scope.quote: The primary purpose of this paper is to examine the extent of earnings management in the period leading to the scandals and prior to SOX, and the changes in such activities after the passage of SOX.

We formally examine the determinants of earnings management in our multivariate analysis next.

sample.quote: We collect our sample from the Compustat annual industrial and research files for the period 1987–2005.

We restrict our sample to all nonfinancial firms with available data, and require at least eight observations in each two-digit SIC grouping per year. The sample obtained from Compustat consists of 8,157 firms representing 87,217 firm-year observations.

evidence.quote: To summarize the data, we regress each of the variables on a time-trend variable, Time, defined as the difference between the year and 1987, and two dummy variables, SCA, which takes the value of 1 in the scandal period (years 2000 and 2001), and 0 otherwise, and SOX, which takes the value of 1 in the post-SOX period (years 2002, 2003, and 2005), and 0 otherwise. scope.quote: The primary purpose of this paper is to examine the extent of earnings management in the period leading to the scandals and prior to SOX, and the changes in such activities after the passage of SOX.
Thus, to provide a more complete study of the trends in earnings management activities in the periods before and after SOX, we also examine real earnings management activities over the sample period.
Table 2, Panel A summarizes time-trends of the accrual and real earnings management proxies.
We formally examine the determinants of earnings management in our multivariate analysis next.

sample.quote: We collect our sample from the Compustat annual industrial and research files for the period 1987–2005.

review_notes: Applying the principal-question hierarchy, Table 2 all observations is retained as the principal regression for the substantive question of whether annual cash effective tax rates predict long-run cash effective tax rates. The paper explicitly describes this predictive assessment as one of its core objectives; the CASH ETR measures are deterministic ratios and require no fitted construction regression.

The Table 2 rows conditional on CASH ETR1 ranges are follow-up partitions. Table 3 changes the dependent variable to next-year CASH ETR1 and examines annual-rate persistence; it is a complementary analysis, not the principal long-run prediction regression. The group-specific Table 3 rows are also not included.
The source does not identify the underlying estimator, and the Table 2 note does not detail the random-draw procedure or selected fiscal year for CASH ETR1 observations; these remain unresolved.

review_notes: Source-first scope: the introduction identifies discretionary accruals, real-activities manipulation, and AAER incidence as the three main earnings-management outcomes. Retained the full-sample ABS_DA model in Table 3, all four distinct outcomes in the paper’s main real-activities family in Table 4, and both AAER outcomes in Table 5 Panel B. The paper does not name the underlying estimator for its multiple-regression models or its construction regressions. Table 5 calls Equation (3) a logistic regression, while the printed equation presents Pr(AAER=1) as a linear expression plus an error and supplies no link; this source inconsistency remains unresolved. The two-digit SIC-year advertising-intensity aggregation and total-accrual component calculation are not reported. The annual industry classification for the discretionary-accrual construction and all supporting-fit cell Ns are not reported.

Table 1 states 20 observations per regression fit. Section V separately says portfolios contain 22 firms; the paper does not reconcile the counts and the stated removal of high eps1/P0 observations.

Table 1 also shows rMPEG, rPEG, rPE, and T-Bond comparator columns. The frozen baseline target is Regression (15) and its implied r_Δagr/Δagr parameters; the special-case comparator estimates are outside this fitted baseline.

review_notes: Source-first scope: Regression (15) is the paper’s central estimated measurement model, run separately within annual PEG-sorted portfolios to estimate portfolio expected returns and long-run abnormal-growth changes. The PE/PEG formulas are parameter-free comparison cases; later correlations, matching variants, and firm-characteristic comparisons do not add another fitted baseline regression.

The supplied reading includes coordinator-verified transcriptions for Regression (15), Equation (5), and Table 1 coefficient mapping, with original garbled text preserved. Equation (15) is now populated from that supplied verified math. Preserve the source’s Equation (5)/adjacent-prose discrepancy in the construction of ceps2. The estimator remains unspecified; Table 1 gives 20 observations per fit, while Section V says 22 firms per formation portfolio. The paper also removes the highest eps1/P0 observations without a stated count or cutoff, so it does not explain the relationship between those counts.
descriptive_reason: No data-value descriptive statistics for the retained observed variables ceps_{j,2}/P_{j,0} and eps_{j,1}/P_{j,0} were located in the complete reading. Table 1 reports medians of fitted coefficients, adjusted R², and implied return/growth model outputs; the paper’s abstract also summarizes model-output estimates rather than these observed variables.
results_review_notes: All 19 annual Table 1 rows plus the All row are retained as separate median-across-fits result sets for the frozen Regression (15) model. The printed annual percentage text is preserved as shown: percent signs appear on the 1981 and All values for r_Δagr and Δagr, while the 1982–1999 cells omit the sign.

independent_variables.name: RNOA_t
independent_variables.definition: Current RNOA = OI / Average NOA. OI = CNI + NFE. CNI is net income/loss (#172) minus preferred dividends (#19) plus the change in marketable-securities adjustment (#238) and the change in cumulative translation adjustment in retained earnings (#230). NFE = interest expense (#15) × (1−MTR) + preferred dividends (#19) − interest income (#62) × (1−MTR) + lagged #238 − current #238. MTR is the applicable highest federal rate plus 0.02: federal rates are 34% for 1989–1992 and 35% for 1993–2005. NOA = NFO + CSE + minority interest (#38), where NFO = FO − FA; FO = current debt (#34) + long-term debt (#9) + preferred stock (#130) − preferred treasury stock (#227) + preferred dividends in arrears (#242); FA = cash/short-term investments (#1) + long-term receivables, investments and advances to affiliated companies (#32); CSE = common equity (#60) + preferred treasury stock (#227) − preferred dividends in arrears (#242). The source preserves change notation for #238/#230 and does not give an arithmetic averaging interval for Average NOA.

independent_variables.name: RNOA_t
independent_variables.definition: Current RNOA = OI / Average NOA. OI = CNI + NFE. CNI is net income/loss (#172) minus preferred dividends (#19) plus the change in marketable-securities adjustment (#238) and the change in cumulative translation adjustment in retained earnings (#230). NFE = interest expense (#15) × (1−MTR) + preferred dividends (#19) − interest income (#62) × (1−MTR) + lagged #238 − current #238. MTR is the applicable highest federal rate plus 0.02: federal rates are 34% for 1989–1992 and 35% for 1993–2005. NOA = NFO + CSE + minority interest (#38), where NFO = FO − FA; FO = current debt (#34) + long-term debt (#9) + preferred stock (#130) − preferred treasury stock (#227) + preferred dividends in arrears (#242); FA = cash/short-term investments (#1) + long-term receivables, investments and advances to affiliated companies (#32); CSE = common equity (#60) + preferred treasury stock (#227) − preferred dividends in arrears (#242). The source preserves change notation for #238/#230 and does not give an arithmetic averaging interval for Average NOA.

estimation_procedure.description: Estimate the full-sample Model 1 direct future-profitability regression for this life-cycle classification. Its five profitability controls and four non-reference stage indicators are the complete nine RHS terms. The three classification schemes are separate competing specifications, not separate fits within stages. The table reports total stage effects (reference intercept plus incremental indicator effect); t-statistics test increments relative to the reference. The source does not name the underlying estimator. Model 2 is a separately motivated interaction extension and is excluded.

CNI is net income/loss (#172) minus preferred dividends (#19) plus the change in marketable-securities adjustment (#238) and the change in cumulative translation adjustment in retained earnings (#230). NFE = interest expense (#15) × (1−MTR) + preferred dividends (#19) − interest income (#62) × (1−MTR) + lagged #238 − current #238. MTR is the applicable highest federal rate plus 0.02: federal rates are 34% for 1989–1992 and 35% for 1993–2005. NOA = NFO + CSE + minority interest (#38), where NFO = FO − FA; FO = current debt (#34) + long-term debt (#9) + preferred stock (#130) − preferred treasury stock (#227) + preferred dividends in arrears (#242); FA = cash/short-term investments (#1) + long-term receivables, investments and advances to affiliated companies (#32); CSE = common equity (#60) + preferred treasury stock (#227) − preferred dividends in arrears (#242). The source preserves change notation for #238/#230 and does not give an arithmetic averaging interval for Average NOA.

evidence.quote: Return on net operating assets (RNOA) 1⁄4 Operating Income (OI)/Average Net Operating Assets (NOA).
Operating Income (OI) 1⁄4 Comprehensive Net Income (CNI) plus Net Financial Expense (NFE);
Net Operating Assets (NOA) 1⁄4 Net Financial Obligation (NFO) plus Common Equity (CSE)

NFE_t = Compustat15_t*(1-MarginalTaxRate_t) + Compustat19_t - Compustat62_t*(1-MarginalTaxRate_t) + Compustat238_(t-1) - Compustat238_t.

estimation_procedure.description: Estimate the full-sample Model 1 direct future-profitability regression for this life-cycle classification. Its five profitability controls and four non-reference stage indicators are the complete nine RHS terms. The three classification schemes are separate competing specifications, not separate fits within stages. The table reports total stage effects (reference intercept plus incremental indicator effect); t-statistics test increments relative to the reference. The source does not name the underlying estimator. Model 2 is a separately motivated interaction extension and is excluded.

We follow prior literature and perform analyses of those accruals measures generally
considered to be most representative of managements’ discretion in the financial reporting

the raw and absolute values of these measures, but we also posit that studying the association between auditor tenure and signed accruals is important because auditors could constrain income-increasing accruals to a greater or lesser extent than income-decreasing accruals, and auditor tenure could have differential effects on this constraint. <sup>9</sup> By using

measures. Panel A reveals that the coefficients for Tenure are negative and significant for
both Discretionary and Current Accruals. That is, extended auditor tenure reduces the dispersion of both measures, consistent with the notion that longer auditor tenure results in
higher audit quality.

PADCA is DCA minus the median DCA in the same two-digit SIC by prior-year ROA-decile portfolio, with the focal firm excluded; DCA = CA − ECA, and PADCA is deflated by assets.
dependent_variable.formula: ln(|PADCA_i|); PADCA_i = DCA_i − median(DCA_j in same two-digit SIC × prior-year ROA decile portfolio, j ≠ i); DCA = CA − ECA; ECA = αhat_1*(1/Lag1asset) + αhat_2*(ΔRev − ΔAR); CA = (Compustat item 123 + item 125 − item 308) / beginning-of-year total assets. scope.quote:
Our first set of tests examine whether FJN’s discretionary accruals results are sensitive
to the measurement of discretionary accruals. Recent research suggests that the discretionary
accrual measure used by FJN systematically rejects the null hypothesis of no-biased financial reporting at much higher-than-stated rates because the measure does not account for
the impact of performance on accruals (Kothari et al. 2002). We calculate two measures of
discretionary current accruals that control for the impact of firm performance in the estimation of discretionary accruals. The first method measures performance-adjusted discretionary current accruals as the difference between a firm’s estimated d

We calculate two measures of
discretionary current accruals that control for the impact of firm performance in the estimation of discretionary accruals. The first method measures performance-adjusted discretionary current accruals as the difference between a firm’s estimated discretionary current
accruals and the median discretionary current accruals from an industry- and performancematched portfolio. The second approach follows Kothari et al. (2002) and includes a control
for firm performance in the regression model used to estimate nondiscretionary current
accruals.

scope.quote:

to the measurement of discretionary accruals. Recent research suggests that the discretionary
accrual measure used by FJN systematically rejects the null hypothesis of no-biased financial reporting at much higher-than-stated rates because the measure does not account for
the impact of performance on accruals (Kothari et al. 2002). We calculate two measures of
discretionary current accruals that control for the impact of firm performance in the estimation of discretionary accruals. The first method measures performance-adjusted discretionary current accruals as the difference between a firm’s estimated d

accruals and the median discretionary current accruals from an industry- and performancematched portfolio. The second approach follows Kothari et al. (2002) and includes a control
for firm performance in the regression model used to estimate nondiscretionary current
accruals.

For firms reporting zero nonaudit fees, we set the nonaudit fee to one dollar to allow for the log transformation.
An alternative to transforming the fee variables by their natural log is to scale the fee variables by total assets.
We elect not to use this transformation because our focus is on the magnitude of fees, which we argue capture
the economic bonding of the auditor to the client. The descriptive statistics reported in Panel B of Table 1
indicate that scaling total fees by total assets results in a measure that reflects the relative cost of audit-related
services to the client as opposed to the economic dependence of the auditor on the client.

scope.quote:
Our first set of tests examine whether FJN’s discretionary accruals results are sensitive
to the measurement of discretionary accruals. Recent research suggests that the discretionary
accrual measure used by FJN systematically rejects the null hypothesis of no-biased financial reporting at much higher-than-stated rates because the measure does not account for
the impact of performance on accruals (Kothari et al. 2002). We calculate two measures of
discretionary current accruals that control for the impact of firm performance in the estimation of discretionary accruals. The first method measures performance-adjusted discretionary current accruals as the difference between a firm’s estimated d

We calculate two measures of
discretionary current accruals that control for the impact of firm performance in the estimation of discretionary accruals. The first method measures performance-adjusted discretionary current accruals as the difference between a firm’s estimated discretionary current
accruals and the median discretionary current accruals from an industry- and performancematched portfolio. The second approach follows Kothari et al. (2002) and includes a control
for firm performance in the regression model used to estimate nondiscretionary current
accruals.

Consistent with FJN, we document a positive association between the absolute value
of firms’ discretionary current accruals

Table 4 reports the results of our unsigned discretionary accruals tests. We find a
positive relation between FEERATIO and the absolute value of PADCA and the absolute
value of REDCA . We find no significant association between TOTAL and either unsigned
estimate of discretionary accruals. The results on AUDIT and NONAUDIT are conditional
on the discretionary accrual estimate used. The coefficient on NONAUDIT is positive and
significant only in the PADCA model, whereas the coefficient on AUDIT is negative
and significant only in the REDCA model. The coefficients on the control variables are, in
general, significant and stable regardless of fee metric or discretionary accruals measure.

dependent_variable.formula: ln(|REDCA|); REDCA = CA − ECAPC; ECAPC = γhat_1*(1/Lag1asset) + γhat_2*(ΔRev − ΔAR) + γhat_3*Lag1ROA; CA = (Compustat item 123 + item 125 − item 308) / beginning-of-year total assets. evidence.quote:
Our second measure of discretionary accruals, REDCA, follows Kothari et al. (2002)
by including lagged ROA in the accruals regression to control for firm performance. Kothari
et al. (2002) report that matching on lagged ROA, as opposed to contemporaneous ROA,
eliminates any mechanical relation between current period’s discretionary accrual estimate
and the performance metric. The calculation of REDCA begins by estimating the following

scope.quote:

to the measurement of discretionary accruals. Recent research suggests that the discretionary
accrual measure used by FJN systematically rejects the null hypothesis of no-biased financial reporting at much higher-than-stated rates because the measure does not account for
the impact of performance on accruals (Kothari et al. 2002). We calculate two measures of
discretionary current accruals that control for the impact of firm performance in the estimation of discretionary accruals. The first method measures performance-adjusted discretionary current accruals as the difference between a firm’s estimated d

accruals and the median discretionary current accruals from an industry- and performancematched portfolio. The second approach follows Kothari et al. (2002) and includes a control
for firm performance in the regression model used to estimate nondiscretionary current
accruals.

scope.quote:
Our first set of tests examine whether FJN’s discretionary accruals results are sensitive
to the measurement of discretionary accruals. Recent research suggests that the discretionary
accrual measure used by FJN systematically rejects the null hypothesis of no-biased financial reporting at much higher-than-stated rates because the measure does not account for
the impact of performance on accruals (Kothari et al. 2002). We calculate two measures of
discretionary current accruals that control for the impact of firm performance in the estimation of discretionary accruals. The first method measures performance-adjusted discretionary current accruals as the difference between a firm’s estimated d

We calculate two measures of
discretionary current accruals that control for the impact of firm performance in the estimation of discretionary accruals. The first method measures performance-adjusted discretionary current accruals as the difference between a firm’s estimated discretionary current
accruals and the median discretionary current accruals from an industry- and performancematched portfolio. The second approach follows Kothari et al. (2002) and includes a control
for firm performance in the regression model used to estimate nondiscretionary current
accruals.

models.method_details: OLS cross-sectional regression of the natural log of the absolute performance-adjusted discretionary-current-accrual measure on one fee metric and the listed controls.

dependent_variable.name: ln |REDCA|
dependent_variable.definition: Natural logarithm of the absolute value of ROA-in-Estimation Discretionary Current Accruals (REDCA). REDCA = CA − ECAPC, where Equation (4) estimates current accruals with lagged ROA and Equation (5) forms expected current accruals; the measure is deflated by assets.
dependent_variable.formula: ln(|REDCA|); REDCA = CA − ECAPC; ECAPC = γhat_1*(1/Lag1asset) + γhat_2*(ΔRev − ΔAR) + γhat_3*Lag1ROA; CA = (Compustat item 123 + item 125 − item 308) / beginning-of-year total assets. ΔRev and ΔAR are current-minus-prior sales (item 12) and receivables (item 2), each divided by beginning-of-year assets; Lag1ROA is prior-year ROA.

evidence.quote:
Our second measure of discretionary accruals, REDCA, follows Kothari et al. (2002)
by including lagged ROA in the accruals regression to control for firm performance. Kothari
et al. (2002) report that matching on lagged ROA, as opposed to contemporaneous ROA,
eliminates any mechanical relation between current period’s discretionary accrual estimate
and the performance metric. The calculation of REDCA begins by estimating the following

Equation (4): CA = gamma_1*(1/lag1asset) + gamma_2*DeltaRev + gamma_3*Lag1ROA + epsilon.
Equation (5): ECAPC = gammahat_1*(1/Lag1asset) + gammahat_2*(DeltaRev - DeltaAR) + gammahat_3*Lag1ROA.

the economic bonding of the auditor to the client. The descriptive statistics reported in Panel B of Table 1

services to the client as opposed to the economic dependence of the auditor on the client.

independent_variables.name: PADCA
independent_variables.definition: Portfolio-adjusted discretionary current accruals: the firm’s DCA less the median DCA in its two-digit SIC and prior-year ROA decile portfolio, with the focal firm excluded. DCA equals current accruals minus expected current accruals.

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Generic inverse Mills ratio and selection-corrected Equation (3), physical PDF page 3):
Let s = alphahat_0prime*Z + alphahat_1prime*X. The printed expression is MILLS = E(u|D) = phi(s)/Phi(s) if D=1, and -phi(s)/(1-Phi(s)) if D=0. phi and Phi are the normal density and cumulative distribution functions. Equation (3) is Y = beta_prime*X + theta*D + rho*sigma*MILLS + epsilon. Footnote 2 explicitly states that Equations (2) and (3) can be estimated using the traditional two-step approach OR maximum likelihood. This generic discussion establishes the printed formula and possible methods, not which method was actually used in a later empirical table.

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Generic inverse Mills ratio and selection-corrected Equation (3), physical PDF page 3):
Let s = alphahat_0prime*Z + alphahat_1prime*X. The printed expression is MILLS = E(u|D) = phi(s)/Phi(s) if D=1, and -phi(s)/(1-Phi(s)) if D=0. phi and Phi are the normal density and cumulative distribution functions. Equation (3) is Y = beta_prime*X + theta*D + rho*sigma*MILLS + epsilon. Footnote 2 explicitly states that Equations (2) and (3) can be estimated using the traditional two-step approach OR maximum likelihood. This generic discussion establishes the printed formula and possible methods, not which method was actually used in a later empirical table.

independent_variables.name: MILLSit
independent_variables.definition: Inverse Mills ratio calculated from the auditor-choice models in Table 3.
independent_variables.formula: For the estimated first-stage index s_it: φ(s_it)/Φ(s_it) if Bigit=1; −φ(s_it)/(1−Φ(s_it)) if Bigit=0, where φ and Φ are the standard normal density and cumulative distribution functions. The index is from the selected Table 3 auditor-choice fit.

evidence.quote: inverse Mills’ ratio calculated from the auditor-choice models in Table 3
The inverse Mills’ ratios (MILLSit) in Columns (1) and (2) are calculated from Model 1 of Table 3.

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Generic inverse Mills ratio and selection-corrected Equation (3), physical PDF page 3):
Let s = alphahat_0prime*Z + alphahat_1prime*X. The printed expression is MILLS = E(u|D) = phi(s)/Phi(s) if D=1, and -phi(s)/(1-Phi(s)) if D=0. phi and Phi are the normal density and cumulative distribution functions. Equation (3) is Y = beta_prime*X + theta*D + rho*sigma*MILLS + epsilon. Footnote 2 explicitly states that Equations (2) and (3) can be estimated using the traditional two-step approach OR maximum likelihood. This generic discussion establishes the printed formula and possible methods, not which method was actually used in a later empirical table.

independent_variables.formula: For the estimated first-stage index s_it: φ(s_it)/Φ(s_it) if Bigit=1; −φ(s_it)/(1−Φ(s_it)) if Bigit=0, where φ and Φ are the standard normal density and cumulative distribution functions. The index is from the selected Table 3 auditor-choice fit.

evidence.quote: inverse Mills’ ratio calculated from the auditor-choice models in Table 3

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Generic inverse Mills ratio and selection-corrected Equation (3), physical PDF page 3):
Let s = alphahat_0prime*Z + alphahat_1prime*X. The printed expression is MILLS = E(u|D) = phi(s)/Phi(s) if D=1, and -phi(s)/(1-Phi(s)) if D=0. phi and Phi are the normal density and cumulative distribution functions. Equation (3) is Y = beta_prime*X + theta*D + rho*sigma*MILLS + epsilon. Footnote 2 explicitly states that Equations (2) and (3) can be estimated using the traditional two-step approach OR maximum likelihood. This generic discussion establishes the printed formula and possible methods, not which method was actually used in a later empirical table.

Source-first scope: Section IV Tables 3–4 are the principal full-sample empirical illustration of how selection-model inferences change with exclusion restrictions. Table 4 retains all three stated outcomes (audit fees, cost of equity, going-concern opinions) and the authors’ selection-corrected and OLS/probit comparisons; Table 3 auditor-choice fits are included only because their fitted indices generate the Table 4 MILLS terms. This applies the sweep clarification by selecting the substantive relationship tests before considering the auxiliary MILLS construction.

Tables 1–2 report descriptive survey counts rather than fitted regressions. review_notes: Source-first scope: Table 4, column 2 is retained as the fully controlled market-choice test. For the central contract-design comparison, Tables 5–7 selection-corrected specifications are retained for spread, maturity, and collateralization. The authors motivate this design by nonrandom debt-market choice and compare the AQ coefficients across loan and bond regimes. Table 4 columns 1 and 3, the within-market OLS/probit columns in Tables 5–7, the univariate Table 3 comparisons, and later robustness/validation analyses are excluded as reduced or supplemental tests; column 3 specifically tests the separate AQ-by-growth interaction (H1b).

The supplied verified reading derivative includes coordinator-verified formulas for AQ, Default Risk, Market-to-Book, Asset Maturity, and Appendix B equations (1)–(5). I used those verified transcriptions and visually checked rendered physical pages 9–11, 16–20, and 22–25. The equation renderer found no embedded equation images on pages 24–25; the relevant vector-text regions were rendered and inspected directly.

Unresolved source details: the Not Rated indicator is coded oppositely in Section III (page 11) and Appendix A (page 23); Tables 5 and 6 footnotes refer to selection specification 2 in Table 3 while the method prose identifies Table 4; Table 7 reports year dummies only while the general method description says year and loan/bond-purpose dummies for Tables 5–7. The underlying estimator for the reported continuous-outcome switching fits is not explicitly identified, and per-industry-year accrual-fit estimators and counts are not reported.
results_review_notes: Extraction follows the frozen baseline family: Table 4 column 2; Table 5 endogenous-switching loan and bond columns; Table 6 endogenous-switching loan and bond columns; Table 7 sample-selection loan and bond columns. OLS columns, Table 4 column 3, Table 7 plain probit columns, AQ-quintile low-versus-high hypothesis tests, and correlations are excluded.

Relevant descriptive rows for retained variables are reported in Tables 1–3 and prose. Table 2 Panel D and Table 3 Panel B AQ-quintile means are included; the associated low-versus-high t-test columns are excluded as inference. The paper does not report descriptives for retained Capital Market Access or Asset Maturity; available summary locations were reviewed.

The source defines Not Rated=1 in the absence of a credit rating on page 11, but Appendix A on page 23 defines Not Rated=1 when the firm has a rating; the sign/coding conflict is not resolvable from the paper.

Tables 5–6 identify endogenous switching and report clustered heteroscedasticity-corrected SEs, but do not explicitly name the estimator for the selected continuous-outcome equations. No estimator was inferred.

Tables 6–7 legends as printed show “**, ***” while naming three significance levels (10, 5, 1 percent); threshold mapping is ambiguous. All markers are preserved verbatim, and no marker-derived p bounds are emitted.
Table 7 note says year dummies are included; the page 20 design description says year and loan/bond-purpose dummies are included for Tables 5–7. Both statements are retained.

Tables 5–7 footnotes identify the selection-model specification as specification 2 in Table 3; page 21 prose says the selection model is the same as specification 2 of Table 4. The discrepancy is preserved without changing the selected baseline fits.

review_notes: Source-first scope: retain the full-sample, full-control outcome regressions in Table 4 Panel A (absolute abnormal accruals), Table 5 Panels A and B (small positive earnings and small earnings increases), and Table 6 Panel A (going-concern report). In each table the selected specification includes INFLUENCE, matching the authors’ stated primary discussion of models with that control. The signed-accrual panels and financially distressed going-concern panel are supplemental partitions. The central next-year bankruptcy accuracy comparison uses a chi-square test after categorizing offices as small/large, so it is recorded as checked but is not a regression model.

The supplied verified reading derivative includes coordinator-verified transcriptions of the performance-adjusted Jones fit, the generic accrual equation, probit Equations (3)–(4), the Altman bankruptcy score, and the footnote-5 Z-score formula. I used those transcriptions and visually checked physical pages 7–9, 12–13, and 19–26. The equation renderer found no embedded equation images on pages 7–9; the relevant vector-text formulas were rendered and inspected directly.

Unresolved details: the source names TA as total accruals but does not state how TA itself is calculated; the clustered robust errors in the probit models are not assigned to a stated clustering dimension; Table 6’s note calls GCREPORT the independent variable even though Equation (4), the table title, and the surrounding text treat it as the dependent variable.
results_review_notes: Extraction is limited to the four frozen full-sample baseline result sets and the related office-fee/client-variable descriptives. Table 4 Panels B and C, Table 5 without-INFLUENCE columns, Table 6 Panel B, and later sensitivity or accuracy analyses are outside this enrichment.
The Table 5 Panel A lnOFFICE coefficient has a table-reported two-tailed p=.171 and a separate one-tailed p=.085 in the selected-results prose; both are retained with distinct roles.
The source states all models are significant at p < .01; these model-level bounds are stored as auxiliary rows in their selected result sets.

models.sample_description: Monthly country panel using dividend-yield cost-of-equity observations for 32 countries from January 1986 to December 1998; coverage is incomplete for some country-months.
models.method_details: The paper reports a panel time-series regression with country fixed effects and country-specific heteroscedasticity/autocorrelation corrections, but does not identify the underlying estimator.

dependent_variable.name: Cost of equity
dependent_variable.definition: Country-level cost of equity estimated from the constant-growth dividend-discount model using current dividend yield and current dividend growth; the current growth rate is assumed to be the best forecast of future dividend growth (random-walk assumption).
dependent_variable.formula: Current dividend yield × (1 + current dividend growth rate) + current dividend growth rate.

evidence.quote: the estimated cost of equity = current dividend yield x (1 + current growth rate of dividends) + current growth rate of dividends
which implies that we assume that dividend growth rates follow a random walk

independent_variables.name: Earnings aggressiveness
independent_variables.definition: For each country-year, the measure is the median across firms of accruals scaled by lagged total assets; accruals equal change in current assets minus change in current liabilities minus change in cash plus change in the current portion of long-term debt included in current liabilities minus depreciation and amortization expense plus change in income taxes payable, all divided by total assets in t−1. The two debt/tax inputs are set to zero when missing. The country-year median is ranked across country-years into deciles 1–10; higher rank denotes more aggressiveness. The regressions use the rank lagged one year.
independent_variables.formula: Rank_{country-year}(median_firm[((Δcurrent assets − Δcurrent liabilities − Δcash + Δcurrent portion of long-term debt in current liabilities − depreciation/amortization + Δincome taxes payable) / total assets_{t−1})]); enter at t−1.

evidence.quote: We scale accruals by lagged total assets for each firm, determine its median in the cross-section of firms per country per year, and then rank these medians across years and across countries
This rank is the "earnings aggressiveness" time-series variable per country
We use lagged earnings opacity measures from year t- 1 in all our tests to proxy for investor expectations about earnings opacity in year t
This motivates us to measure earnings aggressiveness of a country at a point in time as the median for country i, year t, of accruals divided by lagged total assets
ACCk, = (ACAk, - ACLk, - ACASHkt + ASTDk, - DEPkt + ATPkt)/TAkt-, (1)
ACAkt = change in total current assets
change in total current liabilities for firm k, year t
change in cash for firm k, year t
ASTDkt = change in current portion of long-term debt included in total current liabilities
depreciation and amortization expense for firm k, year t
change in income taxes payable
total assets for firm k, year t-1
we assume them to be zero
We rank all the raw time-series earnings aggressiveness median observations, across countries and years, into deciles, with higher ranks associated with greater earnings aggressiveness

we rank all the raw time-series loss avoidance ratios, across countries and years, into deciles, with higher ranks associated with greater loss avoidance

independent_variables.definition: For each country-year, the measure is the median across firms of accruals scaled by lagged total assets; accruals equal change in current assets minus change in current liabilities minus change in cash plus change in the current portion of long-term debt included in current liabilities minus depreciation and amortization expense plus change in income taxes payable, all divided by total assets in t−1. This motivates us to measure earnings aggressiveness of a country at a point in time as the median for country i, year t, of accruals divided by lagged total assets
ACCk, = (ACAk, - ACLk, - ACASHkt + ASTDk, - DEPkt + ATPkt)/TAkt-, (1)

total assets for firm k, year t-1
we assume them to be zero

independent_variables.definition: For each country-year, the measure is the median across firms of accruals scaled by lagged total assets; accruals equal change in current assets minus change in current liabilities minus change in cash plus change in the current portion of long-term debt included in current liabilities minus depreciation and amortization expense plus change in income taxes payable, all divided by total assets in t−1. The two debt/tax inputs are set to zero when missing. The country-year median is ranked across country-years into deciles 1–10; higher rank denotes more aggressiveness. The regressions use the rank lagged one year.
independent_variables.formula: Rank_{country-year}(median_firm[((Δcurrent assets − Δcurrent liabilities − Δcash + Δcurrent portion of long-term debt in current liabilities − depreciation/amortization + Δincome taxes payable) / total assets_{t−1})]); enter at t−1.

evidence.quote: We scale accruals by lagged total assets for each firm, determine its median in the cross-section of firms per country per year, and then rank these medians across years and across countries

We use lagged earnings opacity measures from year t- 1 in all our tests to proxy for investor expectations about earnings opacity in year t
This motivates us to measure earnings aggressiveness of a country at a point in time as the median for country i, year t, of accruals divided by lagged total assets
ACCk, = (ACAk, - ACLk, - ACASHkt + ASTDk, - DEPkt + ATPkt)/TAkt-, (1)
ACAkt = change in total current assets
change in total current liabilities for firm k, year t
change in cash for firm k, year t
ASTDkt = change in current portion of long-term debt included in total current liabilities
depreciation and amortization expense for firm k, year t
change in income taxes payable
total assets for firm k, year t-1
we assume them to be zero
We rank all the raw time-series earnings aggressiveness median observations, across countries and years, into deciles, with higher ranks associated with greater earnings aggressiveness

Source-first scope: the abstract and introduction state that the paper measures earnings opacity, then tests whether it affects the return shareholders demand and how much they trade (physical pages 2–4). Retain the full-control four-proxy families in Table 4 (dividend-yield cost of equity), Table 5 Panel B (risk-adjusted cost-of-equity residual), and Table 6 (trade). These are the principal relationship tests, and the two distinct cost-of-equity approaches are both central. Table 5 Panel A and its country–world and country–FX ARCH fits are supporting because their fitted residuals and conditional covariance are required by the retained Table 5 Panel B models. The opacity measures themselves are medians, count ratios, cross-sectional correlations, and ranks, not fitted regressions. Descriptive/cross-sectional ranking tables and later VAR robustness are excluded.

The assigned reading is the supplied coordinator-verified derivative, whose provenance records independent PDF-crop review of the Table 4, Table 5, and Table 6 math. Its verified math is used as supplied; no worker-authored transcription was added. This worker independently viewed physical PDF pages 26–29 and 31.

Table 5 numbering differs across locations: the body calls the international risk-adjustment model Equation (2), while Table 5 labels it Equation 1; Table 5 labels the residual regression Equation 2. The ARCH system is body Equation (3). Locations and model labels preserve those distinct labels.

independent_variables.name: Q-score_t
independent_variables.definition: Overall earnings-quality score equal to the equally weighted sum of Q^A and Q^B. Q^A is the change in the firm’s C-score from t−1 to t. Q^B is the year-t C-score minus the year-t median C-score among firms in the same two-digit SIC industry. The C-score is the estimated reserve from conservative accounting divided by net operating assets (NOA). The reserve is the sum of the disclosed LIFO inventory reserve, estimated capitalized R&D assets amortized with Lev and Sougiannis (1996) industry coefficients, and estimated advertising-created brand assets capitalized and amortized by the sum-of-the-years-digits method over two years. For non-LIFO firms the inventory reserve is zero. NOA is operating assets less operating liabilities, excluding financial assets and liabilities; the paper also supplies a Compustat-item implementation. A positive Q-score indicates reserve growth and a temporary depression of current earnings, while a negative score indicates reserve liquidation and temporary earnings inflation; the score is not an ordinal ranking of earnings quality. The exact Lev–Sougiannis coefficient schedule is not reproduced in this paper.
independent_variables.formula: C_it = (INVres_it + RDres_it + ADVres_it) / NOA_it; Q_it = 0.5 × (C_it − C_i,t−1) + 0.5 × (C_it − median_{two-digit-SIC,t}(C_it)). NOA = CommonEquity + FinancialObligations − FinancialAssets + MinorityInterest; CommonEquity = item60 + item227 − item242; FinancialObligations = item34 + item9 + item130 − item227 + item242; FinancialAssets = item1 + item32; MinorityInterest = item38.

evidence.quote: C_it = (INVres_it + RDres_it + ADVres_it)/NOA_it. INVres is reported LIFO reserve; RDres capitalizes R&D and amortizes using Lev and Sougiannis (1996) industry coefficients; ADVres capitalizes advertising and amortizes with sum-of-years-digits over two years. Q^A_it = ER_it/NOA_it - ER_i,t-1/NOA_i,t-1. Q^B_it = ER_it/NOA_it - industry_median(ER_it/NOA_it), with two-digit SIC industry median. Q_it = 0.5*Q^A_it + 0.5*Q^B_it.
Q_it = 0.5*(C_it - C_i,t-1) + 0.5*(C_it - industry_median(C_it)) = C_it - (0.5*C_i,t-1 + 0.5*industry_median(C_it)).
C_it = ER_it/NOA_it, where ER is the estimated reserve and NOA is net operating assets.
Net operating assets, NOA, is the book value of operating assets minus operating liabilities.

NOA = CommonEquity + FinancialObligations - FinancialAssets + MinorityInterest. CommonEquity = item60 + item227 - item242. FinancialObligations = item34 + item9 + item130 - item227 + item242. FinancialAssets = item1 + item32. MinorityInterest = item38. Item32 is labelled Investments and Advances - Other; the dash in that item label does not introduce an additional mathematical variable.
Inventory reserve (INVresit ) equals the LIFO reserve reported in the financial statement footnotes.

R&D reserve (RDresit ) is calculated as the estimated amortized R&D assets that would have been on the balance sheet if R&D had not been expensed. We capitalize R&D expenditures, then amortize them using the industry coefficients estimated by Lev and Sougiannis (1996).

Advertising reserve (ADVresit ) is the estimated brand assets created by advertising expenditures. We capitalize advertising expenses and then amortize them using a sum-of-the-year’s digits method over two years.
we weight the two measures equally
there were 22,313 non-LIFO cases (where the reserve is 0).

estimation_procedure.description: Equations (2) and (3) are jointly estimated as the Mishkin system by iterative generalized nonlinear least squares in two stages. The first stage leaves valuation coefficients γ*_q unrestricted from their forecasting counterparts γ_q. The second stage jointly re-estimates under rational-pricing equality constraints γ*_q = γ_q for individual components and reported combinations of components. The likelihood-ratio statistic compares constrained and unconstrained residual sums of squares, with degrees of freedom equal to the number of restrictions. Table 2 reports the unrestricted coefficient estimates and likelihood-ratio tests; the principal abnormal-accrual restriction is γ*_3 = γ_3. The fitted forecasting and valuation equations are separate records in the same estimation group.

evidence.quote: As in Mishkin (1983), I estimate equations (2) and (3) jointly using an iterative generalized nonlinear least squares estimation procedure, proceeding in two stages.

evidence.quote: I use the 1995 CRSP monthly returns file to measure annual buy-and-hold returns (RETURNt) for the 12-month period ending three months after the firm’s fiscal year end.

I use the CRSP size decile breakpoints to classify each firm into a size decile according to its market value of equity at the beginning of the calendar year in which the 12-month return period begins.

Equation (3): SIZEAJR_t+1 = alpha + beta*(EARN_t+1 - gamma_0 - gamma_star_1*CFO_t - gamma_star_2*NAC_t - gamma_star_3*ABNAC_t) + epsilon_t+1. The outer intercept is alpha; gamma_0 is the unstarred intercept inside the innovation. The coefficients gamma_star_1, gamma_star_2 and gamma_star_3 are estimated valuation parameters, not observed regressors. The equation is part of the same Nonlinear Generalized Least Squares system as Equation (2).

estimation_procedure.description: Equations (2) and (3) are jointly estimated as the Mishkin system by iterative generalized nonlinear least squares in two stages. The first stage leaves valuation coefficients γ*_q unrestricted from their forecasting counterparts γ_q. The second stage jointly re-estimates under rational-pricing equality constraints γ*_q = γ_q for individual components and reported combinations of components. The likelihood-ratio statistic compares constrained and unconstrained residual sums of squares, with degrees of freedom equal to the number of restrictions. Table 2 reports the unrestricted coefficient estimates and likelihood-ratio tests; the principal abnormal-accrual restriction is γ*_3 = γ_3. The fitted forecasting and valuation equations are separate records in the same estimation group.

dependent_variable.name: ACCR_t / TA_{t−1}

review_notes: Selected the Table 2 Mishkin system as the principal regression family. The source says the central question is whether the market prices Jones-model abnormal accruals consistently with their one-year-ahead earnings implications; the Mishkin system directly compares forecast and valuation coefficients. Retain the full earnings-component system (CFO, NAC, ABNAC) and its jointly estimated forecasting and valuation equations. The Table 3 hedge portfolio is corroborating portfolio evidence, not a regression family; alternative Jones measures and the refined-accrual/Table 4 analyses are sensitivity analyses.

The Jones-model construction is retained as a supporting fitted equation because its predicted values and residuals generate NAC and ABNAC in the Table 2 baseline system. Pre-1988 CFO is arithmetic construction, not another fitted model. Equation (2) estimated alone by OLS is discussed only for interpretation; that does not replace the joint generalized nonlinear least squares estimator used for Table 2.

Equation (1), equations (2) and (3), timing, scaling, and the equation (3) parameterized earnings innovation were checked against the supplied coordinator-verified mathematical transcriptions and rendered physical PDF pages 4, 5, and 7. No worker-generated mathematical transcription was used.

estimation_procedure.description: The study compares INTCONT auditor-change companies with a matched NOPROB control sample. For each INTCONT company, one NOPROB company was randomly selected from other auditor changes, matched by industry and exchange; three-digit SIC was used where possible, with two-digit codes for 29 observations and one-digit codes for 14 when a three-digit match was unavailable. Controls also had no other reportable events or disagreements. The randomization procedure shuffles the dependent variable across observations, re-estimates the model 1,000 times, and compares the shuffled coefficients with the original coefficient.

evidence.quote: For each company in the INTCONT sample, a random choice for the control sample was made from among the companies that changed auditors using three criteria
Industry matching was based on three-digit SIC codes.
Where it was not possible to match on three digits, two digits (29 observations) and one digit (14 observations) were used
Each INTCONT company was matched with a NOPROB company on the exchange on which the company was listed.
The final sample has 128 INTCONT companies and 128 NOPROB companies.
The test is conducted by shuffling the dependent variable randomly across the observations and estimating the logit model.
This process is repeated 1,000 times

preprocessing.description: Financial variables pertain to the last fiscal year of the predecessor auditor. Audit committee characteristics were measured using proxy statements dated near the auditor change; proxy filing dates averaged 46 days after the change for INTCONT firms and 39 days for NOPROB firms, with a 53-day median in both groups.

evidence.quote: The financial variables (obtained from the Disclosure database) pertain to the last fiscal year of the predecessor auditor.
On average, the proxy filing dates were 46 (39) days after the date of auditor change for the INTCONT (NOPROB) sample.
The median difference between the proxy date and the auditor change date is 53 days for both samples.

evidence.quote: Intercept

estimation_procedure.description: The study compares INTCONT auditor-change companies with a matched NOPROB control sample. For each INTCONT company, one NOPROB company was randomly selected from other auditor changes, matched by industry and exchange; three-digit SIC was used where possible, with two-digit codes for 29 observations and one-digit codes for 14 when a three-digit match was unavailable. Controls also had no other reportable events or disagreements. The randomization procedure shuffles the dependent variable across observations, re-estimates the model 1,000 times, and compares the shuffled coefficients with the original coefficient.

evidence.quote: For each company in the INTCONT sample, a random choice for the control sample was made from among the companies that changed auditors using three criteria
Industry matching was based on three-digit SIC codes.
Where it was not possible to match on three digits, two digits (29 observations) and one digit (14 observations) were used
Each INTCONT company was matched with a NOPROB company on the exchange on which the company was listed.
The final sample has 128 INTCONT companies and 128 NOPROB companies.
The test is conducted by shuffling the dependent variable randomly across the observations and estimating the logit model.
This process is repeated 1,000 times

preprocessing.description: Financial variables pertain to the last fiscal year of the predecessor auditor. Audit committee characteristics were measured using proxy statements dated near the auditor change; proxy filing dates averaged 46 days after the change for INTCONT firms and 39 days for NOPROB firms, with a 53-day median in both groups.

evidence.quote: The financial variables (obtained from the Disclosure database) pertain to the last fiscal year of the predecessor auditor.
On average, the proxy filing dates were 46 (39) days after the date of auditor change for the INTCONT (NOPROB) sample.
The median difference between the proxy date and the auditor change date is 53 days for both samples.

preprocessing.description: TENURE is truncated for nine companies because the available Disclosure database history began in 1988; the paper reports qualitatively unchanged results after excluding those observations.

evidence.quote: For nine companies, I had to rely on the Disclosure database, but because my access to that database goes back only to 1988, the measure of tenure is truncated.
However, the results remained qualitatively unchanged when I dropped these nine observations.

review_notes: Source-first scope: retain Table 4 binary logit for incidence and Table 5 multinomial logit for severity as baseline fits of the central internal-control-quality question. Table 5 gives two category-vs-NOPROB contrasts and one coefficient difference within one multinomial model. Table 6 alternatives/partitions are sensitivity analyses; Table 3 is descriptive.

The article describes logit models and prints complete coefficient tables but no formal regression equation; equation_text is null. Table 4 and Table 5 each report n=256 per fit. The exact matched sample record has 128 INTCONT case firms, matched to 128 NOPROB controls.

ASHARE’s construction dimensions are described, but the exact numerator/denominator formula is not. The Zmijewski PRBANK formula is not reproduced. Table 5 prints RECASSET while Table 2 and Table 4 print RECASST; Table 5 spelling is retained and linked to the Table 2 ratio definition.

Table 2 defines ACCTEXP as CPA certification or prior public-accounting experience; the narrative coding sentence mentions public-accounting experience without separately clarifying CPA certification alone.
descriptive_reason: Table 2 provides means and medians for all retained predictors in the INTCONT and NOPROB groups. Table 1 supplies year and exchange-category counts related to retained YEAR and NYAM variables, and the selected regression tables report exact category counts for ICPROB and ICSEV. Table 2 univariate test statistics are excluded because they are hypothesis tests, not descriptive statistics. Table 1 industry composition is not linked because industry is a matching criterion and is not a baseline predictor or fixed effect.
results_review_notes: The selected focal predictors are ACSIZE, ACINDEP, and ACEXP; the source defines these three as audit-committee quality measures. Other baseline predictors are classified as controls in the source context.

Table 4 and Table 5 report conventional logistic p-values and Noreen randomization p-values in separate columns. Separate result sets retain both methods while repeating the same printed coefficient estimate; coefficient stars stay with the conventional-logit result sets, while column (7) stars stay with its randomization-based contrast.
Randomization p-values are absent where the source shows a dash and states that no test statistic is constructed when no sign is predicted.
Table 5 column (7) coefficient differences are included as selected baseline results. Their exact randomization p-values are not printed; displayed stars are retained.
Table 5 spells the receivables ratio RECASSET while Table 2 and Table 4 spell it RECASST; the frozen schema-1 base links the Table 5 row to the Table 2 definition.
Global Chi-squared statistics, Pseudo R-squared values, and correlation/univariate test results are not parameter estimates and are excluded.

calculation_provenance.policy: strict; no guessed degrees of freedom or normal approximations

dependent_variable.name: ADA

review_notes: Source-first selection: the central question is whether Big 4 treatment effects reflect client characteristics. The authors emphasize propensity-score matching across three coequal audit-quality proxies; full-sample regression findings are described as indirect support. Retained the full-model propensity-score-matched multivariate families in Tables 2 (ADA), 5 (RPEG), and 8 (ACCY), their separate propensity-logit fits, and the KLW fit required to construct ADA. Excluded unmatched full-sample outcome columns, attribute-specific matched-sample Tables 3/6/9, univariate difference-in-means columns, and later robustness/sensitivity analyses.

Needs review: the paper does not identify the post-exclusion control set in the propensity models; the KLW estimator, per-year/SIC N and aggregate N, and exact ΔSALES operational definition are not reported; RPEG and the exact VAR dispersion statistic lack formulas; ACCY aggregation and ZMIJ inputs are not reported; Equation (4) indexes LOG_MKT and EL at t while their definitions state t+1; the fixed-effect industry coding is unspecified.
results_review_notes: Tables 1, 4, and 7 provide means and standard deviations for retained outcomes and predictors plus the reported raw market-value input to LOG_MKT. Full-sample and matched auditor strata are represented separately; table-level No. Obs. counts are included in group descriptions, not assigned as variable-specific N.

The selected descriptive tables show Big 4 and non-Big 4 sample counts but do not print a separate BIG4 mean or standard deviation; no dummy statistic was calculated. Total Assets rows were excluded because they are not retained baseline variables or a same-time upstream component of a retained predictor.

Current-sweep PDF evidence replaces prior-run PDF citations. Source prose p-value comparison glyphs were resolved by visual inspection of the original PDF; the Table 2 common control statement is strict p<0.01.

calculation_provenance.policy: strict; no guessed degrees of freedom or normal approximations

models.sample_description: The analysis starts from the hand-classified 2002–2005 8-K restatement sample (83 errors and 105 irregularities; n=188). Errors were randomly sampled at about one quarter of the eligible error population while all irregularities were retained; the regression loses 16 observations to missing data, leaving 172 observations in each Table 5 fit. The models apply population-proportion weights to account for disproportionate sampling.
models.method_details: The authors state that they estimate logistic regressions. Table 5 reports weighted logistic estimates for the three turnover outcomes.

review_notes: Source-first selection: the paper proposes distinguishing errors from irregularities to test consequences of intentional versus unintentional misreporting for executive turnover. Table 5 is the principal multivariate test and reports separate full-control weighted logistic regressions for CEO, CFO, and CEO-or-CFO turnover. Retained all three outcome models and the primary 13-month window; excluded classification validation and descriptive comparisons, the alternative CAR-severity models in Table 6, and later PRE/POST analyses in Tables 8–9.

Needs review: Table 5 duplicates CFO Turnover in its first two printed headers while the results narrative discusses CEO first; Equation (1) and the Table 5 note conflict on the turnover-window anchor and CEO_EQUITY timing; SUBSIDIARY, IRREGULARITY, and ROA use differing wording across model definitions and the Table 5 note; CEO_EQUITY construction is not specified; Table 3 winsorization is not explicitly tied to the Table 5 regressions; fixed effects and the standard-error correction are unreported.
results_review_notes: Table 5 columns 1–3 are the only retained baseline result columns. Table 5 Pseudo-R², log likelihood, and n cells are retained as auxiliary fit-statistic rows; predicted probabilities discussed in prose and later sensitivity tests are not added.

Table 5 parenthetical values are chi-square statistics, not standard errors. The subtype, null, degrees of freedom, and reference distribution are not identified. Exact p-values are not reported; significance markers are preserved with the one-tailed-when-predicted note and row-specific alternatives only where the table prints a prediction sign.

The selected descriptive evidence is Table 3 for retained controls and Total Assets inputs used by ratios/size quintiles, plus Table 4 turnover percentages for retained outcomes. Table 3 precedes regression missing-data deletion; Table 4 error-frequency counts are weighted.

No separate descriptive rows are reported for IRREGULARITY, SUBSIDIARY, their interaction, ANNUAL, the retained CAR window, or the size-quintile indicators; no moments were calculated. Figures 1–2 report announcement-window CARs, not the retained CAR from days −240 to −8.
Table 3 and Table 4 group-comparison markers are preserved in reported labels; their t/Wilcoxon/chi-square tests are not represented as data-value statistics.

dependent_variable.name: SHELTERit
dependent_variable.definition: Indicator equal to one when the firm’s estimated Wilson sheltering probability is in the top quartile for that year, and zero otherwise. The score applies the displayed Wilson (2009) probability equation using BTD, DA, leverage, log assets, ROA, foreign-income indicator and R&D.
dependent_variable.formula: SHELTERit = 1{SHELTER_PROBit is in the top quartile in year t}; otherwise 0. SHELTER_PROBit = -4.86 + 5.20*BTDit + 4.08*DAit - 0.41*LEVit + 0.76*ATit + 3.51*ROAit + 1.72*FOREIGN INCOMEit + 2.43*R&Dit.

evidence.quote: We use Wilson’s (2009) sheltering probability to capture incidence of the most aggressive avoidance practices

dependent_variable.name: DTAXit
dependent_variable.definition: Frank et al. (2009) discretionary permanent book-tax difference: the residual εit from the regression of PERMDIFFit on INTANGit, UNCONit, MIit, CSTEit, ∆NOLit and LAGPERMit, estimated by two-digit SIC code and fiscal year. Missing MII, TXFO, ESUB or TXS are set to zero; missing TXFED is imputed as TXT−TXFO−TXS−TXDI; missing INTAN is set to zero, and INTANG="C" is replaced with GDWL.
dependent_variable.formula: DTAXit = εit; PERMDIFFit = BIit − [(CFTEit + CFORit)/STRit] − (DTEit/STRit).

evidence.quote: Frank et al. (2009) discretionary permanent book-tax difference for firm i in year t

PERMDIFFit =β0 +β1 INTANGit + β2 UNCONit+ β3 MIit+ β4 CSTEit + β5 ∆NOLit+ β6
LAGPERMit + εit;
PERMDIFFit = BIit – [(CFTEit+ CFORit) / STRit] – (DTEit / STRit);
We follow the method in Frank et al. (2009) to handle the missing value problems in estimating DTAXit.
intangibles (INTANG) is missing on Compustat, then we set the value for INTANG to 0.
then we set the value of INTANG to that for goodwill (GDWL).

models.sample_description: Firm-year observations from 2003–2009, excluding utilities (SIC 4900–4949) and finance companies (SIC 6000–6999), with the relevant tax-avoidance measure and required controls available. The paper identifies 11,006 as the initial firm-year sample and reports outcome-specific final N in Table 3.
models.method_details: The authors report logistic regressions for SHELTER and OLS for DTAX, DD_BT, and CETR.

dependent_variable.name: DTAXit
dependent_variable.definition: Frank et al. (2009) discretionary permanent book-tax difference: the residual εit from the regression of PERMDIFFit on INTANGit, UNCONit, MIit, CSTEit, ∆NOLit and LAGPERMit, estimated by two-digit SIC code and fiscal year. Missing MII, TXFO, ESUB or TXS are set to zero; missing TXFED is imputed as TXT−TXFO−TXS−TXDI; missing INTAN is set to zero, and INTANG="C" is replaced with GDWL.
dependent_variable.formula: DTAXit = εit; PERMDIFFit = BIit − [(CFTEit + CFORit)/STRit] − (DTEit/STRit).

evidence.quote: Frank et al. (2009) discretionary permanent book-tax difference for firm i in year t
DTAXit is the εit from the following regression estimated by 2-digit SIC code and fiscal year
PERMDIFFit =β0 +β1 INTANGit + β2 UNCONit+ β3 MIit+ β4 CSTEit + β5 ∆NOLit+ β6
LAGPERMit + εit;
PERMDIFFit = BIit – [(CFTEit+ CFORit) / STRit] – (DTEit / STRit);
We follow the method in Frank et al. (2009) to handle the missing value problems in estimating DTAXit.
intangibles (INTANG) is missing on Compustat, then we set the value for INTANG to 0.
then we set the value of INTANG to that for goodwill (GDWL).

review_notes: Source-first scope: Table 3 Panel A is the principal full-sample CSR–aggressive-tax-avoidance family. It reports both irresponsible-CSR measures (NEG_CSR and HIGH_NEG_CSR) for four parallel outcomes (SHELTER, DTAX, DD_BT, CETR), so all eight full specifications are retained. Table 3 Panel B is a selection correction; FIN 48 tests, propensity-score matching, firm-level averages, Fama–MacBeth estimates, subgroup splits, and sensitivity analyses are outside this baseline family.

Construction review: DTAX is the residual from the Appendix A PERMDIFF regression and DD_BT is generated by its stated firm fixed-effect regression. The baseline control ABS_DA requires a discretionary-accrual fit, which the paper describes but does not fully specify. The SHELTER probability uses a published fixed-coefficient score; no local probability-estimation regression is required.

The supplied verified reading includes coordinator-verified crop transcriptions at the ends of physical pages 41 and 42; those page-linked transcriptions were used for CETR, IO, CASH, and ROA. The remaining method/sample/construction gaps are limited to the fitted constructions noted above.

dependent_variable.name: CONACCi
dependent_variable.definition: Accrual-based conservatism proxy: the negative of the six-year mean of total accruals before depreciation, scaled by assets. Total accruals before depreciation are net income before extraordinary items plus depreciation expense less operating cash flows.
dependent_variable.formula: CONACCi = −mean_{1993–1998}[(NI before extraordinary items + depreciation expense − operating cash flows) / assets].

evidence.quote: Specifically, we use the sum of total accruals excluding depreciation (net income before extraordinary items plus depreciation expense less operating cash flows) deflated by assets and averaged within each of the two sample periods, 1993–1998 and 1987–1992, respectively, as our accrual-based proxy for conservatism.
We also multiply this measure by –1 so it is increasing in the amount of negative accruals, and refer to it as CONACC.

estimation_procedure.description: The 11-category SURPRISE outcome yields ten threshold-specific equations, one for each k from −4¢ through 5¢. The equations are jointly estimated by maximum likelihood and coefficients vary across k. The Appendix imposes the adjacent-threshold constraint −xβ_k ≥ −xβ_{k−1} for all k so cumulative category probabilities sum to one. To ensure that the sum of cumulative probabilities across all k equals 1, we impose the constraint

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Appendix probability and cross-threshold constraints, physical PDF page 25):
Pr(SURPRISE < k | x) = F(-x beta_k), where F(-x beta_k) = exp(-x beta_k)/(1+exp(-x beta_k)). The printed adjacent-threshold constraint is -x beta_k >= -x beta_k-1 for all k. Odds_k(x) = Pr(SURPRISE >= k|x)/Pr(SURPRISE < k|x) = [1-F(-x beta_k)]/F(-x beta_k) = exp(x beta_k). F is the cumulative logistic distribution.

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Appendix probability and cross-threshold constraints, physical PDF page 25):
Pr(SURPRISE < k | x) = F(-x beta_k), where F(-x beta_k) = exp(-x beta_k)/(1+exp(-x beta_k)). The printed adjacent-threshold constraint is -x beta_k >= -x beta_k-1 for all k. Odds_k(x) = Pr(SURPRISE >= k|x)/Pr(SURPRISE < k|x) = [1-F(-x beta_k)]/F(-x beta_k) = exp(x beta_k). F is the cumulative logistic distribution.

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Appendix probability and cross-threshold constraints, physical PDF page 25):
Pr(SURPRISE < k | x) = F(-x beta_k), where F(-x beta_k) = exp(-x beta_k)/(1+exp(-x beta_k)). The printed adjacent-threshold constraint is -x beta_k >= -x beta_k-1 for all k. Odds_k(x) = Pr(SURPRISE >= k|x)/Pr(SURPRISE < k|x) = [1-F(-x beta_k)]/F(-x beta_k) = exp(x beta_k). F is the cumulative logistic distribution.

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Appendix probability and cross-threshold constraints, physical PDF page 25):
Pr(SURPRISE < k | x) = F(-x beta_k), where F(-x beta_k) = exp(-x beta_k)/(1+exp(-x beta_k)). The printed adjacent-threshold constraint is -x beta_k >= -x beta_k-1 for all k. Odds_k(x) = Pr(SURPRISE >= k|x)/Pr(SURPRISE < k|x) = [1-F(-x beta_k)]/F(-x beta_k) = exp(x beta_k). F is the cumulative logistic distribution.

To ensure that the sum of cumulative probabilities across all k equals 1, we impose the constraint

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Appendix probability and cross-threshold constraints, physical PDF page 25):
Pr(SURPRISE < k | x) = F(-x beta_k), where F(-x beta_k) = exp(-x beta_k)/(1+exp(-x beta_k)). The printed adjacent-threshold constraint is -x beta_k >= -x beta_k-1 for all k. Odds_k(x) = Pr(SURPRISE >= k|x)/Pr(SURPRISE < k|x) = [1-F(-x beta_k)]/F(-x beta_k) = exp(x beta_k). F is the cumulative logistic distribution.

Odds_k = Pr(SURPRISE_it >= k)/Pr(SURPRISE_it < k) = exp(beta_0,k + beta_1,k*NOA_it + beta_kprime*CONTROLS_it). SURPRISE is actual EPS minus consensus forecast, measured in pennies and treated as ordinal. Coefficients can vary by k. This display contains no disturbance term inside the exponential.

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Appendix probability and cross-threshold constraints, physical PDF page 25):
Pr(SURPRISE < k | x) = F(-x beta_k), where F(-x beta_k) = exp(-x beta_k)/(1+exp(-x beta_k)). The printed adjacent-threshold constraint is -x beta_k >= -x beta_k-1 for all k. Odds_k(x) = Pr(SURPRISE >= k|x)/Pr(SURPRISE < k|x) = [1-F(-x beta_k)]/F(-x beta_k) = exp(x beta_k). F is the cumulative logistic distribution.

Source-first scope decision: the paper’s substantive question is whether beginning net operating assets constrain the likelihood of larger positive or smaller negative earnings surprises. Table 5 / Equation (2) is the principal full-sample family. Because NOA is used to answer this empirical question, the extraction retains the full-surprise generalized ordered-logit design rather than treating NOA development as a method contribution.

The ten thresholds k = −4¢ through 5¢ are ten equations in one jointly estimated baseline system, as the paper states; the equations share estimation_group_id. Table 5 Panel B is a summary of those same thresholds, not a second outcome family.

Table 3’s abnormal-accrual fit is used to validate that NOA is associated with past income-increasing accruals. Its residuals do not construct the retained NOA predictor, so it is not an indispensable dependency. Table 6 component splits and the OLS/regular ordered-logit sensitivity fits are excluded as robustness analyses.

The supplied verified reading appends coordinator-checked math to pages 9, 17, and 25. Table 5 page 17 prints +v_it inside the exponent, while Equation (2) on page 9 and the Appendix on page 25 omit it; the source discrepancy is preserved. Physical PDF page 17 was viewed.

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Expected core earnings Equations (1)/(2) and ATO, physical PDF page 11):
ATO_t = Sales_t / ((NOA_t + NOA_t-1)/2); the denominator uses a PLUS between current and lagged NOA. Average NOA must be positive. NOA = OperatingAssets - OperatingLiabilities; OperatingAssets = #6 - #1 - #32; OperatingLiabilities = #6 - (#9 + #34) - (#60 + #130) - #38. models.model_label: Primary FERC model: returns on earnings, future earnings/returns, smoothing, and smoothing interactions
models.sample_description: Firm-year observations from the 2004 version of Compustat's combined industrial annual data, for 1993–2000. Firms in financial and regulated industries (SIC 4000–4999 and 6000–6999) are excluded. The income-smoothing measure requires current-year and prior-four-year changes in discretionary accruals and pre-discretionary income. The primary test requires nonmissing earnings, operating cash flows, and accruals for past, current, and future three years, and returns for current and future three years. The authors trim observations in the top or bottom 1 percent of the stated distributions and remove extreme observations where earnings, operating cash flows, or total accruals in the past/current/future three years exceed 10 times or fall below −10 times market equity, or future three-year compound returns exceed 10 or fall below −10. The resulting primary-test sample is 17,019 firm-years. The accrual-construction fits use Compustat data from 1988–2000.

review_notes: Source-first baseline choice: Regression (4), Table 3 Panel C, is the authors’ primary full-sample test of whether income smoothing improves the informativeness of current returns about future earnings. Regression (5)/Panel A is expressly confirmatory; Regression (3)/Panel B is a CKSS benchmark; Panel D and later specifications are decomposition/robustness tests and are excluded. The income-smoothing measure is developed to answer this substantive question, so it does not make the article a measurement-method paper.

The only indispensable fitted construction is modified Jones/Kothari Regression (1): residual DAP enters the rolling income-smoothing measure; fitted NDAP is used to define DAP; PDI=NI−DAP. The correlation and reversed fractional rank themselves are deterministic, so no other construction fit is included.

scope.quote: We analyze how investors and information intermediaries perceive auditor tenure.
This study focuses on how investors and information intermediaries perceive auditor tenure.
We use earnings response coefficients (ERCs) from contemporaneous returns-earnings regressions to measure investor perceptions of earnings quality.
We analyze the perceptions of three primary users of audited financial statements: investors, independent rating agencies, and financial analysts.

models.equation_text: FEPS_t = α + β_1 EPS_{t−1} + β_2 |ΔEPS|_{t−1} + β_3(EPS_{t−1} × Tenure) + β_4(|ΔEPS|_{t−1} × Tenure) + β_5 Tenure + Σ_{j=1}^{9} β_{6+2(j−1)}(EPS_{t−1} × Control_j) + Σ_{j=1}^{9} β_{7+2(j−1)}(|ΔEPS|_{t−1} × Control_j) + Σ_{j=1}^{9} β_{23+j} Control_j + ε; Control_j order: FirmAge, Big4, Growth, Volatility, Beta, Size, Leverage, Regulation, Analysts.

preprocessing.description: The sample construction deletes the top and bottom 1 percent of E, ΔE, annual EPS, and absolute changes in annual EPS; excludes observations with absolute CAR above 100 percent; and winsorizes the top and bottom 1 percent of Growth, Persistence, Volatility, Beta, and Leverage.

evidence.quote: We impose the following restrictions on the sample: (1) we delete the top and bottom 1 percent of observations for the level of earnings
we remove all observations with the absolute value of cumulative market-adjusted returns ( CAR ) greater than 100 percent
we also winsorize the top and bottom 1 percent of observations for Growth, Persistence, Volatility, Beta, and Leverage

scope.quote: We analyze how investors and information intermediaries perceive auditor tenure.
This study focuses on how investors and information intermediaries perceive auditor tenure.
We analyze the perceptions of three primary users of audited financial statements: investors, independent rating agencies, and financial analysts.

Finally, after controlling for factors that affect analysts’ earnings forecasts, we find that the influence of past earnings on one-year-ahead earnings forecasts becomes larger over extended auditor-client relationships.

review_notes: Source-first scope retains the full-sample, full-control specifications for four central outcomes of the paper: investor CAR/ERC (Table 3 column 2), S&P common stock rankings (Table 5 column 2), S&P senior debt ratings (Table 6 column 2), and one-year-ahead analyst EPS forecasts (Table 7 column 2). These represent the three user groups identified by the authors: investors, independent rating agencies, and analysts.

Reduced models (no controls), restricted-sample estimates, Table 4 CAR-window/deflator sensitivity analyses, the unreported investment/non-investment-grade split, and minimum-analyst-count sensitivity analyses are excluded. The four selected outcomes are parallel tests of the same principal perception question, not an attempt to collect every robustness or partition result.

Every selected model uses Equation (1) with 32 actual RHS terms plus an intercept. The generic nine-control equation and term count are supported by the coordinator-verified transcription in the supplied reading. The Table 7 model uses EPS for E and absolute change in EPS for ΔE, and its nine controls substitute Analysts for Persistence.

The annual cross-sectional estimator is not named in the paper, so method remains null. Coefficients are averaged over 11 annual fits, with time-series standard errors; stock-ranking and debt-rating t-statistics involving Tenure additionally use the described autocorrelation correction.
descriptive_reason: Table 1 Panel A reports 56 retained cells for CAR, E, ΔE, Stock Rankings, Debt Ratings, FEPS, Tenure, and FirmAge. It provides no standalone moments for the full control set, interactions, or Table 7 EPS_{t−1}/|ΔEPS|_{t−1} inputs; Table 2 is a correlation matrix only. Table 1 Tenure and FirmAge links to Table 7 remain unclear because Table 7 states all controls are measured at t−1, while the Table 1 rows are not time-indexed.
results_review_notes: Only the frozen full-control baseline columns are selected: Table 3 full sample (2), Table 5 full sample (2), Table 6 full sample (2), and Table 7 full sample (2). Reduced columns, restricted samples, sensitivity analyses, ordered probit models, and unreported subsample results are excluded.

The reported full-sample column coefficients are averages across 11 annual regressions from 1990–2000, not coefficients from one pooled regression. Per-year observation ranges are kept in the result-set population descriptions and are not summed.

Tables 3, 5, 6, and 7 suppress separate coefficients for earnings-by-control-variable interactions; only each pair sum is reported. The raw enrichments preserve each printed sum as an auxiliary parameter and explicitly mark both individual interaction coefficients unavailable.
No individual coefficient p-values or time-series t degrees of freedom are reported. The sources provide t-statistics, two-tailed significance markers, and source-specific legends.

models.model_label: Mandatory IFRS adoption and cost of equity (full-period pooled regression, Table 4 Panel A)
models.sample_description: The full-sample pooled firm-year regression covers 6,456 observations from 18 EU countries during 1995–2006, representing 1,084 distinct firms. Firms must have data in both the pre- and post-mandatory periods and the data needed for the specified controls; the main sample excludes firms in the three stated classes exempted from 2005 mandatory adoption. Compustat Global provides financial-statement and adoption data; I/B/E/S provides the stock prices and analyst forecasts used to construct COC. Price and forecast inputs are taken seven months after fiscal year-end. The estimation sample requires current stock-price data, positive analyst mean consensus earnings forecasts for at least two periods ahead, all four implied cost-of-equity measures, and available controls; cost-of-equity estimates below 0 or above 1 are omitted.
models.method_details: Table 4 Panel A labels the fit “Pooled Regressions.” The reviewed equation, design description, and table notes do not identify the underlying estimator, so it remains unknown.

dependent_variable.name: COC
dependent_variable.definition: Mean of four implied cost-of-equity estimates: Claus and Thomas (2001), Gebhardt et al. (2001), Gode and Mohanram (2003), and Easton (2004). The estimates are based on current stock prices and analysts’ forecasts; the price and forecast inputs are measured seven months after fiscal year-end.
dependent_variable.formula: Arithmetic mean of the four implied cost-of-equity estimates

evidence.quote: COC       - the mean of the four implied cost of equity estimates based

I use a measure that relies on four estimation models: the industry ROE model in Gebhardt et al. (2001), the economywide growth model in Claus and Thomas (2001), the unrestricted abnormal earnings growth model in Gode and Mohanram (2003), and the restricted abnormal earnings growth model in Easton (2004).

These price and forecast data are in local currencies and are taken seven months after the fiscal year-end to ensure the financial data are publicly available and priced at the time of estimation (Hail and Leuz 2006).
