estimation_procedure.description: Difference-in-differences design: compare the change in COC between the pre-mandatory period (1995–2004) and post-mandatory period (2005–2006) for mandatory adopters with the corresponding change for voluntary adopters. The fitted baseline is one pooled regression over the full 1995–2006 sample; the interaction between mandatory-adopter and post-period indicators is the central treatment contrast. The 2004/2005-excluded regression is a sensitivity fit; Table 4 Panels B and C reconstruct 2×2 comparisons from Panel A coefficients rather than reporting separate fits.

evidence.quote: This difference-in-differences design, which analyzes the population of both mandatory and voluntary adopters over the full period from 1995 to 2006, compares the change in the cost of equity for mandatory adopters before and after the mandatory switch relative to the corresponding change in the cost of equity for voluntary adopters.
Therefore, for ease of exposition, Panel B reports the reconstructed coefficients and the significance levels in a 2 - 2 analysis for the full sample period.
Panel B reports the 2 - 2 analysis of mandatory adopters versus voluntary adopters by period for the full sample, constructed using the coefficients in Panel A.

preprocessing.description: The COC inputs are based on current stock price data and analyst mean consensus earnings forecasts for at least two periods ahead. Prices and forecasts are taken seven months after fiscal year-end; forecasts must be positive; long-term EPS growth forecasts are used when three- through five-year-ahead forecasts are missing.

evidence.quote: These price and forecast data are in local currencies and are taken seven months after the fiscal year-end to ensure the financial data are publicly available and priced at the time of estimation (Hail and Leuz 2006).
To be included in the sample, I require each firm-year observation to have current stock price data and analyst mean consensus earnings forecasts for at least two periods ahead.
All earnings forecasts are restricted to be positive, and the long-term earnings growth rate forecasts are used if the three-year- through five-year-ahead earnings forecasts are missing.

preprocessing.description: The dividend payout ratio is the historic three-year firm average, replaced by the country-year median if missing or outside 0–1. All four individual implied cost-of-equity measures are required to compute COC; estimates below 0 or above 1 are omitted.

evidence.quote: The dividend payout ratio is computed using the historic three-year average for each firm,
and is replaced by the country-year median payout ratio when missing or out of the range of 0 to 1 (Hail and Leuz 2006).
I further require that all four individual measures of cost of equity be available in order to calculate the average cost of equity measure.
Cost of equity estimates below 0 and above 1 are omitted.

preprocessing.description: Winsorize firm-level continuous variables at the top and bottom 1 percent of their distributions, except firm size (log of total assets).

evidence.quote: I winsorize all firm-level continuous variables at the top and bottom 1 percent of their distributions, with the exception of firm size (log of total assets).

preprocessing.description: The author manually checked accounting-standard coding against annual reports and/or company websites and corrected 34 firm-year misclassifications.

review_notes: Source-first scope selection: Table 4 Panel A, full period 1995–2006, Equation (1) is the principal full-sample test of the mandatory IFRS effect on COC. The full-sample DID specification retains the author’s complete control set and central mandatory-adopter × post-period interaction.

Excluded the transition-period specification as sensitivity analysis, Table 4 Panels B/C as algebraically reconstructed two-by-two comparisons rather than separate fits, and Table 6 legal-enforcement/disclosure/comparability conditioning analyses as follow-up heterogeneity/mechanism tests. Later bid-ask, sample restriction, and self-selection analyses are sensitivity checks. These exclusions follow the one-principal-family scope rule.

COC is the average of four established implied-cost-of-equity valuation estimates. The paper identifies those inputs and their required price/forecast data and screening, but reports no separate fitted regression needed to generate them; they are outcome measurement inputs, so dependencies remain empty.
Underlying estimator remains unknown: “pooled regressions” and firm/year cluster-adjusted t-statistics do not establish OLS or another estimator.

dependent_variable.name: Standardized difference: avoid quarterly losses
dependent_variable.definition: Burgstahler–Dichev standardized difference for the avoid-loss threshold (quarterly earnings level deflated by beginning-of-quarter-t stock price) in year y, evaluated in the earnings bin just left of zero. It is the actual observation count minus the expected count, divided by the estimated standard deviation of that difference; the expected count is the average of the two adjacent bins. The authors compute the threshold-year statistic using a standardized N of 1,000 based on the actual bin proportion. Bins have width .0025. A negative value indicates threshold achievement; |statistic| ≥ 2.33 is the stated one-tailed threshold criterion.

dependent_variable.name: Standardized difference: avoid negative quarterly earnings surprises

It is the actual observation count minus the expected count, divided by the estimated standard deviation of that difference; the expected count is the average of the two adjacent bins. need time to plan and implement tax planning strategies.

The measures are constructed so that higher values represent an
increase in financial constraints.

RankDKZ is intended to capture changes in firms’ investment-related constraints and equals the
decile rank of the change in the firm’s investment-related constraints, based on the Kaplan and Zingales (1997) financial
constraint index. Decile rank values range from 0 to 9.
KZ = -1.00*((IB+DP)/lag(PPENT)) + 0.28*((AT+PRCC_F*CSHO-CEQ-TXDB)/AT) + 3.13*((DLTT+DLC)/(DLTT+DLC+SEQ)) - 39.36*((DVC+DVP)/lag(PPENT)) - 1.31*(CHE/lag(PPENT)).

H1: Increases (decreases) in financial constraints are associated with decreases (increases) in cash effective tax rates.

review_notes: Source-first scope decision: the selected family is H1, the full-sample relation between earnings-management magnitude and relationship-specific-investment proxies. Section III calls industry-level variables the “first approach” (p. 7); it calls the identified actual-partner subset the “second approach” (p. 9). Section IV begins “Determinants of Earnings Management Using Industry-Level Variables,” tests H1 by OLS, and presents Table 2 (pp. 13–16). Retain Table 2 Models 1 and 2 as the parallel R&D and alliance/JV proxy specifications.

Exclude Table 2 Models 3–4 because they add Zscore Dummy interactions (financial-health moderation), not additional controls or baseline proxy fits. Exclude Tables 3–4 actual-partner regressions: the paper labels them as a separate second approach and later analysis; pp. 19–20 describe them as addressing potential simultaneity/endogeneity, with smaller supplier/customer samples and only 895 firm-years when both partners’ R&D are measurable. Footnote 18 says Table 2 does not use 2SLS because endogeneity is less relevant for industry-level regressors. The direct-partner/2SLS fits are therefore follow-up analyses, not indispensable components of the selected full-sample H1 design.
Exclude later income-smoothing/large-earnings-increase analyses and H2 consequence/duration outcomes as distinct subsequent questions or decompositions.

The volatility controls require at least five observations, but their estimation-window length is not reported. The alliance/JV proxy counts announcements during 1984–2003, but the paper does not specify the event-year aggregation and denominator year for the firm-year regressions.

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Differential-timeliness Equation (1), physical PDF page 4):
EPS_jt/Price_(j,t-1) = alpha_0 + beta_0*DUM_jt + beta_1*Return_jt + beta_2*(DUM_jt*Return_jt) + epsilon_jt. EPS is earnings per share from continuing operations. estimation_procedure.description: Equation (1) is pooled over all years relevant to the IAS-versus-matched-NIAS post-adoption comparison. Its residuals are pooled by IAS/NIAS group to compute the variance of AM*. Differences in metrics are assessed using the empirical-distribution J-test: observations are assigned to comparison groups by resampling with replacement, repeated 1,000 times.

evidence.quote: For example, when comparing IAS and NIAS firms in the postadoption period, we pool all sample years in the postadoption period.
For this comparison, the variability of AM* is the variance of the IAS and NIAS firms' respective residuals from equation (1) in the postadoption period.

With the exception of the tests for the frequency of small positive and
large negative net income, for which we test for significance of regression
coefficients, we test for differences in each metric using a J-testbased on
the empirical distribution of the differences.

We obtain
the empirical distribution of this difference by repeating this procedure
1,000 times.

estimation_procedure.description: Equation (2) is pooled over all years relevant to the post-adoption IAS-versus-matched-NIAS comparison. The metric is the ratio of the group-specific variances of residuals from equations (1) and (2), AM* over ACF*. Metric differences are assessed by the J-test empirical distribution from 1,000 resamples with replacement.

evidence.quote: For example, when comparing IAS and NIAS firms in the postadoption period, we pool all sample years in the postadoption period.

Our resulting second metric is the ratio of
the variability of AM* to variability of A CF*.

With the exception of the tests for the frequency of small positive and
large negative net income, for which we test for significance of regression
coefficients, we test for differences in each metric using a J-testbased on
the empirical distribution of the differences.

We obtain
the empirical distribution of this difference by repeating this procedure
1,000 times.

estimation_procedure.description: Equations (3) and (4) are pooled over the post-adoption comparison observations. Their residuals CF* and ACC* form the partial Spearman correlation outcome, computed separately by IAS/NIAS group. Group metric differences are tested using a J-test empirical distribution from 1,000 resamples with replacement.

evidence.quote: Our third earnings smoothing metric is based on the Spearman correlation between accruals and cash flows.
we compare correlations of residuals from equations (3) and (4), CF* and ACC*

With the exception of the tests for the frequency of small positive and
large negative net income, for which we test for significance of regression
coefficients, we test for differences in each metric using a J-testbased on
the empirical distribution of the differences.

We obtain
the empirical distribution of this difference by repeating this procedure
1,000 times.

preprocessing.description: The authors winsorize at the 5% level all variables used to construct the accounting-quality metrics to mitigate outlier effects; the paper does not state a more detailed cutoff rule.

evidence.quote: The sample size reflects our having winsorized at the 5% level all variables used to construct our metrics to mitigate the effects of outliers on our inferences.

scope.quote: As the primary test of our predictions, we compare accounting quality metrics for IAS firms and NIAS firms in the period after the IAS firms adopt IAS, that is,the postadoption period.
Table 3 presents results comparing the quality of accounting amounts for IAS and NIAS firms in the postadoption period.

equation.quote: CFit = a0 + ot\SIZEu + a^GROWTHu + ot$EISSUEit + a4LEVit + a5DISSUEit + UPTURNit+ a7AUDit + a8NUMEXit + a9XLISTit + a10 CLOSEit + sit (3)

sample.quote: We select as the matched NIAS firm the nonapplying firm from the IAS firm's country whose equity market value is closest to the IAS firm's at the end of itsadoption year.
Our analyses include all firm-years for which the IAS firm and itsmatched NIAS firm both have data.
Our sample comprises 1,896 firm-year observations for 327 firms that adopted IAS between 1994 and 2003
We obtain our sample of IAS firms from WorldScope, which identifies the set of accounting standards a firm uses to prepare itsfinancial statements.
We gather financial and accounting data from DataStream.
The periods after IAS firms adopted IAS, that is, the postadoption period, ends in 2003.

estimation_procedure.description: Equations (3) and (4) are pooled over the post-adoption comparison observations. Their residuals CF* and ACC* form the partial Spearman correlation outcome, computed separately by IAS/NIAS group. Group metric differences are tested using a J-test empirical distribution from 1,000 resamples with replacement.

evidence.quote: Our third earnings smoothing metric is based on the Spearman correlation between accruals and cash flows.
we compare correlations of residuals from equations (3) and (4), CF* and ACC*

With the exception of the tests for the frequency of small positive and
large negative net income, for which we test for significance of regression
coefficients, we test for differences in each metric using a J-testbased on
the empirical distribution of the differences.

We obtain
the empirical distribution of this difference by repeating this procedure
1,000 times.

preprocessing.description: The authors winsorize at the 5% level all variables used to construct the accounting-quality metrics to mitigate outlier effects; the paper does not state a more detailed cutoff rule.

evidence.quote: The sample size reflects our having winsorized at the 5% level all variables used to construct our metrics to mitigate the effects of outliers on our inferences.

scope.quote: As the primary test of our predictions, we compare accounting quality metrics for IAS firms and NIAS firms in the period after the IAS firms adopt IAS, that is,the postadoption period.
Table 3 presents results comparing the quality of accounting amounts for IAS and NIAS firms in the postadoption period.

equation.quote: ACCit = a0 + <*iSIZEu + a2GROWTHit + a3EISSUEit + a4LEVit + ctbDISSUEit + aeTURNit + a7AUDit + a8NUMEXit + a9 XLISTit + aio CLOSEit+ eit (4)

sample.quote: We select as the matched NIAS firm the nonapplying firm from the IAS firm's country whose equity market value is closest to the IAS firm's at the end of itsadoption year.
Our analyses include all firm-years for which the IAS firm and itsmatched NIAS firm both have data.
Our sample comprises 1,896 firm-year observations for 327 firms that adopted IAS between 1994 and 2003
We obtain our sample of IAS firms from WorldScope, which identifies the set of accounting standards a firm uses to prepare itsfinancial statements.
We gather financial and accounting data from DataStream.
The periods after IAS firms adopted IAS, that is, the postadoption period, ends in 2003.

evidence.quote:
Following Lang,
Raedy, and Wilson [2006], we measure RETURN as the natural logarithm
of the ratio of the stock price three months after fiscal year-end to the stock

estimation_procedure.description: Two-stage reverse earnings-return procedure: first regress NI/P on country and industry fixed-effect indicators to form [NI/P]*, then regress [NI/P]* on natural-log RETURN for the indicated IAS/NIAS group and good/bad-news sample. The specific footnote 21 rule determines good/bad membership using the sign of the dividend- and split-adjusted price relative from nine months before to three months after fiscal year-end; the RETURN regressor itself is the natural logarithm of that price ratio. Table 3 describes the partition as nonnegative/negative RETURN; under source-specificity clarification 03 this less detailed wording is read using footnote 21. Adjusted R-squared is reported, with IAS-versus-NIAS metric differences assessed using a J-test empirical distribution from 1,000 resamples with replacement.

evidence.quote: We regress the residuals from this regression, [NI/P]*, on annual stock return

Following Lang, Raedy, and Wilson [2006], we measure RETURN as the natural logarithm of the ratio of the stock price three months after fiscal year-end to the stock price nine months before fiscal year-end, adjusted for dividends and stock splits.

Because RETURN is the natural logarithm of a price ratio and therefore can be negative even when stock prices increase during the 12-month window, when determining whether an observation belongs in the good news or bad news regression, we measure return as the stock price three months after fiscal year-end relative to the stock price nine months before fiscal year end, adjusted for dividends and stock splits.
The good/bad news regression is based on a two-stage regression.
Good (bad) news observations are those for which RETURN is nonnegative (negative).
Adjusted R2 is from the second-stage regressions.

With the exception of the tests for the frequency of small positive and
large negative net income, for which we test for significance of regression
coefficients, we test for differences in each metric using a J-testbased on
the empirical distribution of the differences.

We obtain
the empirical distribution of this difference by repeating this procedure
1,000 times.

dependent_variable.name: Log(Price Impact)
dependent_variable.definition: Natural logarithm of the firm-year median Amihud illiquidity measure. The daily measure is the absolute price change in percent divided by U.S.-dollar trading volume measured in thousands; zero-return days are omitted from the median. The appendix states that the price-impact metric is multiplied by 1,000 for exposition, and the firm-year measurement period is months −5 through +7 relative to fiscal year-end.
dependent_variable.formula: ln(yearly median daily price impact).

evidence.quote: Log(Price
Impact)

We measure illiquidity as the median daily price impact over the year (or month in the country-month analyses) and follow Amihud [2002] in computing price impact as the daily absolute price change in percent divided by US$ trading volume (measured in thousands)

To avoid the misclassification of days with no or low trading activity (i.e., days potentially yielding a price impact of zero), we omit zero-return days from the computation of the yearly or monthly medians
multiply the price impact metric by 1,000. Again, the measurement period starts in month −5 and runs through month +7 relative to the firm’s fiscal year-end

dependent_variable.name: Log(Total Trading Costs)
dependent_variable.definition: Natural logarithm of the yearly estimate of round-trip transaction costs. In Appendix A.3, latent true returns follow a market relation and observed returns are censored by estimated negative- and positive-information transaction-cost thresholds; the measure is the estimated upper threshold minus the lower threshold. Daily stock and equal-weighted local market-index returns are used in a separate firm-year likelihood fit over months −5 through +7 relative to fiscal year-end; each fit requires at least 24 daily returns and at least 20% nonzero returns.

models.sample_description: Firm-year observations from 2001 through 2005; the Table 5 base specification combines the IFRS treatment sample with a maximum of 150 randomly selected firms from each non-mandating benchmark country. This outcome is observed in up to 36 countries.
models.method_details: The paper states that the firm-year regressions report OLS coefficient estimates. Inference is based on firm-clustered robust standard errors.

dependent_variable.name: Cost of Capital
dependent_variable.definition: Firm-year average of four implied cost-of-equity estimates from the Claus–Thomas, Gebhardt–Lee–Swaminathan (GLS), Ohlson–Juettner–Nauroth (OJ), and Easton modified PEG models. Each estimate is the internal rate of return that equates the stock price with its model-specific expected sequence of residual income or abnormal earnings. CT uses forecast EPS and beginning-of-year book value through T=5, clean-surplus book-value forecasts and a constant payout fraction; terminal residual income grows at expected inflation, proxied by the annualized country-specific median of one-year-ahead realized monthly inflation. GLS uses three explicit forecast years, then linearly fades forecast ROE toward the historic three-year average ROE in a country-year within Campbell industries; negative yearly target returns are replaced by country-industry medians, and residual income is constant from T=12. OJ combines one-year-ahead EPS and dividends with short-term growth equal to the mean of forecast EPS growth from years 1 to 2 and the I/B/E/S five-year growth forecast, and long-term growth equal to expected inflation; a positive forecast earnings change is required. Modified PEG uses one- and two-year-ahead EPS and year-1 dividends, assumes abnormal-earnings growth persists, and requires positive forecast earnings changes including reinvested dividends. Required inputs are the current price, mean analyst EPS forecasts for years 1 and 2, and either year-3 EPS or long-term growth; missing year-3-to-5 EPS forecasts are filled recursively using long-term growth, and missing long-term growth is imputed from the forecast EPS change from years 2 to 3. Prices and mean forecasts are measured at month +7 after fiscal year-end; prices are shifted to the beginning of the fiscal year for full-year discounting. Forecast dividends use the firm’s historic three-year payout ratio, with the country-year median substituted when missing or outside [0,1]. Long-run inflation growth is country-specific; negative inflation is replaced by the country historical median over 1980–2005. IRRs are solved iteratively until imputed and actual prices differ by at most 0.001; only positive estimates are retained.
dependent_variable.formula: mean(r_CT, r_GLS, r_OJ, r_PEG)

evidence.quote: Cost of Capital is the average cost of capital estimate implied by the mean I/B/E/S analyst consensus forecasts and stock prices using the Claus and Thomas [2001] model, the Gebhardt, Lee, and Swaminathan [2001] model, the Ohlson and Juettner-Nauroth [2005] model, and the Easton [2004] model.

For each model, we substitute market price and analyst forecasts from I/B/E/S into the valuation equation and back out the cost of capital as the internal rate of return that equates current stock price and the expected future sequence of residual incomes or abnormal earnings. We average over the four models to obtain a single estimate per firm-year observation.
We assume clean surplus, that is, future book values are imputed from current book values, forecasted earnings, and dividends. Dividends are set equal to a constant fraction of forecasted earnings.

At time T = 5, it is assumed that (nominal) residual income grows at rate g equal to the expected inflation. As a proxy for g, we use the (annualized) median of country-specific, one-year-ahead realized monthly inflation rates.
After the explicit forecast period of three years, the residual income series is derived by linearly fading the forecasted accounting return on equity to the industryspecific median return.

We compute the historic three-year average return on equity in a given country and year based on the industry classification in Campbell [1996]. Negative yearly target returns are replaced by countryindustry medians. From T = 12 on residual income is assumed to remain constant.

Following Gode and Mohanram [2003], the short-term growth rate, gst, is estimated as the average between the forecasted percentage change in earnings from year t +1 to t +2 and the five-year growth forecast provided by financial analysts on I/B/E/S.

The model embeds the assumption that growth in abnormal earnings persists in perpetuity after the initial period. Note that it requires positive changes in forecasted earnings (including reinvested dividends) to yield a numerical solution.
OJ long-run abnormal-earnings growth g_lt equals expected inflation, the annualized country-specific median of one-year-ahead realized monthly inflation.
Missing explicit year3-5 EPS forecasts are filled recursively as xhat_(t+tau)=xhat_(t+tau-1)*(1+ltg). The sample requires price, forecastEPS1 and2, and either forecastEPS3 or ltg.
Stock prices and analyst forecasts are measured as of month +7 after the fiscal year-end.
Move the month+7 price back to beginning fiscal year with the imputed cost of capital, then use full-year discounting, equivalent to partial-year discount factors.
Dividend payout is each firm’s historic3year average; if missing or outside[0,1], substitute the country-year median payout.
Long-run terminal growth uses annualized country-specific median one-year-ahead monthly inflation; negative values are replaced by historical country inflation median over1980-2005.
We stop iterating if the imputed price falls within a 0.001 difference of its actual value. Implied cost of equity capital estimates are restricted to be positive and set to missing otherwise.

models.sample_description: Annual June 30 cross-sections of NYSE and AMEX stocks with available data, 1979–1995. The main sample requires CRSP/Compustat coverage, required accounting and market data, and one- and two-year-ahead I/B/E/S EPS forecasts. The paper reports annual firm counts from 1,018 to 1,333, but not the exact N for each annual fit.
models.method_details: The authors report annual Fama–MacBeth regressions. The underlying estimator for each annual cross-sectional fit is not identified in the paper.

dependent_variable.name: r_i,t − r_f,t (implied risk premium)
dependent_variable.definition: Annualized year-t implied risk premium for firm i, measured in percent as the firm-specific internal rate of return from a 12-year Edwards–Bell–Ohlson residual-income valuation less the end-of-month yield on a 10-year Treasury bond. The valuation equates the June 30 stock price to beginning book value per share plus discounted residual income and a terminal value. It uses I/B/E/S mean EPS forecasts for years 1 and 2; year-3 EPS is forecast as year-2 EPS times (1+Ltg), using the growth implicit in FY1 and FY2 when Ltg is unavailable. ROE is forecast explicitly for the first three years, then linearly mean-reverted to a moving median ROE for profitable firms in the same Fama–French 48 industry, calculated from at least five and up to ten past years; reported results use T=12 and a terminal value beyond T. Future book values use clean-surplus accounting, with dividends based on the latest fiscal-year payout ratio; the payout ratio excludes share repurchases, divides dividends by earnings (or by 0.06 times total assets when earnings are negative), and is bounded to [0,1]. Until reported book value becomes available four months after fiscal year-end, book value is forecast using prior book value plus earnings less dividends; thereafter the actual Compustat value is used.
dependent_variable.formula: r_e solved from the 12-year EBO price equation − end-of-month 10-year Treasury yield, as of June 30

evidence.quote: Equation(5): P_t = B_t + ((FROE_(t+1)-r_e)/(1+r_e))*B_t + ((FROE_(t+2)-r_e)/(1+r_e)^2)*B_(t+1) + TV. Equation(6): TV = sum_(i=3)^(T-1) [((FROE_(t+i)-r_e)/(1+r_e)^i)*B_(t+i-1)] + ((FROE_(t+T)-r_e)/(r_e*(1+r_e)^(T-1)))*B_(t+T-1). T=12 in reported results.
The reported horizon is T=12. Industry target ROE is the moving median of past ROEs from profitable firms in the same Fama-French48 industry, using at least five and up to ten past years.

First/two-year-ahead forecasts are IBES mean EPS; year3 forecast is FEPS_(t+2)*(1+Ltg). When Ltg is missing (including before1981), use the growth implicit in the year1/year2 forecasts to forecast year3.
From announcement month through four months after fiscal year-end, synthetic B_t=B_(t-1)+EPS_t-D_t; after the fourth month use actual reported Compustat book value as continued on page11.

Expected payout k is latest-fiscal-year actual dividends divided by earnings for that period, excluding share repurchases. For negative earnings, use dividends/(0.06*totalAssets). Set payout below0 to0 and above1 to1.

We estimate the IRR for each firm at the end ofJune each year by substituting the forecasted future earnings, book values, and terminal values into equation (5) and solving the resulting non-linear equation. We then subtract the end-of-month yield on long-term (10-year) Treasury bonds from the IRR measure to obtain an (annualized) implied risk premium for each firm in the sample.
Response is the firm’s implied risk premium derived from the twelve-year EBO model in percent.

dependent_variable.name: DACC_bs
dependent_variable.definition: Discretionary accruals under the balance-sheet approach, computed as ACC_bs minus predicted NDACC_bs. ACC_bs uses changes in current assets, current liabilities, cash, short-term debt and depreciation, with the Equation (1) variables deflated by lagged total assets. NDACC_bs uses fitted modified-Jones coefficients with ΔRev−ΔAR_bs and gross PPE; ΔAR_bs is measured from subsequent balance sheets. Table 3 coefficient entries are printed in percent units.

review_notes: Scope decision: the principal question is whether balance-sheet and cash-flow discretionary-accrual measures lead to different earnings-management inferences when the partition coincides with a non-articulation event. The paper describes this as its most significant finding, and Table 3 Panel B directly tests it. Retained six annual specifications: two primary accrual measures crossed with three partition indicators. Excluded Table 3 Panel A bias calculations, Table 2 accrual-measurement-error characterization, and later Tables 4–6 and portfolio applications.

Each Table 3 Panel B specification is estimated separately by year from 1988 through 1997. The All Years row summarizes ten annual estimates; it is not a pooled regression. The 14,558 firm-years is the overall sample, not any single annual regression N.

Retained six year-by-industry modified-Jones construction fits because their estimated coefficients generate the NDACC components of the retained DACC outcomes. The fits use firm-years without the specified non-articulation event and apply the parameters to ΔRev−ΔAR and PPE. Footnote 12 distinguishes balance-sheet and cash-flow sources of ΔAR.

Applied Section II event definitions to the generic Table 3 PART notes: Compustat annual footnote code #1 for M&A; Compustat #66 discontinued operations greater than $10,000; and Compustat #150 foreign-currency gain/loss greater than $10,000. The body’s more specific item-code and threshold rules refine the table definitions rather than conflict with them.

The Table 3 equations and Equation (1) are supported by coordinator-verified transcriptions appended to the assigned reading. Equations (10a/b) and (11a/b) are readable in the supplied page text with damaged Greek labels only; no worker-created transcription was added to the reading.
results_review_notes: Table 1 raw ACCbs and ACCcf summaries are retained as components of the selected DACCbs and DACCcf outcomes; DIFF rows are omitted because they are not inputs to those outcomes.
Table 3 Panel A is used only for the reported standard deviations of retained PART indicators. Its bias estimates and correlations are outside the selected baseline results.
No direct DACCbs or DACCcf data-value descriptives were found in the reviewed source sections; Table 1 reports their raw accrual components instead.

Source-first scope: the paper’s principal question is whether simple historical accounting signals can sort high book-to-market firms into portfolios that separate future winners from losers. Section 3.3 identifies portfolio formation on F-SCORE as the primary methodology; the tests compare high-score firms with low-score firms and with the full high-BM portfolio using return distributions, t-statistics, and bootstrap comparisons (Table 3). These are portfolio sorts and return-difference tests, not regression equations.

Reconsidered the prior zero-model decision against the source. F-SCORE is the sum of nine binary signals and the paper explicitly says its investment decision does not require an estimated probability model or year-by-year fitted data (Section 2.3.4). No fitted regression is required to construct the score or primary portfolio test.

Table 7 is an actual cross-sectional regression, but Section 5 introduces it to control for size, book-to-market, momentum, accruals, and equity issuance as other sources of return variation after the primary portfolio tests. It is outside the principal baseline family under the selected scope. No-baseline status is retained because the primary analysis contains no eligible regression, not because the score is deterministic.

dependent_variable.definition: Absolute abnormal accruals, |DACC|, measuring abnormal-accrual magnitude. DACC = TA − ETA (Equation (3)); ETA uses Equation (1) coefficient estimates with (ΔREV − ΔREC) (Equation (2)). dependent_variable.name: |DACC|

review_notes: The principal question is whether joint national and city-office auditor industry expertise is associated with audit quality. Retain the authors’ primary fully controlled Model 3 for the paper’s three central outcome measures (absolute abnormal accruals, MEET, and going-concern opinion), for both specialist definitions. The abstract and Introduction identify all three outcomes as audit-quality tests; the authors call Model 3 the primary model of interest for Equation (4) and report it as Model 3 for Equations (5) and (6).

Excluded Equation (4) Models 1 and 2 because the paper identifies Model 3 as its primary test; excluded Table 6 income-increasing/income-decreasing abnormal-accrual decompositions because the paper explicitly labels these as robustness tests; excluded Fama–MacBeth, continuous-market-share interaction, size partitions, and other sensitivity analyses.

Equation (1) is retained as the sole supporting fitted construction because its coefficients generate expected total accruals used for DACC. Equation (2) applies those fitted coefficients algebraically and Equation (3) forms a difference; neither is an additional fitted regression.

Needs review remains for source-reported gaps: Equation (4) versus Table 3 give incompatible σ(CFO) windows; the paper does not specify the ΔREC scaling in Equation (2), Altman-score formula, or ROA operational formula; and the reported Rogers-style inference does not identify the correction or grouping dimension.

Source-first principal-family decision: the paper’s central contribution is a large-sample test of the debt-covenant hypothesis using covenant-slack distributions for the current-ratio and net-worth covenant samples. The authors state (physical PDF p. 18): “We present our main results in a series of histograms that document the empirical distributions of covenant slack over loan life.” Their primary smoothness test compares expected and observed bin counts around zero (p. 19); the randomization-based robustness test uses the ratio of observations in bin 0 to bin −1 and shuffles covenant thresholds against accounting realizations (p. 27). These are distributional and randomization tests, not fitted regression equations.

The rest of the paper does not supply an eligible regression for this selected family: Table 3 reports Spearman rank correlations (p. 17); Table 5 reports violation frequencies (p. 29); Table 6 compares sample medians across loan-quarter groups (pp. 30–31). Covenant slack is computed as actual covenant-variable realization minus the threshold (p. 15), a deterministic difference, not a regression. Therefore models=[] with status no_baseline_regression is retained.

The family covers both current-ratio and net-worth covenant samples and the paper’s main full and follow-up histogram partitions. The assigned sample record is the current-ratio histogram sample (sample_id current_ratio_covenant), while the source also reports the parallel net-worth covenant sample; neither contains a fitted regression.
descriptive_reason: No baseline regression models are selected in the frozen specification or inventory, so no model-related descriptive statistics apply to this enrichment. The paper’s primary results are covenant-slack distributions/histograms, Spearman correlations, randomization tests, violation frequencies and medians (source pages 15–18 and 27–31), outside the frozen regression-results family.
results_review_notes: Source pages 15–18 and 27–32 were read, and original PDF pages 15, 17–18 and 27–32 were rendered and viewed before opening the matching prior.

review_notes: Scope: retain the full piecewise-linear accrual family in Tables 3–5: CF, DD, and Jones accrual specifications; three book proxies and the abnormal-return proxy individually (Tables 3–4); the three book/market proxy pairings and all-proxy combination (Table 5); and both pooled full-sample and repeated three-digit-SIC industry fits. The central source question is how accruals asymmetrically recognize timely gains/losses, and the paper states that it reports evidence on all proxies individually and in combinations (physical PDF pp. 1, 8, 12–20). Table 1 is the conventional linear replication/benchmark and Table 2 reports proxy overlap; these do not estimate the new piecewise baseline. Later time-trend, robustness, subgroup, and future-cash-flow analyses address extensions outside this one principal family.

The actual estimator for the Table 3–5 regressions is not identified; method is null and flagged in every model. For DD fits, the paper does not specify whether lagged and lead cash flows use average assets of their own years or year t; formula fields remain null and the timing gap is flagged. Industry-specific N values in tables are counts of qualifying fits, not per-fit observation counts; sample_size is null for those models.

In Table 4 and the combined Table 5 fits, the specific note names continuous accounting variables for annual tail deletion; treatment of abnormal-return tails is not separately stated in that note, while the general sample description states annual tail exclusions for each variable. This source detail is preserved without asserting an incompatible rule.

In Table 5 Panel D Jones columns, the table reports no standalone CF_t coefficient row while reporting DCF_t × CF_t. The RHS inventory follows the printed column; the omission rationale is not separately identified beyond the paper’s general collinearity note.
descriptive_reason: Targeted search of the complete assigned paper text for descriptive/summary statistics and summary terms related to retained variables (including means, standard deviations, minima/maxima, medians, percentiles, and variable names) found no data-value summaries for the selected baseline outcomes, predictors, raw inputs, or components. Table 1 is a linear benchmark outside the retained family; Table 2 reports proxy correlations and chi-square tests, which are not variable descriptives; later results concern additional or robustness analyses. Table notes reporting coefficient means and average observations per industry are fit summaries, not data-variable descriptives.
results_review_notes: All 48 frozen baseline result sets from Tables 3–5 were compared with the selected original table cells, including intercepts, all predictor estimates and parenthetical statistics; parameter identities and frozen RHS links were reviewed.

The source labels industry-specific parentheticals as t-statistics based on the cross-sectional coefficient distribution; Student-t is used with df unknown and that dispersion is not treated as a sampling SE. Pooled parenthetical cells are not labeled t or z and retain kind other with test context/reference unknown.

No coefficient standard errors, exact coefficient p-values, significance markers, or significance legend are printed for Tables 3–5. Each selected fit now includes source-printed No. of obs. and Adj. R² (%) as explicit auxiliary rows.

Jones-model intercepts remain on the printed scale with unit multiplier, consistent with the later source explanation; Table 5 Panel D individual coefficients carry the source multicollinearity caution.

models.method_details: The authors say they estimate a regression but do not identify its estimator.

dependent_variable.name: VDIF
dependent_variable.definition: Percentage difference between the analysts’ accounting-based equity value estimate and share price: VDIF=(AV−P)/P. AV is book value plus discounted expected abnormal earnings for years 1–4 and a terminal abnormal-earnings term at year 5. Mean analyst EPS forecasts supply t+1 and t+2; for t+3 through t+5 expected EPS uses the mean long-term growth forecast times prior-year EPS. Expected book value rolls forward prior book value plus expected EPS less expected dividends; expected dividends equal expected EPS times PAYOUT. PAYOUT averages the prior three years’ dividend-to-net-income ratio; for this calculation, negative net income is set to 6% of total assets. Cost of equity is the greater of the market-model return estimate and the 10-year Treasury rate; negative AV is set to zero. The supplied reading text has a corrupted summation glyph in the printed A1 value formula; the candidate transcription is documented in the worker report and remains unverified.
dependent_variable.formula: VDIF_t=(AV_t−P_t)/P_t

evidence.quote: Specifically, we first set VDIF = ( AVt  - Pt ) /Pt, where Pt is share price and
E t ( EPSt + i ) equals time t mean analyst forecast of earnings per share for year t + i, for i = 1 , 2.
Thus, we set E t ( EPSt + i ) equal to the time t mean analyst long-term earnings growth forecast times EPSt + i −1, for i = 3 through 5.
E t ( BVE t + i ) equals BVE t + i −1 + E t ( EPSt + i ) − E t ( DIVt + i ), where DIVt is dividends in year t .
We set E t ( DIVt + i ) equal to E t ( EPSt + i ) × PAYOUT, where PAYOUT is the firm’s dividend payout ratio.

The firm’s cost of equity capital, r, equals the greater of R f + β ( Rm - R f ) or R f, where β is estimated from the market model, R f is the 10-year Treasury Bill rate, and ( Rm - R f ) is 7.6%, following Ibbotson Associates [1996].
If AVt is negative, we set it to zero.

We define the dividend payout ratio as the average of the prior three years ratio of dividends-to-net income. Consistent with Frankel and Lee [1998], among others, if net income in a particular year is negative, for purposes of this calculation, we set it equal to 6% of total assets.

estimation_procedure.description: Estimate a separate accounting function for each firm-year using the 16 previous quarterly observations. Table 1 describes 71,295 such fits, not 71,295 observations within one fit. To construct pairwise comparability, evaluate both firm i and firm j functions at the SAME firm-i quarterly return: fitted_Earnings_ii = alpha_i + beta_i*Return_i and fitted_Earnings_ij = alpha_j + beta_j*Return_i. CompAcct_ij is the negative average absolute difference between those predictions over the 16-quarter window. Rank peer values from highest to lowest: CompAcct4 is the mean for the four highest-comparability peers, and CompAcctInd is the median across peers in the same two-digit SIC industry. The peer universe has fiscal year ends in March, June, September or December. Reported pairing exclusions remove holding/Group/ADR/LP-name variants and highly similar firm names using five-or-more letter words while avoiding generic words; the complete implementation/stop-word list is not reported. These subsequent predictions/aggregations are deterministic uses of the same fitted function, not additional estimated regression equations. No December-only analyst sample restriction is imported into the broader fit sample.

models.sample_description: Two-digit SIC industry-year matched-pairing panel, 1983–1995. independent_variables.definition: Differential relative firm-specific return variation: the high-Ψ minus low-Ψ group ratio of summed residual sums of squares to summed total sums of squares from weekly firm-return fits, aggregated within each two-digit SIC industry-year. evidence.quote: It is calculated as the ratio of residual sum of squares to total sum of squares (residual plus explained sum of squares) from the regressions of firm return on market and two-digit industry value-weighted indexes (constructed excluding own return) performed on weekly data.

independent_variables.name: TRANS
independent_variables.definition: Aggregate firm-level transparency measure: average of the scaled percentile ranks of ANALYST, R ACCURACY, INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC); if R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the remaining four components. ANALYST is the average number of analysts forecasting year t earnings over the SMTH estimation period. R ACCURACY is the residual from a fitted regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS; ACCURACY is the negative absolute I/B/E/S mean annual forecast error (mean forecast less reported actual earnings) scaled by prior fiscal-year-end stock price, SUE is absolute unexpected earnings (actual less mean forecast) scaled by prior-year price, and BIAS is the signed I/B/E/S forecast error scaled by prior fiscal-year-end price. INTGAAP S indicates a firm reporting under IFRS or U.S. GAAP with above-median transparency excluding INTGAAP and a mandatory or voluntary international-standards adoption. BIG5 indicates a Big-5-affiliated auditor. DIS SMTHC is the average scaled percentile rank of the residuals from the SMTH1 and SMTH2 fundamental-smoothness fits. The percentile-rank reference population and scaling convention are not reported.
independent_variables.formula: average(scaled_percentile_rank(ANALYST), scaled_percentile_rank(R ACCURACY), scaled_percentile_rank(INTGAAP S), scaled_percentile_rank(BIG5), scaled_percentile_rank(1−DIS SMTHC)); when R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the four remaining scaled percentile ranks

evidence.quote: TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

Accordingly, we define serious adopters ( INTGAAP S = 1), our final transparency indicator, to be adopting firms that have an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable) and either a) are mandated by country regulations to adopt international accounting standards, or b) voluntarily adopted international standards
ANALYST is equal to the average number of analysts making a forecast for year t ’s earnings over the SMTH estimation period

ACCURACY is the absolute value of the forecast error multiplied by −1, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S

BIAS is the signed value of the forecast error, scaled by stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S
SUE is the absolute value of unexpected earnings, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior year, where unexpected earnings is actual earnings less the mean analyst forecast
BIG5 is equal to one if the firm is audited by a “BIG5” auditing firm, and zero otherwise
R ACCURACY is equal to the residual value from a regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS.

INTGAAP S is an indicator variable equal to one if the firm reports under IFRS or U.S. GAAP during the year and has an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable).
DIS SMTHC is the average of the scaled percentile rank of DIS SMTH1 and DIS SMTH2, where DIS SMTH1 & 2 are the residual values from the fundamental earnings smoothness model described in appendix A.

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

estimation_procedure.description: Table 5 Panel A reports a separate OLS fit for the LOW ASDI partition; its grouping dimension is ASDI relative to the sample median. scope.quote: Our primary interest is in variation in the strength of the relation between firm-level transparency and liquidity across economic environments.
one of our primary goals is to document the extent to which the importance of firm-level transparency varies with a firm’s characteristics and its environment.

We consider three aspects of the firm’s environment that are likely to increase investor demand for information: poor country-level institutions, time periods with high aggregate levels of investor uncertainty, and firm-level governance problems.

independent_variables.name: TRANS
independent_variables.definition: Aggregate firm-level transparency measure: average of the scaled percentile ranks of ANALYST, R ACCURACY, INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC); if R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the remaining four components. ANALYST is the average number of analysts forecasting year t earnings over the SMTH estimation period. R ACCURACY is the residual from a fitted regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS; ACCURACY is the negative absolute I/B/E/S mean annual forecast error (mean forecast less reported actual earnings) scaled by prior fiscal-year-end stock price, SUE is absolute unexpected earnings (actual less mean forecast) scaled by prior-year price, and BIAS is the signed I/B/E/S forecast error scaled by prior fiscal-year-end price. INTGAAP S indicates a firm reporting under IFRS or U.S. GAAP with above-median transparency excluding INTGAAP and a mandatory or voluntary international-standards adoption. BIG5 indicates a Big-5-affiliated auditor. DIS SMTHC is the average scaled percentile rank of the residuals from the SMTH1 and SMTH2 fundamental-smoothness fits. The percentile-rank reference population and scaling convention are not reported.
independent_variables.formula: average(scaled_percentile_rank(ANALYST), scaled_percentile_rank(R ACCURACY), scaled_percentile_rank(INTGAAP S), scaled_percentile_rank(BIG5), scaled_percentile_rank(1−DIS SMTHC)); when R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the four remaining scaled percentile ranks

evidence.quote: TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

Accordingly, we define serious adopters ( INTGAAP S = 1), our final transparency indicator, to be adopting firms that have an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable) and either a) are mandated by country regulations to adopt international accounting standards, or b) voluntarily adopted international standards
ANALYST is equal to the average number of analysts making a forecast for year t ’s earnings over the SMTH estimation period

ACCURACY is the absolute value of the forecast error multiplied by −1, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S

BIAS is the signed value of the forecast error, scaled by stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S
SUE is the absolute value of unexpected earnings, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior year, where unexpected earnings is actual earnings less the mean analyst forecast
BIG5 is equal to one if the firm is audited by a “BIG5” auditing firm, and zero otherwise
R ACCURACY is equal to the residual value from a regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS.

INTGAAP S is an indicator variable equal to one if the firm reports under IFRS or U.S. GAAP during the year and has an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable).
DIS SMTHC is the average of the scaled percentile rank of DIS SMTH1 and DIS SMTH2, where DIS SMTH1 & 2 are the residual values from the fundamental earnings smoothness model described in appendix A.

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

fixed_effects.details: Country, industry, and year fixed effects; industry fixed effects use the firm’s two-digit ICB code.

evidence.quote: We include country (C), industry (I), and year (Y) fixed effects in all models, but do not report the coefficients. Industry fixed effects are based on the firm’s two-digit ICB code.

standard_errors.details: Two-sided p-values use robust standard errors clustered at firm level (one clustering dimension); this fit has 10,967 firm clusters. Table 5 cross-partition tests use a different country-industry cluster, as recorded in estimation_procedure.

evidence.quote: The table reports OLS coefficient estimates and p-values (two-sided) based on robust standard errors clustered at the firm-level.

estimation_procedure.description: Table 5 Panel A reports a separate OLS fit for the HIGH ASDI partition; its grouping dimension is ASDI relative to the sample median. The table’s cross-partition HIGH–LOW coefficient test is based on a fully interacted specification that lets all variables and fixed effects vary by partition and clusters standard errors at the country-industry level; the table reports 589 country-industry clusters for this comparison. This comparison fit is described in the source but has no separately printed full equation.
grouping_variables: ASDI relative to the country-level sample median

evidence.quote: In panel A, regressions are run separately for high and low ASDI, DISCLOSE, and MEDIA subgroups

Assessments of significance across partitions are made based on the standard errors (clustered at the country-industry level) of the coefficient on the interaction of TRANS and the partitioning variable in a fully interacted specification, i.e., we allow each variable, including the fixed effects, to vary by the partitioning variable.

preprocessing.description: All continuous nonlogarithmic variables are truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles.

scope.quote: Our primary interest is in variation in the strength of the relation between firm-level transparency and liquidity across economic environments.
one of our primary goals is to document the extent to which the importance of firm-level transparency varies with a firm’s characteristics and its environment.

We consider three aspects of the firm’s environment that are likely to increase investor demand for information: poor country-level institutions, time periods with high aggregate levels of investor uncertainty, and firm-level governance problems.

independent_variables.name: TRANS
independent_variables.definition: Aggregate firm-level transparency measure: average of the scaled percentile ranks of ANALYST, R ACCURACY, INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC); if R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the remaining four components. ANALYST is the average number of analysts forecasting year t earnings over the SMTH estimation period. R ACCURACY is the residual from a fitted regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS; ACCURACY is the negative absolute I/B/E/S mean annual forecast error (mean forecast less reported actual earnings) scaled by prior fiscal-year-end stock price, SUE is absolute unexpected earnings (actual less mean forecast) scaled by prior-year price, and BIAS is the signed I/B/E/S forecast error scaled by prior fiscal-year-end price. INTGAAP S indicates a firm reporting under IFRS or U.S. GAAP with above-median transparency excluding INTGAAP and a mandatory or voluntary international-standards adoption. BIG5 indicates a Big-5-affiliated auditor. DIS SMTHC is the average scaled percentile rank of the residuals from the SMTH1 and SMTH2 fundamental-smoothness fits. The percentile-rank reference population and scaling convention are not reported.
independent_variables.formula: average(scaled_percentile_rank(ANALYST), scaled_percentile_rank(R ACCURACY), scaled_percentile_rank(INTGAAP S), scaled_percentile_rank(BIG5), scaled_percentile_rank(1−DIS SMTHC)); when R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the four remaining scaled percentile ranks

evidence.quote: TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

Accordingly, we define serious adopters ( INTGAAP S = 1), our final transparency indicator, to be adopting firms that have an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable) and either a) are mandated by country regulations to adopt international accounting standards, or b) voluntarily adopted international standards
ANALYST is equal to the average number of analysts making a forecast for year t ’s earnings over the SMTH estimation period

ACCURACY is the absolute value of the forecast error multiplied by −1, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S

BIAS is the signed value of the forecast error, scaled by stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S
SUE is the absolute value of unexpected earnings, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior year, where unexpected earnings is actual earnings less the mean analyst forecast
BIG5 is equal to one if the firm is audited by a “BIG5” auditing firm, and zero otherwise
R ACCURACY is equal to the residual value from a regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS.

INTGAAP S is an indicator variable equal to one if the firm reports under IFRS or U.S. GAAP during the year and has an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable).
DIS SMTHC is the average of the scaled percentile rank of DIS SMTH1 and DIS SMTH2, where DIS SMTH1 & 2 are the residual values from the fundamental earnings smoothness model described in appendix A.

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

evidence.quote: We include country (C), industry (I), and year (Y) fixed effects in all models, but do not report the coefficients. Industry fixed effects are based on the firm’s two-digit ICB code.

standard_errors.details: Two-sided p-values use robust standard errors clustered at firm level (one clustering dimension); this fit has 4,940 firm clusters. Table 5 cross-partition tests use a different country-industry cluster, as recorded in estimation_procedure.

evidence.quote: The table reports OLS coefficient estimates and p-values (two-sided) based on robust standard errors clustered at the firm-level.

estimation_procedure.description: Table 5 Panel A reports a separate OLS fit for the LOW DISCLOSE partition; its grouping dimension is DISCLOSE relative to the sample median. The table’s cross-partition HIGH–LOW coefficient test is based on a fully interacted specification that lets all variables and fixed effects vary by partition and clusters standard errors at the country-industry level; the table reports 589 country-industry clusters for this comparison. This comparison fit is described in the source but has no separately printed full equation.
grouping_variables: DISCLOSE relative to the country-level sample median

evidence.quote: In panel A, regressions are run separately for high and low ASDI, DISCLOSE, and MEDIA subgroups

Assessments of significance across partitions are made based on the standard errors (clustered at the country-industry level) of the coefficient on the interaction of TRANS and the partitioning variable in a fully interacted specification, i.e., we allow each variable, including the fixed effects, to vary by the partitioning variable.

preprocessing.description: All continuous nonlogarithmic variables are truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles.

evidence.quote: All continuous nonlogarithmic variables are truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles.

scope.quote: Our primary interest is in variation in the strength of the relation between firm-level transparency and liquidity across economic environments.
one of our primary goals is to document the extent to which the importance of firm-level transparency varies with a firm’s characteristics and its environment.

We consider three aspects of the firm’s environment that are likely to increase investor demand for information: poor country-level institutions, time periods with high aggregate levels of investor uncertainty, and firm-level governance problems.
Our primary interest is in comparing the strength of the relation between TRANS and ILLIQ across the high and low ASDI, DISCLOSE, and MEDIA subsamples.

method.quote: The table reports OLS coefficient estimates and p-values (two-sided) based on robust standard errors clustered at the firm-level.

independent_variables.name: TRANS
independent_variables.definition: Aggregate firm-level transparency measure: average of the scaled percentile ranks of ANALYST, R ACCURACY, INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC); if R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the remaining four components. ANALYST is the average number of analysts forecasting year t earnings over the SMTH estimation period. R ACCURACY is the residual from a fitted regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS; ACCURACY is the negative absolute I/B/E/S mean annual forecast error (mean forecast less reported actual earnings) scaled by prior fiscal-year-end stock price, SUE is absolute unexpected earnings (actual less mean forecast) scaled by prior-year price, and BIAS is the signed I/B/E/S forecast error scaled by prior fiscal-year-end price. INTGAAP S indicates a firm reporting under IFRS or U.S. GAAP with above-median transparency excluding INTGAAP and a mandatory or voluntary international-standards adoption. BIG5 indicates a Big-5-affiliated auditor. DIS SMTHC is the average scaled percentile rank of the residuals from the SMTH1 and SMTH2 fundamental-smoothness fits. The percentile-rank reference population and scaling convention are not reported.
independent_variables.formula: average(scaled_percentile_rank(ANALYST), scaled_percentile_rank(R ACCURACY), scaled_percentile_rank(INTGAAP S), scaled_percentile_rank(BIG5), scaled_percentile_rank(1−DIS SMTHC)); when R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the four remaining scaled percentile ranks

evidence.quote: TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

Accordingly, we define serious adopters ( INTGAAP S = 1), our final transparency indicator, to be adopting firms that have an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable) and either a) are mandated by country regulations to adopt international accounting standards, or b) voluntarily adopted international standards
ANALYST is equal to the average number of analysts making a forecast for year t ’s earnings over the SMTH estimation period

ACCURACY is the absolute value of the forecast error multiplied by −1, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S

BIAS is the signed value of the forecast error, scaled by stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S
SUE is the absolute value of unexpected earnings, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior year, where unexpected earnings is actual earnings less the mean analyst forecast
BIG5 is equal to one if the firm is audited by a “BIG5” auditing firm, and zero otherwise
R ACCURACY is equal to the residual value from a regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS.

INTGAAP S is an indicator variable equal to one if the firm reports under IFRS or U.S. GAAP during the year and has an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable).
DIS SMTHC is the average of the scaled percentile rank of DIS SMTH1 and DIS SMTH2, where DIS SMTH1 & 2 are the residual values from the fundamental earnings smoothness model described in appendix A.

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

evidence.quote: The table reports OLS coefficient estimates and p-values (two-sided) based on robust standard errors clustered at the firm-level.

estimation_procedure.description: Table 5 Panel A reports a separate OLS fit for the HIGH DISCLOSE partition; its grouping dimension is DISCLOSE relative to the sample median. The table’s cross-partition HIGH–LOW coefficient test is based on a fully interacted specification that lets all variables and fixed effects vary by partition and clusters standard errors at the country-industry level; the table reports 589 country-industry clusters for this comparison. This comparison fit is described in the source but has no separately printed full equation.
grouping_variables: DISCLOSE relative to the country-level sample median

evidence.quote: In panel A, regressions are run separately for high and low ASDI, DISCLOSE, and MEDIA subgroups

Assessments of significance across partitions are made based on the standard errors (clustered at the country-industry level) of the coefficient on the interaction of TRANS and the partitioning variable in a fully interacted specification, i.e., we allow each variable, including the fixed effects, to vary by the partitioning variable.

preprocessing.description: All continuous nonlogarithmic variables are truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles.

evidence.quote: All continuous nonlogarithmic variables are truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles.

scope.quote: Our primary interest is in variation in the strength of the relation between firm-level transparency and liquidity across economic environments.
one of our primary goals is to document the extent to which the importance of firm-level transparency varies with a firm’s characteristics and its environment.

We consider three aspects of the firm’s environment that are likely to increase investor demand for information: poor country-level institutions, time periods with high aggregate levels of investor uncertainty, and firm-level governance problems.
Our primary interest is in comparing the strength of the relation between TRANS and ILLIQ across the high and low ASDI, DISCLOSE, and MEDIA subsamples.

method.quote: The table reports OLS coefficient estimates and p-values (two-sided) based on robust standard errors clustered at the firm-level.

equation.quote: ILLIQ t = αt + β1LNMVEt + β2BM t + β3LOSSt + β4STDRET t + β5ADR EX t + β6ADR NEX t + β7%CLHLD Ht + β8%CLHLD Lt + β9FUND SMTHCt + β10TRANSt + FIXED EFFECTS + εt

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.

sample.quote: The sample comprises firm-year observations between 1994 and 2007.

dependencies.quote: FUND SMTHC is the average of the scaled percentile rank of FUND SMTH1 and FUND SMTH2, where FUND SMTH1 & 2 are the predicted values from the fundamental earnings smoothness model described in appendix A.

R ACCURACY is equal to the residual value from a regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS.

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.

dependent_variable.name: ILLIQ
dependent_variable.definition: Combined illiquidity measure: average of the scaled percentile ranks of available ZERORET and LN(BIDASK); if BIDASK is unavailable, use the percentile rank of ZERORET. ZERORET is the percent of fiscal-year trading days with no price change. BIDASK is the fiscal-year median relative bid–ask spread, (ASK−BID)/((ASK+BID)/2), and LN(BIDASK) is the transformed component. The reference population and scaling convention for “scaled percentile rank” are not reported.
dependent_variable.formula: average(scaled_percentile_rank(ZERORET), scaled_percentile_rank(ln(BIDASK))) when BIDASK available; scaled_percentile_rank(ZERORET) otherwise

ZERORET is equal to the percent of days in the fiscal year for which the stock price does not change
BIDASK is equal to the median bid ask spread over the fiscal year, where the bid ask spread is equal to (ASK−BID)/((ASK+BID)/2)).

independent_variables.name: TRANS
independent_variables.definition: Aggregate firm-level transparency measure: average of the scaled percentile ranks of ANALYST, R ACCURACY, INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC); if R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the remaining four components. ANALYST is the average number of analysts forecasting year t earnings over the SMTH estimation period. R ACCURACY is the residual from a fitted regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS; ACCURACY is the negative absolute I/B/E/S mean annual forecast error (mean forecast less reported actual earnings) scaled by prior fiscal-year-end stock price, SUE is absolute unexpected earnings (actual less mean forecast) scaled by prior-year price, and BIAS is the signed I/B/E/S forecast error scaled by prior fiscal-year-end price. INTGAAP S indicates a firm reporting under IFRS or U.S. GAAP with above-median transparency excluding INTGAAP and a mandatory or voluntary international-standards adoption. BIG5 indicates a Big-5-affiliated auditor. DIS SMTHC is the average scaled percentile rank of the residuals from the SMTH1 and SMTH2 fundamental-smoothness fits. The percentile-rank reference population and scaling convention are not reported.
independent_variables.formula: average(scaled_percentile_rank(ANALYST), scaled_percentile_rank(R ACCURACY), scaled_percentile_rank(INTGAAP S), scaled_percentile_rank(BIG5), scaled_percentile_rank(1−DIS SMTHC)); when R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the four remaining scaled percentile ranks

evidence.quote: TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

Accordingly, we define serious adopters ( INTGAAP S = 1), our final transparency indicator, to be adopting firms that have an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable) and either a) are mandated by country regulations to adopt international accounting standards, or b) voluntarily adopted international standards
ANALYST is equal to the average number of analysts making a forecast for year t ’s earnings over the SMTH estimation period

ACCURACY is the absolute value of the forecast error multiplied by −1, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S

BIAS is the signed value of the forecast error, scaled by stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S
SUE is the absolute value of unexpected earnings, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior year, where unexpected earnings is actual earnings less the mean analyst forecast
BIG5 is equal to one if the firm is audited by a “BIG5” auditing firm, and zero otherwise
R ACCURACY is equal to the residual value from a regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS.

INTGAAP S is an indicator variable equal to one if the firm reports under IFRS or U.S. GAAP during the year and has an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable).
DIS SMTHC is the average of the scaled percentile rank of DIS SMTH1 and DIS SMTH2, where DIS SMTH1 & 2 are the residual values from the fundamental earnings smoothness model described in appendix A.

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.
