independent_variables.name: TRANS
independent_variables.definition: Aggregate firm-level transparency measure: average of the scaled percentile ranks of ANALYST, R ACCURACY, INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC); if R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the remaining four components. ANALYST is the average number of analysts forecasting year t earnings over the SMTH estimation period. R ACCURACY is the residual from a fitted regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS; ACCURACY is the negative absolute I/B/E/S mean annual forecast error (mean forecast less reported actual earnings) scaled by prior fiscal-year-end stock price, SUE is absolute unexpected earnings (actual less mean forecast) scaled by prior-year price, and BIAS is the signed I/B/E/S forecast error scaled by prior fiscal-year-end price. INTGAAP S indicates a firm reporting under IFRS or U.S. GAAP with above-median transparency excluding INTGAAP and a mandatory or voluntary international-standards adoption. BIG5 indicates a Big-5-affiliated auditor. DIS SMTHC is the average scaled percentile rank of the residuals from the SMTH1 and SMTH2 fundamental-smoothness fits. The percentile-rank reference population and scaling convention are not reported.
independent_variables.formula: average(scaled_percentile_rank(ANALYST), scaled_percentile_rank(R ACCURACY), scaled_percentile_rank(INTGAAP S), scaled_percentile_rank(BIG5), scaled_percentile_rank(1−DIS SMTHC)); when R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the four remaining scaled percentile ranks

evidence.quote: TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

Accordingly, we define serious adopters ( INTGAAP S = 1), our final transparency indicator, to be adopting firms that have an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable) and either a) are mandated by country regulations to adopt international accounting standards, or b) voluntarily adopted international standards
ANALYST is equal to the average number of analysts making a forecast for year t ’s earnings over the SMTH estimation period

ACCURACY is the absolute value of the forecast error multiplied by −1, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S

BIAS is the signed value of the forecast error, scaled by stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S
SUE is the absolute value of unexpected earnings, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior year, where unexpected earnings is actual earnings less the mean analyst forecast
BIG5 is equal to one if the firm is audited by a “BIG5” auditing firm, and zero otherwise
R ACCURACY is equal to the residual value from a regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS.

INTGAAP S is an indicator variable equal to one if the firm reports under IFRS or U.S. GAAP during the year and has an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable).
DIS SMTHC is the average of the scaled percentile rank of DIS SMTH1 and DIS SMTH2, where DIS SMTH1 & 2 are the residual values from the fundamental earnings smoothness model described in appendix A.

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

independent_variables.name: TRANS
independent_variables.definition: Aggregate firm-level transparency measure: average of the scaled percentile ranks of ANALYST, R ACCURACY, INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC); if R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the remaining four components. ANALYST is the average number of analysts forecasting year t earnings over the SMTH estimation period. R ACCURACY is the residual from a fitted regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS; ACCURACY is the negative absolute I/B/E/S mean annual forecast error (mean forecast less reported actual earnings) scaled by prior fiscal-year-end stock price, SUE is absolute unexpected earnings (actual less mean forecast) scaled by prior-year price, and BIAS is the signed I/B/E/S forecast error scaled by prior fiscal-year-end price. INTGAAP S indicates a firm reporting under IFRS or U.S. GAAP with above-median transparency excluding INTGAAP and a mandatory or voluntary international-standards adoption. BIG5 indicates a Big-5-affiliated auditor. DIS SMTHC is the average scaled percentile rank of the residuals from the SMTH1 and SMTH2 fundamental-smoothness fits. The percentile-rank reference population and scaling convention are not reported.
independent_variables.formula: average(scaled_percentile_rank(ANALYST), scaled_percentile_rank(R ACCURACY), scaled_percentile_rank(INTGAAP S), scaled_percentile_rank(BIG5), scaled_percentile_rank(1−DIS SMTHC)); when R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the four remaining scaled percentile ranks

evidence.quote: TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

Accordingly, we define serious adopters ( INTGAAP S = 1), our final transparency indicator, to be adopting firms that have an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable) and either a) are mandated by country regulations to adopt international accounting standards, or b) voluntarily adopted international standards
ANALYST is equal to the average number of analysts making a forecast for year t ’s earnings over the SMTH estimation period

ACCURACY is the absolute value of the forecast error multiplied by −1, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S

BIAS is the signed value of the forecast error, scaled by stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S
SUE is the absolute value of unexpected earnings, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior year, where unexpected earnings is actual earnings less the mean analyst forecast
BIG5 is equal to one if the firm is audited by a “BIG5” auditing firm, and zero otherwise
R ACCURACY is equal to the residual value from a regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS.

INTGAAP S is an indicator variable equal to one if the firm reports under IFRS or U.S. GAAP during the year and has an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable).
DIS SMTHC is the average of the scaled percentile rank of DIS SMTH1 and DIS SMTH2, where DIS SMTH1 & 2 are the residual values from the fundamental earnings smoothness model described in appendix A.

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

estimation_procedure.description: Table 5 Panel B runs separate OLS regressions for GOV SCORE groups 0, 1, 2, and 3. The adjacent-group RIGHT–LEFT coefficient tests use fully interacted specifications that let every variable and fixed effect vary across the comparison, with country-industry clustered standard errors; the table reports 436, 348, and 201 country-industry clusters for the adjacent comparisons. The source does not print a separate full equation for those comparison fits.

evidence.quote: In panel B, regressions are run separately for GOV SCORE subgroups.

GOV SCORE is an aggregate variable composed of the three country-level institutional variables in panel A where a country receives a value of one for each of the individual institutional variables for which it is above the sample median with possible scores taking integer values between 0 and 3.

Assessments of significance across partitions are made based on the standard errors (clustered at the country-industry level) of the coefficient on the interaction of TRANS and the partitioning variable in a fully interacted specification, i.e., we allow each variable, including the fixed effects, to vary by the partitioning variable.

scope.quote: Our primary interest is in variation in the strength of the relation between firm-level transparency and liquidity across economic environments.
one of our primary goals is to document the extent to which the importance of firm-level transparency varies with a firm’s characteristics and its environment.

We consider three aspects of the firm’s environment that are likely to increase investor demand for information: poor country-level institutions, time periods with high aggregate levels of investor uncertainty, and firm-level governance problems.
There are two primary takeaways from this analysis.
the magnitude of the TRANS coefficient increases monotonically, moving across partitions from strongest to weakest overall governance environments.

independent_variables.name: TRANS
independent_variables.definition: Aggregate firm-level transparency measure: average of the scaled percentile ranks of ANALYST, R ACCURACY, INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC); if R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the remaining four components. ANALYST is the average number of analysts forecasting year t earnings over the SMTH estimation period. R ACCURACY is the residual from a fitted regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS; ACCURACY is the negative absolute I/B/E/S mean annual forecast error (mean forecast less reported actual earnings) scaled by prior fiscal-year-end stock price, SUE is absolute unexpected earnings (actual less mean forecast) scaled by prior-year price, and BIAS is the signed I/B/E/S forecast error scaled by prior fiscal-year-end price. INTGAAP S indicates a firm reporting under IFRS or U.S. GAAP with above-median transparency excluding INTGAAP and a mandatory or voluntary international-standards adoption. BIG5 indicates a Big-5-affiliated auditor. DIS SMTHC is the average scaled percentile rank of the residuals from the SMTH1 and SMTH2 fundamental-smoothness fits. The percentile-rank reference population and scaling convention are not reported.
independent_variables.formula: average(scaled_percentile_rank(ANALYST), scaled_percentile_rank(R ACCURACY), scaled_percentile_rank(INTGAAP S), scaled_percentile_rank(BIG5), scaled_percentile_rank(1−DIS SMTHC)); when R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the four remaining scaled percentile ranks

evidence.quote: TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

Accordingly, we define serious adopters ( INTGAAP S = 1), our final transparency indicator, to be adopting firms that have an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable) and either a) are mandated by country regulations to adopt international accounting standards, or b) voluntarily adopted international standards
ANALYST is equal to the average number of analysts making a forecast for year t ’s earnings over the SMTH estimation period

ACCURACY is the absolute value of the forecast error multiplied by −1, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S

BIAS is the signed value of the forecast error, scaled by stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S
SUE is the absolute value of unexpected earnings, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior year, where unexpected earnings is actual earnings less the mean analyst forecast
BIG5 is equal to one if the firm is audited by a “BIG5” auditing firm, and zero otherwise
R ACCURACY is equal to the residual value from a regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS.

INTGAAP S is an indicator variable equal to one if the firm reports under IFRS or U.S. GAAP during the year and has an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable).
DIS SMTHC is the average of the scaled percentile rank of DIS SMTH1 and DIS SMTH2, where DIS SMTH1 & 2 are the residual values from the fundamental earnings smoothness model described in appendix A.

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

standard_errors.details: Two-sided p-values use robust standard errors clustered at firm level (one clustering dimension); this fit has 3,255 firm clusters. Adjacent-group comparison tests cluster at country-industry level, as described in estimation_procedure.

evidence.quote: The table reports OLS coefficient estimates and p-values (two-sided) based on robust standard errors clustered at the firm-level.

estimation_procedure.description: Table 5 Panel B runs separate OLS regressions for GOV SCORE groups 0, 1, 2, and 3. The adjacent-group RIGHT–LEFT coefficient tests use fully interacted specifications that let every variable and fixed effect vary across the comparison, with country-industry clustered standard errors; the table reports 436, 348, and 201 country-industry clusters for the adjacent comparisons. The source does not print a separate full equation for those comparison fits.

evidence.quote: In panel B, regressions are run separately for GOV SCORE subgroups.

GOV SCORE is an aggregate variable composed of the three country-level institutional variables in panel A where a country receives a value of one for each of the individual institutional variables for which it is above the sample median with possible scores taking integer values between 0 and 3.

Assessments of significance across partitions are made based on the standard errors (clustered at the country-industry level) of the coefficient on the interaction of TRANS and the partitioning variable in a fully interacted specification, i.e., we allow each variable, including the fixed effects, to vary by the partitioning variable.

preprocessing.description: All continuous nonlogarithmic variables are truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles.

scope.quote: Our primary interest is in variation in the strength of the relation between firm-level transparency and liquidity across economic environments.
one of our primary goals is to document the extent to which the importance of firm-level transparency varies with a firm’s characteristics and its environment.

We consider three aspects of the firm’s environment that are likely to increase investor demand for information: poor country-level institutions, time periods with high aggregate levels of investor uncertainty, and firm-level governance problems.
There are two primary takeaways from this analysis.
the magnitude of the TRANS coefficient increases monotonically, moving across partitions from strongest to weakest overall governance environments.

dependent_variable.name: ILLIQ
dependent_variable.definition: Combined illiquidity measure: average of the scaled percentile ranks of available ZERORET and LN(BIDASK); if BIDASK is unavailable, use the percentile rank of ZERORET. ZERORET is the percent of fiscal-year trading days with no price change. BIDASK is the fiscal-year median relative bid–ask spread, (ASK−BID)/((ASK+BID)/2), and LN(BIDASK) is the transformed component. dependent_variable.formula: average(scaled_percentile_rank(ZERORET), scaled_percentile_rank(ln(BIDASK))) when BIDASK available; scaled_percentile_rank(ZERORET) otherwise

ZERORET is equal to the percent of days in the fiscal year for which the stock price does not change
BIDASK is equal to the median bid ask spread over the fiscal year, where the bid ask spread is equal to (ASK−BID)/((ASK+BID)/2)).

independent_variables.name: TRANS
independent_variables.definition: Aggregate firm-level transparency measure: average of the scaled percentile ranks of ANALYST, R ACCURACY, INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC); if R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the remaining four components. ANALYST is the average number of analysts forecasting year t earnings over the SMTH estimation period. R ACCURACY is the residual from a fitted regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS; ACCURACY is the negative absolute I/B/E/S mean annual forecast error (mean forecast less reported actual earnings) scaled by prior fiscal-year-end stock price, SUE is absolute unexpected earnings (actual less mean forecast) scaled by prior-year price, and BIAS is the signed I/B/E/S forecast error scaled by prior fiscal-year-end price. INTGAAP S indicates a firm reporting under IFRS or U.S. GAAP with above-median transparency excluding INTGAAP and a mandatory or voluntary international-standards adoption. BIG5 indicates a Big-5-affiliated auditor. DIS SMTHC is the average scaled percentile rank of the residuals from the SMTH1 and SMTH2 fundamental-smoothness fits. The percentile-rank reference population and scaling convention are not reported.
independent_variables.formula: average(scaled_percentile_rank(ANALYST), scaled_percentile_rank(R ACCURACY), scaled_percentile_rank(INTGAAP S), scaled_percentile_rank(BIG5), scaled_percentile_rank(1−DIS SMTHC)); when R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the four remaining scaled percentile ranks

evidence.quote: TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

Accordingly, we define serious adopters ( INTGAAP S = 1), our final transparency indicator, to be adopting firms that have an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable) and either a) are mandated by country regulations to adopt international accounting standards, or b) voluntarily adopted international standards
ANALYST is equal to the average number of analysts making a forecast for year t ’s earnings over the SMTH estimation period

ACCURACY is the absolute value of the forecast error multiplied by −1, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S

BIAS is the signed value of the forecast error, scaled by stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S
SUE is the absolute value of unexpected earnings, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior year, where unexpected earnings is actual earnings less the mean analyst forecast
BIG5 is equal to one if the firm is audited by a “BIG5” auditing firm, and zero otherwise
R ACCURACY is equal to the residual value from a regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS.

INTGAAP S is an indicator variable equal to one if the firm reports under IFRS or U.S. GAAP during the year and has an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable).
DIS SMTHC is the average of the scaled percentile rank of DIS SMTH1 and DIS SMTH2, where DIS SMTH1 & 2 are the residual values from the fundamental earnings smoothness model described in appendix A.

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

Assessments of significance across partitions are made based on the standard errors (clustered at the country-industry level) of the coefficient on the interaction of TRANS and the partitioning variable in a fully interacted specification, i.e., we allow each variable, including the fixed effects, to vary by the partitioning variable.

scope.quote: Our primary interest is in variation in the strength of the relation between firm-level transparency and liquidity across economic environments.
one of our primary goals is to document the extent to which the importance of firm-level transparency varies with a firm’s characteristics and its environment.

We consider three aspects of the firm’s environment that are likely to increase investor demand for information: poor country-level institutions, time periods with high aggregate levels of investor uncertainty, and firm-level governance problems.
There are two primary takeaways from this analysis.
the magnitude of the TRANS coefficient increases monotonically, moving across partitions from strongest to weakest overall governance environments.

independent_variables.name: TRANS
independent_variables.definition: Aggregate firm-level transparency measure: average of the scaled percentile ranks of ANALYST, R ACCURACY, INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC); if R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the remaining four components. ANALYST is the average number of analysts forecasting year t earnings over the SMTH estimation period. R ACCURACY is the residual from a fitted regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS; ACCURACY is the negative absolute I/B/E/S mean annual forecast error (mean forecast less reported actual earnings) scaled by prior fiscal-year-end stock price, SUE is absolute unexpected earnings (actual less mean forecast) scaled by prior-year price, and BIAS is the signed I/B/E/S forecast error scaled by prior fiscal-year-end price. INTGAAP S indicates a firm reporting under IFRS or U.S. GAAP with above-median transparency excluding INTGAAP and a mandatory or voluntary international-standards adoption. BIG5 indicates a Big-5-affiliated auditor. DIS SMTHC is the average scaled percentile rank of the residuals from the SMTH1 and SMTH2 fundamental-smoothness fits. The percentile-rank reference population and scaling convention are not reported.
independent_variables.formula: average(scaled_percentile_rank(ANALYST), scaled_percentile_rank(R ACCURACY), scaled_percentile_rank(INTGAAP S), scaled_percentile_rank(BIG5), scaled_percentile_rank(1−DIS SMTHC)); when R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the four remaining scaled percentile ranks

evidence.quote: TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

Accordingly, we define serious adopters ( INTGAAP S = 1), our final transparency indicator, to be adopting firms that have an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable) and either a) are mandated by country regulations to adopt international accounting standards, or b) voluntarily adopted international standards
ANALYST is equal to the average number of analysts making a forecast for year t ’s earnings over the SMTH estimation period

ACCURACY is the absolute value of the forecast error multiplied by −1, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S

BIAS is the signed value of the forecast error, scaled by stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S
SUE is the absolute value of unexpected earnings, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior year, where unexpected earnings is actual earnings less the mean analyst forecast
BIG5 is equal to one if the firm is audited by a “BIG5” auditing firm, and zero otherwise
R ACCURACY is equal to the residual value from a regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS.

INTGAAP S is an indicator variable equal to one if the firm reports under IFRS or U.S. GAAP during the year and has an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable).
DIS SMTHC is the average of the scaled percentile rank of DIS SMTH1 and DIS SMTH2, where DIS SMTH1 & 2 are the residual values from the fundamental earnings smoothness model described in appendix A.

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

estimation_procedure.description: Table 5 Panel B runs separate OLS regressions for GOV SCORE groups 0, 1, 2, and 3. The adjacent-group RIGHT–LEFT coefficient tests use fully interacted specifications that let every variable and fixed effect vary across the comparison, with country-industry clustered standard errors; the table reports 436, 348, and 201 country-industry clusters for the adjacent comparisons. The source does not print a separate full equation for those comparison fits.

evidence.quote: In panel B, regressions are run separately for GOV SCORE subgroups.

GOV SCORE is an aggregate variable composed of the three country-level institutional variables in panel A where a country receives a value of one for each of the individual institutional variables for which it is above the sample median with possible scores taking integer values between 0 and 3.

Assessments of significance across partitions are made based on the standard errors (clustered at the country-industry level) of the coefficient on the interaction of TRANS and the partitioning variable in a fully interacted specification, i.e., we allow each variable, including the fixed effects, to vary by the partitioning variable.

scope.quote: Our primary interest is in variation in the strength of the relation between firm-level transparency and liquidity across economic environments.
one of our primary goals is to document the extent to which the importance of firm-level transparency varies with a firm’s characteristics and its environment.

We consider three aspects of the firm’s environment that are likely to increase investor demand for information: poor country-level institutions, time periods with high aggregate levels of investor uncertainty, and firm-level governance problems.
There are two primary takeaways from this analysis.
the magnitude of the TRANS coefficient increases monotonically, moving across partitions from strongest to weakest overall governance environments.

independent_variables.name: TRANS
independent_variables.definition: Aggregate firm-level transparency measure: average of the scaled percentile ranks of ANALYST, R ACCURACY, INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC); if R ACCURACY is unavailable, average the remaining four components. ANALYST is the average number of analysts forecasting year t earnings over the SMTH estimation period. R ACCURACY is the residual from a fitted regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS; ACCURACY is the negative absolute I/B/E/S mean annual forecast error (mean forecast less reported actual earnings) scaled by prior fiscal-year-end stock price, SUE is absolute unexpected earnings (actual less mean forecast) scaled by prior-year price, and BIAS is the signed I/B/E/S forecast error scaled by prior fiscal-year-end price. scope.quote: Our primary interest is in variation in the strength of the relation between firm-level transparency and liquidity across economic environments.

We consider three aspects of the firm’s environment that are likely to increase investor demand for information: poor country-level institutions, time periods with high aggregate levels of investor uncertainty, and firm-level governance problems.
As a result, the question we ask is whether, following a month of high country-level uncertainty, firm-level illiquidity is more sensitive to transparency.

dependent_variable.definition: Combined illiquidity measure: average of the scaled percentile ranks of available ZERORET and LN(BIDASK); if BIDASK is unavailable, use the percentile rank of ZERORET. ZERORET is the percent of fiscal-year trading days with no price change. BIDASK is the fiscal-year median relative bid–ask spread, (ASK−BID)/((ASK+BID)/2), and LN(BIDASK) is the transformed component. The reference population and scaling convention for “scaled percentile rank” are not reported.

independent_variables.name: %CLHLD H × TRANS
independent_variables.definition: Interaction between %CLHLD H (the closely held-share proportion when above the sample median, zero otherwise) and TRANS. TRANS averages the scaled ranks of analyst following, residual forecast accuracy, serious IFRS/U.S.-GAAP adoption, Big-5 auditor, and one minus discretionary smoothness; it falls back to four components when R ACCURACY is unavailable. The paper uses separate high- and low-ownership interaction terms in full-sample Table 7 column 1.
independent_variables.formula: %CLHLD_H × average(scaled_percentile_rank(ANALYST), scaled_percentile_rank(R ACCURACY), scaled_percentile_rank(INTGAAP S), scaled_percentile_rank(BIG5), scaled_percentile_rank(1−DIS SMTHC)); omit R ACCURACY when unavailable

evidence.quote: % CLHLD H is equal to the percentage of the firm’s shares that are closely held if that proportion is above the sample median value of % CLHLD, and zero otherwise

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY, INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1− DIS SMTHC ). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.

ILLIQ t = αt + β 1 LNMVE t + β 2 BM t + β 3 LOSS t + β 4 STDRET t + β 5 ADR EX t + β 6 ADR NEX t


+ β 7% CLHLD ~~H~~ t + β 8% CLHLD ~~L~~ t + β 9 FUND ~~S~~ MTHC t


+ β 10% CLHLD H <sup>∗</sup> TRANS t + β 11% CLHLD ~~L~~ <sup>∗</sup> TRANS t + FIXED EFFECTS + εt

Accordingly, we define serious adopters ( INTGAAP S = 1), our final transparency indicator, to be adopting firms that have an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable) and either a) are mandated by country regulations to adopt international accounting standards, or b) voluntarily adopted international standards
ANALYST is equal to the average number of analysts making a forecast for year t ’s earnings over the SMTH estimation period

ACCURACY is the absolute value of the forecast error multiplied by −1, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S

BIAS is the signed value of the forecast error, scaled by stock price at the end of the prior fiscal year, where the forecast error is the I/B/E/S analysts’ mean annual earnings forecast less the actual earnings as reported by I/B/E/S
SUE is the absolute value of unexpected earnings, scaled by the stock price at the end of the prior year, where unexpected earnings is actual earnings less the mean analyst forecast
BIG5 is equal to one if the firm is audited by a “BIG5” auditing firm, and zero otherwise
R ACCURACY is equal to the residual value from a regression of ACCURACY on SUE and BIAS.

INTGAAP S is an indicator variable equal to one if the firm reports under IFRS or U.S. GAAP during the year and has an above-median aggregate transparency score (calculated excluding the INTGAAP variable).
DIS SMTHC is the average of the scaled percentile rank of DIS SMTH1 and DIS SMTH2, where DIS SMTH1 & 2 are the residual values from the fundamental earnings smoothness model described in appendix A.

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY , INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1−DIS SMTHC). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.
For parsimony in our later analyses, we combine the transparency variables to create an aggregate measure, TRANS, by ranking each variable, summing the percentile ranks, and taking the average.

research_interest_evidence.quote: More important for our hypotheses, the effect of transparency is particularly strong among firms with the highest levels of ownership concentration, suggesting that, while transparency is associated with greater liquidity at all levels of ownership, the effects are particularly pronounced when ownership concentration (and, hence, the extent of expected agency problems) is high.

independent_variables.research_interest_reason: The ownership-by-TRANS interaction is a stated research focus for whether transparency matters more when ownership concentration is high.

scope.quote: Our primary interest is in variation in the strength of the relation between firm-level transparency and liquidity across economic environments.
one of our primary goals is to document the extent to which the importance of firm-level transparency varies with a firm’s characteristics and its environment.

We consider three aspects of the firm’s environment that are likely to increase investor demand for information: poor country-level institutions, time periods with high aggregate levels of investor uncertainty, and firm-level governance problems.

To examine the effect of firm-level governance, we follow our earlier approach of including separate coefficients for low and high ownership concentration, but we now interact these piecewise coefficients with transparency.

equation.quote:
ILLIQ t = αt + β 1 LNMVE t + β 2 BM t + β 3 LOSS t + β 4 STDRET t + β 5 ADR EX t + β 6 ADR NEX t


+ β 7% CLHLD ~~H~~ t + β 8% CLHLD ~~L~~ t + β 9 FUND ~~S~~ MTHC t


+ β 10% CLHLD H <sup>∗</sup> TRANS t + β 11% CLHLD ~~L~~ <sup>∗</sup> TRANS t + FIXED EFFECTS + εt

The dependent variable in all models is ILLIQ, which is a combined measure of illiquidity equal to the average scaled percentile rank of the available liquidity measures, ZERORET and LN(BIDASK). If BIDASK is unavailable, ILLIQ captures the percentile rank of ZERORET .

TRANS is defined as the average of the scaled percentile rank of the variables: ANALYST, R ACCURACY, INTGAAP S, BIG5, and (1− DIS SMTHC ). If R ACCURACY is unavailable, TRANS captures the average percentile rank of the remaining four measures.

dependent_variable.definition: Negative of the ratio of the rolling standard deviation of income before extraordinary items scaled by average total assets to the rolling standard deviation of cash flow from operations scaled by average total assets; rolling calculation requires at least three and at most five years. Cash flow from operations equals income before extraordinary items minus accruals; accruals equal change in current assets minus change in current liabilities minus change in cash plus change in current debt in current liabilities minus depreciation and amortization. Larger values (closer to zero) indicate smoother earnings.
dependent_variable.formula: − SD(NI before extraordinary items / average total assets) / SD(CFO / average total assets)

Cash flow from operations is equal to net income before extraordinary items minus accruals, where accruals are defined as the change in current assets minus the change in current liabilities minus the change in cash plus the change in current debt in current liabilities minus depreciation and amortization expense.
Both smoothing measures ( SMTH1, SMTH2 ) are multiplied by negative one so that larger values represent firms with smoother earnings.

review_notes: Source-first scope: the authors state that their primary interest is variation in the transparency–liquidity relation across economic environments. Retain the full-control “when transparency matters most” family: Table 5 Panel A’s three country-institution splits (ASDI, DISCLOSE, MEDIA), Panel B’s four GOV SCORE groups, Table 6’s within-firm Model 3, and Table 7’s full-sample column 1. The partition regressions are the author’s chosen design for Table 5; Table 6 Model 3 is the within-firm time-uncertainty design; Table 7 column 1 is the full-sample piecewise-ownership interaction design.

Source inconsistency in Table 5: Table 2 and the Panel A note say lower MEDIA ranks correspond to better media penetration and define HIGH MEDIA as a rank above the median. The surrounding narrative describes the larger transparency coefficient as occurring in weak media-penetration environments, while the printed low-rank coefficient is more negative than the high-rank coefficient. GOV SCORE also counts above-median values for all three indices without stating a direction reversal for MEDIA, yet the discussion interprets the combined score as a governance-strength ranking. Preserve the formula and group labels; do not silently recode MEDIA.

independent_variables.name: PVINCOME
independent_variables.definition: Present value of expected future abnormal earnings for years t+1 through t+3. Expected EPS1, EPS2, and EPS3 are proxied by mean analyst forecasts AF1_post, AF2_post, and AF3_post issued after the year-t earnings announcement. AF3_post is the mean long-term earnings-growth forecast multiplied by AF2_post, as stated. Expected book value rolls forward as BVE1 = BVE + expected EPS1 - expected dividends1 and BVE2 = BVE1 + expected EPS2 - expected dividends2. Expected dividends in years 1 and 2 equal expected EPS times PAYOUT. PAYOUT is the prior-three-year average dividends-to-net-income ratio; if a year has negative net income, that year’s net income is set to 6% of total assets for this calculation. Cost of equity r is max(Rf + beta*(Rm-Rf), Rf); Rf is the year-end 10-year Treasury Note rate and Rm-Rf is fixed at 7.6%. Beta is the estimated coefficient on the CRSP value-weighted index including dividends from a market-model regression using daily returns over the 250 trading days before the year-t earnings announcement.
independent_variables.formula: PVINCOME_it = [E_t(EPS1_it) - r_it*E_t(BVE_it)]/(1+r_it) + [E_t(EPS2_it) - r_it*E_t(BVE1_it)]/(1+r_it)^2 + [E_t(EPS3_it) - r_it*E_t(BVE2_it)]/[(1+r_it)^2*r_it]; E_t(BVE1_it)=BVE_it+E_t(EPS1_it)-E_t(DIV1_it); E_t(BVE2_it)=E_t(BVE1_it)+E_t(EPS2_it)-E_t(DIV2_it); E_t(DIVj_it)=E_t(EPSj_it)*PAYOUT_it (j=1,2); r_it=max(Rf_t+beta_it*(Rm-Rf),Rf_t), Rm-Rf=7.6%.

dependent_variable.name: FError_{s,t+1}
dependent_variable.definition: Monthly analyst forecast error for year t+1 earnings: realized earnings for year t+1 minus the forecast in month s, divided by the stock price at the end of month 1. Month s=1 is the first month after announcement of year-t earnings, and the sequence runs through month 12 or the current-year earnings announcement. dependent_variable.formula: FError_{s,t+1} = (realized EPS_{t+1} - forecast EPS_{t+1,s}) / stock price_{month 1}.

evidence.quote: FError_(s,t+1) = beta_0 + beta_1*PortWCAcc_t + nu_(t+1).
Month s=1,...,12 is relative to the announcement of year-t earnings; forecast error for year-t+1 earnings is realized earnings minus forecast in month s, divided by stock price in month1 for every s.
PortWCAcc ranks annual working-capital-accrual portfolios, converted to[0,1].
WCAcc uses cash-flow-statement working-capital changes items302,303,304,305,307.
Our analyst forecast tests are conducted across fiscal months using the median IBES forecast of the current year annual earnings.

review_notes: Selected the principal intermediary-information question with its two explicitly central outcome families: analyst forecast errors (Table 5) and audit opinions (Table 7). For Table 7, the paper presents the contemporaneous and three subsequent opinion fits as one repeated-horizon specification; each horizon is retained with its year-0 accrual rank and contemporaneous controls. Excluded the initial Sloan replication/market-efficiency analyses (Tables 2–4), the SEC enforcement-action premise check (Table 6), and auditor changes (Table 8), which the authors explicitly describe as supplementary to the audit-opinion tests.

The Table 5 OLS equation and horizon scaling and the Table 7 logit equation/control formulas were checked against the independently verified appended transcriptions in the supplied reading and visually inspected on physical PDF pages 22 and 26.

The log base used for TA=log(Assets) is not specified in the source. Standard-error corrections/clustering are not reported for the selected models; these absent reporting details are distinguished from the stated OLS/logit estimators.
results_review_notes: The retained baseline family is Table 5 monthly OLS forecast-error fits for months 1–12 and Table 7 audit-opinion logit fits for t=0 through t+3. Other model tables, robustness tests, and later additional tests are excluded.

All six frozen RHS terms are mapped and have role evidence. Table 5 reports coefficient estimates and signed t-statistics; Table 7 reports estimates and p-values in parentheses. Coefficient-level standard errors are not directly printed.
Table 1 and Table 6 WCAcc summaries are included only for the continuous raw version of the retained PortWCAcc rank. Table 7 opinion category counts summarize the retained Unclean outcome.

No separate descriptive statistics are reported for the transformed PortWCAcc rank or the Table 7 control variables TA, CFO, LEV, and TIE. Figure 2 shows FError mean trajectories but prints no numeric point values; no values were digitized from it.
Table 5 exact degrees of freedom are unreported. Table 7 does not identify the coefficient-level test type, reference distribution, degrees of freedom, or sidedness; those are left unknown.

estimation_procedure.description: For each target firm-year, estimate the no-intercept proportional relation between the valuation base (share price P) and its single value driver using the restricted harmonic mean for comparable firms from the same middle-level IBES industry and fiscal year t. The target firm is removed from its comparable group (out-of-sample). Each industry-year group has at least five eligible observations, but because the fit is target-specific and per-fit counts are not reported, exact peer N is unknown. For TP columns, predict TP and subtract the target’s book debt per share to obtain predicted equity price. The target prediction error is (actual P − predicted equity value)/actual P; Table 2 reports pooled distributions across the 19,879 target firm-years.

For the results sample, value-driver ratios are trimmed at pooled 1st/99th percentiles, price is at least $2, all included multiples are positive, and each industry-year has at least five observations. independent_variables.name: P1_star_t
independent_variables.definition: Per-share residual-income intrinsic-value measure based on current book value and expected future abnormal earnings. EPS forecasts for years +1 and +2 are IBES means; for fewer than 5% of firm-years, IBES forecasts are available through year +5, and otherwise the mean long-term growth forecast g is applied recursively to the preceding mean forecast for years +3 to +5. Future book value follows the ex-ante clean-surplus relation: prior book value plus forecast EPS minus forecast dividends. Current indicated annual dividends divided by year+1 EPS forecast define the payout ratio; it is held constant for future dividends and winsorized to lie between 10% and 50%. Indicated annual dividends are four times the latest quarter’s declared dividends, and EPS1 is used as deflator. The discount rate k_t is the 10-year Treasury yield on April 1 of t+1 plus beta times a 5% equity risk premium; beta is the same-year median beta of firms in the same beta decile. The underlying beta estimator is not stated. P1 assumes abnormal earnings remain constant after year +5. The Appendix A terminal term is transcribed as printed with unbound s; its horizon/exponent meaning is unresolved.

review_notes: Source-first scope: the principal contribution is the valuation-performance ranking of a comprehensive set of value drivers. The authors call alternative multiple-computation approaches related issues; Table 2 Panel A is explicitly their primary results and uses the traditional no-intercept relation with harmonic-mean same-industry comparables. Retain the 17 actual fitted Panel A driver relations only. Table 2 Panels B/C and Table 3 compare other comparator sets or estimation procedures and are secondary to this principal question; later industry/year partitions and ancillary applications are excluded.

FCF and MCF are omitted because the authors say they were dropped from the remainder of the study before the main results owing to negative values and poor performance. P1*, P2*, P3*, ES1, and ES2 are included as value-driver RHS constructions in the retained price/TP fits, not as separate regressions; only the required return-beta fit is a supporting dependency.

All 17 retained baseline sample_size fields are null because 19,879 is the aggregate out-of-sample target/evaluation population, whereas each coefficient fit is target-specific and the exact peer count is not reported. The aggregate remains in sample_description.

The supplied verified reading provides complete P1*, P2*, P3*, ES1, ES2 formulas. P1’s printed terminal term has an unbound s, and P3’s Table 2 and Appendix A horizons conflict; these source issues remain flagged. The beta estimator/equation is also unreported, so no OLS assumption is made.

The pricing-error distributions in Table 2 are retained as primary model results, not duplicated as descriptive statistics.

independent_variables.name: D × Holder67
independent_variables.definition: CEO option-based overconfidence indicator: C̄ is the value of exercisable unexercised options divided by the number of exercisable unexercised options; X̄ is the fiscal-year-end stock price S̄ minus C̄. Holder67 equals one when C̄/X̄ exceeds 0.67 at least twice during the sample period, zero otherwise. A CEO is classified as overconfident beginning in the first qualifying fiscal year and remains so through the rest of the sample. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

evidence.quote:
NI t = β 0 + β 1 Dt + β 2 Ownt −1 + β 3 MTBt −1 + β 4 Leverage t −1

+ β 25 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Firm Sizet −1 + β 26 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Litigationt −1
+ β 27 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> OverCont −1 + βFirm + βYear + ε, (1)
D is an indicator variable set equal to one if Return is negative, zero otherwise
Return is the annual buy and hold return beginning four months after the prior fiscal year end
Holder67 is equal to one when the ratio of the value of options in-the-money to the average strike price exceeds 0.67 at least twice during the sample period, zero otherwise.

Consistent with Malmendier and Tate [2005] and Campbell et al. [2011], a CEO is classified as overconfident in the first fiscal year he/she exhibits the overconfident behavior and continues to be classified as overconfident for the remainder of the sample.

Second, we subtract ( C <sup> ̄</sup> ) from the stock price ( S <sup> ̄</sup> ) at the

independent_variables.definition: CEO purchase-based overconfidence indicator: net purchases are purchases minus sales; the measure equals one when net purchases are in the top quintile of all CEO net purchases and the purchases increase the CEO’s ownership in the firm by 10% during the fiscal year, zero otherwise. Purchases due to option exercises are excluded. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

evidence.quote:
NI t = β 0 + β 1 Dt + β 2 Ownt −1 + β 3 MTBt −1 + β 4 Leverage t −1

+ β 5 Firm Sizet −1 + β 6 Litigationt −1 + β 7 OverCont −1

+ β 8D t <sup>∗</sup> Ownt −1 + β 9 Dt <sup>∗</sup> MTBt −1 + β 10 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Leverage t −1
+ β 11D t <sup>∗</sup> Firm Sizet −1 + β 12 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Litigationt −1 + β 13 Dt <sup>∗</sup> OverCont −1

+ β 14 Returnt + β 15 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Ownt −1 + β 16 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> MTBt −1

+ β 17 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Leverage t −1 + β 18 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Firm Sizet −1

+ β 19 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Litigationt −1 + β 20 Returnt <sup>∗</sup> OverCont −1

+ β 21 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt + β 22 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> Ownt −1

+ β 27 Dt <sup>∗</sup> Returnt <sup>∗</sup> OverCont −1 + βFirm + βYear + ε, (1)
D is an indicator variable set equal to one if Return is negative, zero otherwise
Return is the annual buy and hold return beginning four months after the prior fiscal year end

Purchase is equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases (purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm by 10%, zero otherwise.

Thus, consistent with
Campbell et al. [2011], we classify a CEO as overconfident using a dichotomous variable where Purchase is set equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases
(purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm
by 10% during the fiscal year, otherwise zero.

In our Purchase measure, we exclude purchases due to option exercises, although our
results remain qualitatively similar to those reported if we include purchases due to option
transactions.

Purchase is equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases (purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm by 10%, zero otherwise.

Thus, consistent with
Campbell et al. [2011], we classify a CEO as overconfident using a dichotomous variable where Purchase is set equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases
(purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm
by 10% during the fiscal year, otherwise zero.

In our Purchase measure, we exclude purchases due to option exercises, although our
results remain qualitatively similar to those reported if we include purchases due to option
transactions.

Purchase is equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases (purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm by 10%, zero otherwise.

Thus, consistent with
Campbell et al. [2011], we classify a CEO as overconfident using a dichotomous variable where Purchase is set equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases
(purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm
by 10% during the fiscal year, otherwise zero.

In our Purchase measure, we exclude purchases due to option exercises, although our
results remain qualitatively similar to those reported if we include purchases due to option
transactions.

independent_variables.name: Purchase
independent_variables.definition: CEO purchase-based overconfidence indicator: net purchases are purchases minus sales; the measure equals one when net purchases are in the top quintile of all CEO net purchases and the purchases increase the CEO’s ownership in the firm by 10% during the fiscal year, zero otherwise. Purchases due to option exercises are excluded. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

evidence.quote:
Cont = β 0 + β 1 OverCont −1 + β 2 Ownt + β 3 MTBt + β 4 Leverage t

+ β 5 Firm Sizet + β 6 Litigationt + β 7 Sales Growtht + β 8 R & D ADt

+ β 9 CFO 1 + β 10 σ Revenuet + βFirm + βYear + ε, (6)

Purchase is equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases (purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm by 10%, zero otherwise.

Thus, consistent with
Campbell et al. [2011], we classify a CEO as overconfident using a dichotomous variable where Purchase is set equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases
(purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm
by 10% during the fiscal year, otherwise zero.

In our Purchase measure, we exclude purchases due to option exercises, although our
results remain qualitatively similar to those reported if we include purchases due to option
transactions.

independent_variables.definition: CEO option-based overconfidence indicator: C̄ is the value of exercisable unexercised options divided by the number of exercisable unexercised options; X̄ is the fiscal-year-end stock price S̄ minus C̄. Holder67 equals one when C̄/X̄ exceeds 0.67 at least twice during the sample period, zero otherwise. A CEO is classified as overconfident beginning in the first qualifying fiscal year and remains so through the rest of the sample. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

Holder67 is equal to one when the ratio of the value of options in-the-money to the average strike price exceeds 0.67 at least twice during the sample period, zero otherwise.

independent_variables.name: Purchase
independent_variables.definition: CEO purchase-based overconfidence indicator: net purchases are purchases minus sales; the measure equals one when net purchases are in the top quintile of all CEO net purchases and the purchases increase the CEO’s ownership in the firm by 10% during the fiscal year, zero otherwise. Purchases due to option exercises are excluded. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

evidence.quote:
Cont = β 0 + β 1 OverCont −1 + β 2 Ownt + β 3 MTBt + β 4 Leverage t

+ β 5 Firm Sizet + β 6 Litigationt + β 7 Sales Growtht + β 8 R & D ADt

+ β 9 CFO 1 + β 10 σ Revenuet + βFirm + βYear + ε, (6)

Purchase is equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases (purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm by 10%, zero otherwise.

Thus, consistent with
Campbell et al. [2011], we classify a CEO as overconfident using a dichotomous variable where Purchase is set equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases
(purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm
by 10% during the fiscal year, otherwise zero.

In our Purchase measure, we exclude purchases due to option exercises, although our
results remain qualitatively similar to those reported if we include purchases due to option
transactions.

method.quote: To test H1a and H1b, we use the firm-specific measures of conservatism in the following regression:

+ β 9 CFO 1 + β 10 σ Revenuet + βFirm + βYear + ε, (6)

Con-ACC is income before extraordinary items less cash flows from operations plus depreciation expense deflated by average total assets, and averaged over the previous three years, multiplied by negative one.

independent_variables.name: Holder67
independent_variables.definition: CEO option-based overconfidence indicator: C̄ is the value of exercisable unexercised options divided by the number of exercisable unexercised options; X̄ is the fiscal-year-end stock price S̄ minus C̄. Holder67 equals one when C̄/X̄ exceeds 0.67 at least twice during the sample period, zero otherwise. A CEO is classified as overconfident beginning in the first qualifying fiscal year and remains so through the rest of the sample. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

evidence.quote:
Cont = β 0 + β 1 OverCont −1 + β 2 Ownt + β 3 MTBt + β 4 Leverage t

+ β 5 Firm Sizet + β 6 Litigationt + β 7 Sales Growtht + β 8 R & D ADt

+ β 9 CFO 1 + β 10 σ Revenuet + βFirm + βYear + ε, (6)
Holder67 is equal to one when the ratio of the value of options in-the-money to the average strike price exceeds 0.67 at least twice during the sample period, zero otherwise.

Consistent with Malmendier and Tate [2005] and Campbell et al. [2011], a CEO is classified as overconfident in the first fiscal year he/she exhibits the overconfident behavior and continues to be classified as overconfident for the remainder of the sample.

First, we obtain the average value per option ( C <sup> ̄</sup> ) by dividing the

Second, we subtract ( C <sup> ̄</sup> ) from the stock price ( S <sup> ̄</sup> ) at the

fiscal year end to obtain the average exercise price per option ( X <sup> ̄</sup> ). Third,
we divide the average value per option ( C <sup> ̄</sup> ) by the average exercise price

we set Holder67 (overconfidence) equal to one when the ratio of the options in-the-money ( C <sup> ̄</sup> / X <sup> ̄</sup> ) exceeds 0.67 at least twice during the sample

independent_variables.name: Purchase
independent_variables.definition: CEO purchase-based overconfidence indicator: net purchases are purchases minus sales; the measure equals one when net purchases are in the top quintile of all CEO net purchases and the purchases increase the CEO’s ownership in the firm by 10% during the fiscal year, zero otherwise. Purchases due to option exercises are excluded. The selected proxy enters at t−1 in the baseline equation.

evidence.quote:
Cont = β 0 + β 1 OverCont −1 + β 2 Ownt + β 3 MTBt + β 4 Leverage t

+ β 5 Firm Sizet + β 6 Litigationt + β 7 Sales Growtht + β 8 R & D ADt

+ β 9 CFO 1 + β 10 σ Revenuet + βFirm + βYear + ε, (6)

Purchase is equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases (purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm by 10%, zero otherwise.

Thus, consistent with
Campbell et al. [2011], we classify a CEO as overconfident using a dichotomous variable where Purchase is set equal to one if the CEO’s net purchases
(purchases−sales) are in the top quintile of the distribution of net purchases by all CEO and those purchases increase their ownership in the firm
by 10% during the fiscal year, otherwise zero.

In our Purchase measure, we exclude purchases due to option exercises, although our
results remain qualitatively similar to those reported if we include purchases due to option
transactions.

review_notes: Source-first scope: the principal question is the relation between managerial overconfidence and accounting conservatism. Retain the full main regression family across the four stated conservatism outcomes and four overconfidence proxies: Table 4/equation (1), plus Tables 5–7/equation (6).

Tables 1–3 are descriptive/correlation analyses. Exclude the Table 8 external-monitoring interaction, CEO-turnover change tests, and other robustness or alternative-estimation exercises as separate follow-up questions.

Equation (5) uses Return_t and RET_t in different interaction blocks. Equation (2) and the page 9 definition identify these as the same annual return measure; the extraction preserves the printed notation and does not treat this as a substantive source conflict.

Underlying estimators are not named for the primary regressions or supporting fits. The Over-Invest construction fit also lacks its exact total-asset-growth formula, industry classification, fit sample, and per-fit N; the C-Score annual construction fit lacks the exact yearly sample and per-fit N.
results_review_notes: Tables 1 and 2 provide relevant raw descriptives for the retained baseline outcomes, proxies, controls, and asymmetric-timeliness variables. Table 3 is a correlation table and is not treated as descriptive statistics. Table 2 reports no exact p-values for its italicized 1% mean/median differences.
The CAPEX high-overconfidence Leverage median is visibly printed as 0.187 in Table 2; it is preserved verbatim rather than silently corrected.

equation.quote: To test HI, i.e., whether differences in domestic accounting standards relative to IAS adversely affect analyst earnings forecast accuracy, we estimate the following regression model:
(c) Set model: FERRORitI = a + j NUMit-1 + B2 MVEit-1 + 3 IASSETi + site

sample.quote: The final sample consists of 80 firms
The Sample is 80 Firms Adopting IAS in 1990, 1991, 1992, or 1993
t- 1 is the Year Prior to IAS Adoption

We eliminated seven firms from Italy and 22 firms from South Africa since firms from these countries could use IAS selectively rather than fully adopt IAS when their domestic-GAAP was silent on an accounting measurement or disclosure issue.
In addition, we deleted one firm from Bermuda because Bermuda did not have a set of domestic-GAAP to benchmark to IAS.
We deleted 53 of the remaining 133 firms voluntarily using IAS in 1993 because they were missing data

review_notes: Source-first scope selection: retain the three Table 4 / equation (1) pre-adoption H1 models, presented first in section 4.1, for the paper’s cross-country relation between domestic-GAAP differences from IAS and analyst forecast errors. Exclude H2 / equation (2) / Table 6 from this extraction because it is a distinct numbered hypothesis and adoption-change question that follows the H1 family. independent_variables.name: OWN
independent_variables.definition: Scaled annual decile rank of CEOOWN, the direct-ownership percentage for the CEO at the beginning of the fiscal year; options shares are excluded.

evidence.quote: OWN is equal to the scaled decile rank of CEOOWN or TOP5 .
OWN represents managerial ownership and is either set equal to RCEOOWN (model 1)
CEOOWN is equal to the percentage of shares held by the CEO in the form of direct ownership (source ExecuComp) at the beginning of the fiscal year.
CEO ownership, CEOOWN, is defined as the number of shares held by the CEO divided by the total number of shares outstanding. Ownership by the top five managers, TOP5, is defined analogously.
In our primary tests, we measure both CEO and top 5 manager ownership excluding shares granted in options.

The scaled decile rank is determined by first ranking observations each year into 10 groups from zero to nine, and then scaling the ranking by nine so that the rank variable falls within the zero-to-one interval.

evidence.quote: RET t ∗ OWN t −1
RET is equal to the buy-and-hold return over the fiscal year.
OWN is equal to the scaled decile rank of CEOOWN or TOP5 .
OWN represents managerial ownership and is either set equal to RCEOOWN (model 1)
CEOOWN is equal to the percentage of shares held by the CEO in the form of direct ownership (source ExecuComp) at the beginning of the fiscal year.
CEO ownership, CEOOWN, is defined as the number of shares held by the CEO divided by the total number of shares outstanding. Ownership by the top five managers, TOP5, is defined analogously.
In our primary tests, we measure both CEO and top 5 manager ownership excluding shares granted in options.

The scaled decile rank is determined by first ranking observations each year into 10 groups from zero to nine, and then scaling the ranking by nine so that the rank variable falls within the zero-to-one interval.

research_interest_evidence.quote: H1: Accounting conservatism is negatively related to managerial ownership.

Concentrating first on model 1, we find that the coefficient on RET ∗ OWN is significantly positive, while the coefficient on RET ∗ NEG ∗ OWN is significantly negative. These results suggest that, as managerial ownership declines, earnings become less timely in recognizing good news and more asymmetrically timely in recognizing bad news.

independent_variables.research_interest_reason: This interaction directly measures how managerial ownership is associated with earnings timeliness for good news (RET×OWN) or incremental bad-news asymmetry (RET×NEG×OWN), the paper’s H1 prediction.

evidence.quote: RET t ∗ OWN t −1
RET is equal to the buy-and-hold return over the fiscal year.
OWN is equal to the scaled decile rank of CEOOWN or TOP5 .
or RTOP5 (model 2).
TOP5 is equal to the percentage of shares held by the top five highest paid executives in the form of direct ownership (source ExecuComp) at the beginning of the fiscal year.
CEO ownership, CEOOWN, is defined as the number of shares held by the CEO divided by the total number of shares outstanding. Ownership by the top five managers, TOP5, is defined analogously.
In our primary tests, we measure both CEO and top 5 manager ownership excluding shares granted in options.

The scaled decile rank is determined by first ranking observations each year into 10 groups from zero to nine, and then scaling the ranking by nine so that the rank variable falls within the zero-to-one interval.

research_interest_evidence.quote: H1: Accounting conservatism is negatively related to managerial ownership.

Concentrating first on model 1, we find that the coefficient on RET ∗ OWN is significantly positive, while the coefficient on RET ∗ NEG ∗ OWN is significantly negative. These results suggest that, as managerial ownership declines, earnings become less timely in recognizing good news and more asymmetrically timely in recognizing bad news.

independent_variables.research_interest_reason: This interaction directly measures how managerial ownership is associated with earnings timeliness for good news (RET×OWN) or incremental bad-news asymmetry (RET×NEG×OWN), the paper’s H1 prediction.

review_notes: Source-first scope: retain the primary H1 relationship in section 4.1 / Table 2, which the authors call their primary results. CEO direct ownership and top-five-manager direct ownership are the two stated primary ownership proxies; each is estimated with the same complete Basu interaction model and controls.

Exclude the later H2 IOS-residualization models (Table 4 ownership prediction and Table 5 conservatism regression) because they test the distinct after-controlling-for-IOS hypothesis and use a subsequent decomposition. The Table 3 options test, director/founder analyses, and three-year Basu measure are follow-up designs. Table 4 is not a dependency of the retained Table 2 models.

The paper identifies annual cross-sectional Fama–MacBeth estimation and Newey–West corrected time-series inference, but does not name the estimator used within each annual cross section. Table 2 reports an average N over 11 fits, not an exact per-fit N.

The SIC 7370 classification for LIT is conflicting: the Table 2 note lists 7370, while descriptive text on physical page 15 lists 7370–7374. Both statements are preserved; the actual coding remains unresolved.
results_review_notes: Table 2 is the selected baseline family. Later specifications in other tables are outside scope.
The coefficient estimates are means across 11 annual regressions, and the t-statistics test those means using Newey–West corrected time-series standard errors. Degrees of freedom are not stated.
Table 1 Panel B reports no per-variable N; the Table 1 Panel A total sample is not used to populate N statistics for each descriptive row.
The LIT SIC coding differs between the Table 1 note and descriptive prose; this source discrepancy is preserved as a review note and the frozen Table 2 coding is unchanged.

scope.quote:
We analyze a procedure common in empirical accounting and finance re
 search where researchers use ordinary least squares to decompose a depen
 dent variable into its predicted and residual components and use the residu
 als as the dependent variable in a second regression. This two-step procedure
 is used to examine determinants of constructs such as discretionary accru
 als, real activities management, discretionary book-tax differences, and abnor
 mal investment. We show that the typical implementation of this procedure
 generates biased coefficients and standard errors that can lead to incorrect
 inferences, with both Type I and Type II errors. We further show that the
 magnitude of the bias in coefficients and standard errors is a function of the
 correlations between model regressors. We illustrate the potential magnitude
 of the bias in accounting research in four commonly used settings.

We use the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell Theorem and simulations to demon
 strate that this two-step procedure produces biased coefficients and
 f-statistics.

To more directly illustrate the possible effects of the two-step regression
 procedure in accounting research, we examine several settings where this
 approach is used. Specifically, we consider the consequences of the two
 step procedure in evaluating proposed determinants of (1) discretionary
 accruals, (2) discretionary expenditures (i.e., real activities management),
 (3) discretionary permanent book-tax differences (i.e., tax aggressiveness),
 and (4) abnormal investment. In each of these settings we estimate coeffi
 cients and /-statistics using single-step regressions and compare the results
 with those obtained from two-step regressions. We do this for several vari
 ables of interest and with different combinations of second-step control
 variables.

scope.quote:
We analyze a procedure common in empirical accounting and finance re
 search where researchers use ordinary least squares to decompose a depen
 dent variable into its predicted and residual components and use the residu
 als as the dependent variable in a second regression. This two-step procedure
 is used to examine determinants of constructs such as discretionary accru
 als, real activities management, discretionary book-tax differences, and abnor
 mal investment. We show that the typical implementation of this procedure
 generates biased coefficients and standard errors that can lead to incorrect
 inferences, with both Type I and Type II errors. We further show that the
 magnitude of the bias in coefficients and standard errors is a function of the
 correlations between model regressors. We illustrate the potential magnitude
 of the bias in accounting research in four commonly used settings.

We use the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell Theorem and simulations to demon
 strate that this two-step procedure produces biased coefficients and
 f-statistics.

To more directly illustrate the possible effects of the two-step regression
 procedure in accounting research, we examine several settings where this
 approach is used. Specifically, we consider the consequences of the two
 step procedure in evaluating proposed determinants of (1) discretionary
 accruals, (2) discretionary expenditures (i.e., real activities management),
 (3) discretionary permanent book-tax differences (i.e., tax aggressiveness),
 and (4) abnormal investment. In each of these settings we estimate coeffi
 cients and /-statistics using single-step regressions and compare the results
 with those obtained from two-step regressions. We do this for several vari
 ables of interest and with different combinations of second-step control
 variables.

Source-first correction: the paper’s principal contribution is methodological. The abstract and introduction identify bias in the common two-step residual regression and use Frisch–Waugh–Lovell analysis and simulations to establish the result. Retain the actually fitted Monte Carlo full-model and standard two-step regressions underlying Tables 3–4; retain the first stage as the residual construction required by the second stage.

Do not treat Table 2 as a regression result: its bias grids are analytically derived; the simulation reported in the text verifies those formulas but is untabulated. Section 4/Table 5 is an accounting application used to illustrate the method, after the method/simulation contribution, and is outside this selected family. The three equations in the simulation comparison are one full OLS fit, the two-step first-stage fit, and its residual second-stage fit.

The previous Table 5 scope relied on matching sample metadata to choose a family; that was not used for this source-first correction. The sample record links to the later Compustat application and does not establish the principal method family.
descriptive_reason: No descriptive-statistics table or prose summary of realized data values for x1, x2, or x3 is reported in the assigned reading. The source specifies zero-mean normal data generation and correlation designs, which are design assumptions rather than sample descriptives. Tables 3–4 report relative-bias performance summaries, not data-value descriptives.
results_review_notes: Tables 3–4 report mean simulated relative bias for the two-step x2 coefficient and its t-statistic, not actual coefficient estimates or individual coefficient tests.

The source defines coefficient-bias and t-statistic-bias ratios in the Table 3–4 notes. Values remain the printed cell summaries over the R1² row and R2² column design grid; no transformations are applied.
The source simulation generates 20,000 observations and reports average bias over 500 OLS samples for each design combination. These are simulation summaries, not standard errors or p-values.
The selected tables contain no actual full-model or stage-two regression coefficient table. Full-model coefficients and stage-two intercept/x2/x3 estimates remain documented as omitted.
The zero-mean normal simulation design is not a descriptive-statistics report for realized x1, x2, x3, or y values.

review_notes: Source-first scope selects the Monte Carlo regressions in Figures 1–4 as the principal family: the paper’s central empirical question concerns size/operating-volatility bias in unsigned-discretionary-accrual tests and the two remedial approaches. The retained specifications include the full standard controls, the full expanded control variants, and the transformed-accrual comparison; univariate nested lines are omitted. AMJT and APMJ are retained as parallel central outcome proxies. The Section 5 equity-compensation model is an expressly final replication/application and is excluded from the principal family.

The supplied reading JSON OCR truncates figure captions on pages 21–22 and 26–27. Those physical PDF pages were visually inspected to confirm the figure outcomes/panel targets and plotted line categories; the reading-backed definitions remain quoted from Appendix B (page 36).

The operating-volatility timing is genuinely inconsistent: the printed Table 1 note says current year plus prior four years, while Appendix B gives t−5 to t. The supplied OCR drops the words “current and” on page 12; I verified the Table 1 line visually. This remains unresolved for σCFO and σREV; the distinct WLS scalar is explicitly t−5 through t−1.

review_notes: Source-first principal family: reversal-aware tests for accrual-based earnings management. Table 2 evaluates specification using randomly selected management years; seeded-power Figures 1–2 evaluate one-year Healy reversal modeling. These are central contexts for the same contribution, with the full joint two-year equation across five coequal accrual-control models and the distinct one-year Healy equation retained.

For Table 2 the five Healy, Jones, Modified Jones, DD, and McNichols models are full joint Equation (5) specifications. The reported b=0, b−c=0, and b−c−d=0 statistics are restrictions on the same fitted equation, not separate nested regressions.

The performance-matched residual t-tests and Panel C serial-correlation summaries are not regressions in the selected inventory. The AAER application and characteristics-correlated tests are separate validation/follow-up contexts, not this principal testing family.

CF has conflicting supplied-paper definitions: Section 3.2.4 states earnings before extraordinary items minus DAP, whereas the Table 2 note states ib minus WC_ACC. Section 2.1 defines DAP generically but does not supply its dataset-specific construction for CF; the table-note formula also leaves ib scaling relative to asset-scaled WC_ACC unresolved.

Figure 1 and Figure 2 seed amounts are reported as percentages of beginning total assets added to WC_ACC, which is itself scaled by lagged assets; the precise numeric scaling step is not explicit. The estimator for pooled regression fits is also unidentified.
results_review_notes: Table 1 Panel A summarizes the unseeded WC_ACC outcome in the full 209,530-observation sample. It is exact for the five Table 2 outcome specifications and a component of the seeded Figure 1–2 outcome.

Table 1 Panel C reports means and standard deviations for years t, t+1, and t+2 by earnings-performance decile. Only year-t summaries are linked to the frozen WC_ACC outcome; later years are outside the selected model horizon.
Table 1 Panel D is an AAER subsample descriptive and only its year-t WC_ACC row is linked; future accrual years are not part of the frozen outcome.
No descriptive-statistics rows are reported for the synthetic PART indicators or the ΔREV, PPE, and CF control terms in the selected model family; the relevant Table 1 panels summarize WC_ACC only.
