independent_variables.name: DecileRank(|ΔEPS|)
independent_variables.definition: Decile ranking (1 for the smallest absolute year-over-year change and 10 for the largest) of |ΔEPS|. Diluted EPS change scaled by fiscal-year-end stock price; earnings and price are adjusted for stock splits. The change is from t−1 to t; missing change values are set to zero; the change is winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles before absolute values are taken.

evidence.quote:
We measure operating changes
by the change in a firm’s diluted EPS from the previous year, scaled by the
fiscal-year-end stock price, and refer to the variable as �EPS .

Also required from the MD&A is managers’ view of the firm’s liquidity
condition and the use and sufficiency of capital resources.

Both earnings and price are adjusted for stock splits. The observations
with stock prices less than 1 are excluded. BigN is 1 if the firm is audited by a Big N ( N is 6, 5, or 4)
accounting firm or it

The change variables are changes from the prior year to the current year and are filled with 0 when the data
are missing. The above independent variables are winsorized at 1% and 99% and then the absolute values
are calculated. LCR is the mean decile ranking of | �Current |, | �Debtdue |, | �Leverage | , and

research_interest_evidence.quote:
Column 2 uses the decile rankings with 1 being the smallest absolute change
group and 10 being the largest. The coefficients can now be compared;
moreover, by using a coarser scale, this approach relaxes the linearity restriction. Because of these advantages, we treat column 2 as our primary
analysis. Column 3 aggregates the liquidity and capital resources variables
into one variable, LCR, which is the mean decile ranking of | �Current | ,
| �Debtdue | , | �Leverage | , and | �FCF |. This approach allows us to compare
the degree of disclosure modifications after changes in operations versus
changes in LCR.

Except for | �Stdret |, all the explanatory variables in column 2 have significantly positive coefficients. The magnitude of the coefficients for operations and liquidity variables is between 0.002 and 0.003, indicating that the
modification scores from firms in the highest decile are on average 0.018
to 0.027 higher than the scores from those in the lowest decile. This difference is equivalent to about half of the difference between either the 10 <sup>th</sup>

and 25 <sup>th</sup> percentiles or between the 25 <sup>th</sup> and 50 <sup>th</sup> percentiles of Score and
is thus material. If a firm is ranked high for more than one variable, the
difference between its modification score and those of other firms would
be even larger. These results suggest that managers with large economic
changes (except for changes in risk exposure) modify the MD&A more
than firms with small economic changes, apparently meeting a minimum
disclosure requirement.

In column 3, LCR has a coefficient of 0.007 with a t -statistic of 13.42,
significantly higher than the coefficient of 0.003 on | �EPS | (Wald-test F =
42.21). This result suggests that managers modify the MD&A to a larger
extent when discussing changes in LCR than when discussing operations.
Given that firms’ earnings announcements, which typically occur a few
weeks before the 10-K filing, convey predominately information about operations, the MD&A is perhaps a better information source about LCR than
about operations.

Except for | �Stdret |, all the explanatory variables in column 2 have significantly positive coefficients. The magnitude of the coefficients for operations and liquidity variables is between 0.002 and 0.003, indicating that the
modification scores from firms in the highest decile are on average 0.018
to 0.027 higher than the scores from those in the lowest decile. This difference is equivalent to about half of the difference between either the 10 <sup>th</sup>

and 25 <sup>th</sup> percentiles or between the 25 <sup>th</sup> and 50 <sup>th</sup> percentiles of Score and
is thus material. If a firm is ranked high for more than one variable, the
difference between its modification score and those of other firms would
be even larger. These results suggest that managers with large economic
changes (except for changes in risk exposure) modify the MD&A more
than firms with small economic changes, apparently meeting a minimum
disclosure requirement.

extent when discussing changes in LCR than when discussing operations.

weeks before the 10-K filing, convey predominately information about operations, the MD&A is perhaps a better information source about LCR than

Column 2 uses the decile rankings with 1 being the smallest absolute change
group and 10 being the largest. The coefficients can now be compared;
moreover, by using a coarser scale, this approach relaxes the linearity restriction. Because of these advantages, we treat column 2 as our primary
analysis. Column 3 aggregates the liquidity and capital resources variables

| �Debtdue | , | �Leverage | , and | �FCF |. This approach allows us to compare
the degree of disclosure modifications after changes in operations versus
changes in LCR.

Except for | �Stdret |, all the explanatory variables in column 2 have significantly positive coefficients. The magnitude of the coefficients for operations and liquidity variables is between 0.002 and 0.003, indicating that the
modification scores from firms in the highest decile are on average 0.018

and 25 <sup>th</sup> percentiles or between the 25 <sup>th</sup> and 50 <sup>th</sup> percentiles of Score and

Except for | �Stdret |, all the explanatory variables in column 2 have significantly positive coefficients. The magnitude of the coefficients for operations and liquidity variables is between 0.002 and 0.003, indicating that the
modification scores from firms in the highest decile are on average 0.018
to 0.027 higher than the scores from those in the lowest decile. This difference is equivalent to about half of the difference between either the 10 <sup>th</sup>

and 25 <sup>th</sup> percentiles or between the 25 <sup>th</sup> and 50 <sup>th</sup> percentiles of Score and
is thus material. If a firm is ranked high for more than one variable, the
difference between its modification score and those of other firms would
be even larger. These results suggest that managers with large economic
changes (except for changes in risk exposure) modify the MD&A more
than firms with small economic changes, apparently meeting a minimum
disclosure requirement.

In column 3, LCR has a coefficient of 0.007 with a t -statistic of 13.42,
significantly higher than the coefficient of 0.003 on | �EPS | (Wald-test F =
42.21). This result suggests that managers modify the MD&A to a larger
extent when discussing changes in LCR than when discussing operations.
Given that firms’ earnings announcements, which typically occur a few
weeks before the 10-K filing, convey predominately information about operations, the MD&A is perhaps a better information source about LCR than
about operations.

review_notes: Source-first principal question is whether firms with larger year-over-year economic changes modify MD&A more than firms with smaller changes. Table 3 column 2 is the authors’ expressly identified primary specification; column 3 is retained as a central LCR-versus-operations comparison within that same question.

Table 3 column 1 raw-value scaling is excluded because the authors designate decile column 2 as primary; column 4 is excluded because it answers a separate question about firm characteristics among firms with similar changes. Investor/analyst, trend, and hand-coded validation regressions are separate questions or follow-up applications.

The Table 3 Score outcome is length-adjusted Rawscore. Appendix B Table B1’s OLS regression on current-year document Length and its first five powers is an indispensable fitted construction and is included as a supporting model.

Table 3 uses year indicators excluding 2003 and Rogers standard errors for within-firm serial correlation; the authors state that firm fixed effects are omitted in the main analysis and that year clustering is not used. The coefficient estimator for the Table 3 fits is not named.

The paper does not report the exact current-ratio construction, the specific debt-due components, or the precise weekly-return volatility statistic. Table B1 does not report its fit-specific observation count or standard-error correction.

evidence.quote:
Another form of economic change is the change in business components. These changes either reflect the execution of a long-term business strategy (e.g., some firms grow by acquisitions while others grow from
within) or the cumulative effects of past operating performances reaching
a threshold (e.g., some units are discontinued or spun off). We use indicators for substantial asset changes to capture such events: Acquire is 1 if total
assets increase by at least one-third from the previous year and 0 otherwise;
Downsize is 1 if total assets decrease by at least one-third from the previous
year and 0 otherwise. <sup>18</sup> Acquire is 1 for 20.7% of our sample and Downsize is
1 for 4.2%.

Our sample period is fiscal years 1997–2006. <sup>13</sup> It starts with 1997 because
we require the previous year’s filings to be on EDGAR and 1996 is the first
fiscal year for which almost all companies filed the 10-K electronically. We
download 10-K filings from EDGAR and extract the MD&A from Item 7 in
each filing. <sup>14</sup> As in Li [2008, 2010], before further processing, we remove
tables from the MD&A. We then merge the EDGAR data with Compustat
using the Central Index Key (CIK) and exclude observations (1) whose
MD&A for the previous year is missing, (2) whose total assets or diluted
earnings per share (EPS) for the current year or the previous year are missing, (3) whose year-end stock price is below $1 (to avoid outliers created
by small scalars), or (4) that changed the month of fiscal year end during
the year. The screening leaves us with 28,142 firm-year observations. This
number is comparable to the number of 28,279 firm-year observations for
1994–2004 in Li [2008]. Table 1 presents descriptive statistics for the sample by fiscal year.

Second, for profit observations, I regress the median frequency of small positive surprise conditional on positive surprise occurring in the fiscal year representing the firm’s fiscal quarter on the fiscal year.

Third, for loss observations, I regress the median frequency of extreme negative surprise conditional on negative surprise occurring in the fiscal year representing the firm’s fiscal quarter on the fiscal year.
The trend and the t-value pertain to the slope coefficient of the univariate regression of the column on fiscal year.

sample.quote: I obtain 176,519 quarterly observations of actual earnings and analyst forecasts spanning the 16 years, 1984–1999.
The only constraints I impose for my principal analyses are that the I/B/E/S file contains the quarterly earnings report date
at least one earnings forecast be made before that date
The averages reported in the all years row are the time-series means of the 16 annual observations.
Earnings are reported quarterly earnings numbers in a given fiscal year.
Losses are reported negative quarterly earnings numbers in the same fiscal year.
Profits are positive quarterly earnings numbers in that fiscal year.
Earnings are occasionally zero cents per share
I include these observations in my earnings sample but I exclude them from my profit and loss samples.

estimation_procedure.description: Difference-in-differences with a joint country-group moderation: estimate the three DMAND × country-group interactions simultaneously, comparing mandatory adopters in each country group with the voluntary-IFRS control firms pooled across all countries. scope.quote: For mandatory adopters domiciled in countries with both strong enforcement regimes and domestic accounting standards that differ substantially from IFRS, we find statistically and economically significant decreases relative to the control firms in both forecast errors and dispersion.

independent_variables.definition: Product of PI (Worldwide pretax income (Compustat PI), scaled by total assets. The source imputes PI as PIDOM + PIFO when PI is missing and both components are available.) and HAVENYEAR (Indicator equal to one if the firm reported at least one material operation in a country classified as a tax haven in year t, and zero otherwise. The static haven list classifies countries identified by at least three of four cited sources as of March 4, 2008.). The authors subtract the mean of all continuous variables before estimating the interaction model; this product is formed from the specified terms, with only continuous components subject to that centering.

evidence.quote: PI ∗ HAVENYEAR
PI is worldwide pretax income (PI).

Using these data, we set the variable HAVENYEAR equal to 1 if the firm has operations in at least one tax haven country in year t, 0 otherwise.
We consider a country to be a tax haven if it was identified as a haven by at least three of four sources as reported at http://www.globalpolicy.org on March 4, 2008.
HAVENYEAR indicates at least one material operation in a tax haven country in year t listed in the firm’s form 10-K, exhibit 21. Tax haven countries are identified as in table 1.

scope.quote: We address two primary research questions in this study. First, do firms with material operations in tax haven countries face lower current tax rates than other firms? Second, do firms with material operations in any of 99 countries face higher or lower current tax rates than firms without operations in a particular country?

We use a new research methodology coupled with public financial accounting data to compute worldwide, federal, and foreign current tax rates on worldwide, domestic, and foreign income in order to examine these questions.
Selected coefficient estimates from equations (9) and (10) are presented in table 8.

sample.quote: Our sample consists of all U.S. incorporated firms in the Compustat database between 1995 and 2007 that have at least $10 million in total assets (TA) and a nonmissing CIK number (CIK) so we can link the firm to data from the Securities and Exchange Commission Web site.
We require firms to have nonmissing values of worldwide current tax expense (TXT−TXDI), federal current tax expense (TXFED), and foreign current tax expense (TXFO).

Visual inspection of several form 10-K filings reveals that many of the missing values for these variables in Compustat should be coded as 0. Thus, to increase our sample size, we replace missing values as follows:
We define a firm as multinational if it has a nonzero value of foreign current tax expense ( TXFO ) or pretax foreign income ( PIFO ).
We match each Compustat firm-year to a data set gathered from each firm-year’s exhibit 21 of form 10-K filed on the Securities and Exchange Commission web page at www.sec.gov.
Imposing these requirements on the data translates into a sample of 15,231 firm- years corresponding to 3,433 unique firms.
If TXFO is missing and TXFED and TXWW are not missing, we set TXFO to TXWW −TXFO.
The first column estimates the model for firm-years with positive pretax income only ( PI > 0). The second column estimates the model for firm-years with negative pretax income only ( PI ≤ 0).

dependencies.quote: we use a regression framework to identify the variation in tax expense measures associated with income earned in different locations.

missing_fields.sample_size: The selected family comprises two separate sign-stratum fits with different reported Ns (10,285 and 4,304), so no single per-fit N applies to this grouped model record; sample_size is null and both exact Ns are retained in sample_description.
missing_fields.sample_description: The multinational classification uses nonzero TXFO or PIFO. The paper’s printed TXFO imputation rule 9 is self-referential, so the intended value for affected missing-TXFO observations—and any resulting effect on sample classification—cannot be established from the source.
missing_fields.specifications.preprocessing: The paper says all continuous variables are mean-centered but does not state whether the reference mean is computed in the full sample or separately within the sign-stratum fits.

review_notes: The source prints a self-referential TXFO missing-value rule (TXFO = TXWW − TXFO); its intended value is unresolved. Because the multinational sample definition also uses TXFO, this may affect sample classification. No correction is inferred.
results_review_notes: Selected result columns are separate robust-regression fits by pretax-income sign. Printed N values count nonzero-weight observations.

estimation_procedure.description: The authors fit the same specification separately by pretax-income sign strata because the income-tax relation is treated as piecewise with a kink at zero. Table 3 partitions by PI; Tables 4–6 partition jointly by PIDOM and PIFO signs. Robust-regression table Ns count nonzero-weight observations, not the total parent sample.

evidence.quote: We believe that tax rates are nonlinear in pretax income with most of the change in slope occurring at 0 pretax income.

In the first column we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pre-tax income ( PIDOM > 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the second column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pretax income ( PIDOM > 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). In the third column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the fourth column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). Standard errors are reported
We report the number of observations with nonzero weights in the N for each regression, which accounts for the slightly varying N from table to table.

preprocessing.description: The authors subtract the mean of all continuous variables before estimation to facilitate interpretation of interaction effects. The reference sample used to calculate means is not stated.

evidence.quote: We subtract the mean of all continuous variables to facilitate the interpretation of the coefficients.

scope.quote: We address two primary research questions in this study. First, do firms with material operations in tax haven countries face lower current tax rates than other firms? Second, do firms with material operations in any of 99 countries face higher or lower current tax rates than firms without operations in a particular country?

We use a new research methodology coupled with public financial accounting data to compute worldwide, federal, and foreign current tax rates on worldwide, domestic, and foreign income in order to examine these questions.
Selected coefficient estimates from equations (9) and (10) are presented in table 8.
to estimate rates of federal taxation on domestic and foreign income, we change the dependent variable in equation (8) to TXFED .

sample.quote: Our sample consists of all U.S. incorporated firms in the Compustat database between 1995 and 2007 that have at least $10 million in total assets (TA) and a nonmissing CIK number (CIK) so we can link the firm to data from the Securities and Exchange Commission Web site.
We require firms to have nonmissing values of worldwide current tax expense (TXT−TXDI), federal current tax expense (TXFED), and foreign current tax expense (TXFO).

Visual inspection of several form 10-K filings reveals that many of the missing values for these variables in Compustat should be coded as 0. Thus, to increase our sample size, we replace missing values as follows:
We define a firm as multinational if it has a nonzero value of foreign current tax expense ( TXFO ) or pretax foreign income ( PIFO ).
We match each Compustat firm-year to a data set gathered from each firm-year’s exhibit 21 of form 10-K filed on the Securities and Exchange Commission web page at www.sec.gov.
Imposing these requirements on the data translates into a sample of 15,231 firm- years corresponding to 3,433 unique firms.
If TXFO is missing and TXFED and TXWW are not missing, we set TXFO to TXWW −TXFO.

In the first column we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pre-tax income ( PIDOM > 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the second column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pretax income ( PIDOM > 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). In the third column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the fourth column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). Standard errors are reported

dependencies.quote: we use a regression framework to identify the variation in tax expense measures associated with income earned in different locations.

missing_fields.sample_size: The selected family comprises four sign-stratum fits with different reported Ns (6,842 2,661 2,398 2,600), so no single per-fit N applies to this grouped model record; sample_size is null and exact group Ns are retained in sample_description.
missing_fields.sample_description: The multinational classification uses nonzero TXFO or PIFO. The paper’s printed TXFO imputation rule 9 is self-referential, so the intended value for affected missing-TXFO observations—and any resulting effect on sample classification—cannot be established from the source.
missing_fields.specifications.preprocessing: The paper says all continuous variables are mean-centered but does not state whether the reference mean is computed in the full sample or separately within the sign-stratum fits.

review_notes: The source prints a self-referential TXFO missing-value rule (TXFO = TXWW − TXFO); its intended value is unresolved. Because the multinational sample definition also uses TXFO, this may affect sample classification. No correction is inferred.

models.equation_text: TXFED_it = a0 + θ1 PIDOM_it + φ1 PIFO_it + θ2 (PIDOM_it × HAVENYEAR_it) + φ2 (PIFO_it × HAVENYEAR_it) + Σ_k θk (PIDOM_it × CONTROL^k_it) + Σ_k φk (PIFO_it × CONTROL^k_it) + u_it, where CONTROL^k is each of HAVENFIRM, NOL, LNAT, DLTT, XAD, and XRD. The fit is estimated separately for the four PIDOM/PIFO sign combinations.

robust regression iteratively assigns weights to observations to mitigate the

We report the number of observations with nonzero weights in the N for each regression, which accounts for the slightly varying N from table to table.

estimation_procedure.description: The authors fit the same specification separately by pretax-income sign strata because the income-tax relation is treated as piecewise with a kink at zero. Table 3 partitions by PI; Tables 4–6 partition jointly by PIDOM and PIFO signs. Robust-regression table Ns count nonzero-weight observations, not the total parent sample.

evidence.quote: We believe that tax rates are nonlinear in pretax income with most of the change in slope occurring at 0 pretax income.

In the first column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pretax income ( PIDOM > 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the second column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pretax income ( PIDOM > 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). In the third column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the fourth column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). Standard errors are reported
We report the number of observations with nonzero weights in the N for each regression, which accounts for the slightly varying N from table to table.

preprocessing.description: The authors subtract the mean of all continuous variables before estimation to facilitate interpretation of interaction effects. The reference sample used to calculate means is not stated.

evidence.quote: We subtract the mean of all continuous variables to facilitate the interpretation of the coefficients.

scope.quote: We address two primary research questions in this study. First, do firms with material operations in tax haven countries face lower current tax rates than other firms? Second, do firms with material operations in any of 99 countries face higher or lower current tax rates than firms without operations in a particular country?

We use a new research methodology coupled with public financial accounting data to compute worldwide, federal, and foreign current tax rates on worldwide, domestic, and foreign income in order to examine these questions.
Selected coefficient estimates from equations (9) and (10) are presented in table 8.
We estimate equation (8), except with TXFED as the dependent variable in table 5.

sample.quote: Our sample consists of all U.S. incorporated firms in the Compustat database between 1995 and 2007 that have at least $10 million in total assets (TA) and a nonmissing CIK number (CIK) so we can link the firm to data from the Securities and Exchange Commission Web site.
We require firms to have nonmissing values of worldwide current tax expense (TXT−TXDI), federal current tax expense (TXFED), and foreign current tax expense (TXFO).

Visual inspection of several form 10-K filings reveals that many of the missing values for these variables in Compustat should be coded as 0. Thus, to increase our sample size, we replace missing values as follows:
We define a firm as multinational if it has a nonzero value of foreign current tax expense ( TXFO ) or pretax foreign income ( PIFO ).
We match each Compustat firm-year to a data set gathered from each firm-year’s exhibit 21 of form 10-K filed on the Securities and Exchange Commission web page at www.sec.gov.
Imposing these requirements on the data translates into a sample of 15,231 firm- years corresponding to 3,433 unique firms.
If TXFO is missing and TXFED and TXWW are not missing, we set TXFO to TXWW −TXFO.

In the first column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pretax income ( PIDOM > 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the second column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pretax income ( PIDOM > 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). In the third column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the fourth column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). Standard errors are reported

dependencies.quote: we use a regression framework to identify the variation in tax expense measures associated with income earned in different locations.

missing_fields.sample_description: The multinational classification uses nonzero TXFO or PIFO. The paper’s printed TXFO imputation rule 9 is self-referential, so the intended value for affected missing-TXFO observations—and any resulting effect on sample classification—cannot be established from the source.
missing_fields.specifications.preprocessing: The paper says all continuous variables are mean-centered but does not state whether the reference mean is computed in the full sample or separately within the sign-stratum fits.

review_notes: The source prints a self-referential TXFO missing-value rule (TXFO = TXWW − TXFO); its intended value is unresolved. Because the multinational sample definition also uses TXFO, this may affect sample classification. No correction is inferred.

models.model_label: Table 6: foreign current tax rates on domestic and foreign pretax income
models.sample_description: U.S.-incorporated Compustat firm-year sample, 1995–2007, with assets of at least $10 million and nonmissing CIK; tax expense/income inputs and pretax income components are required subject to the source’s Table 2 missing-value rules. Multinational firms have nonzero TXFO or PIFO and are linked to material foreign operations using Form 10-K Exhibit 21. Parent pool: 15,231 firm-years and 3,433 unique firms. The four reported sign-stratum Ns are 6,728, 2,312, 2,387, 2,486 in the order PIDOM > 0/PIFO > 0, PIDOM > 0/PIFO ≤ 0, PIDOM ≤ 0/PIFO > 0, and PIDOM ≤ 0/PIFO ≤ 0; each is a separate robust-regression fit and reports nonzero-weight observations.
models.method_details: The authors state that all tables use robust regression to control for outliers. They describe iterative observation weights; zero-weight observations are excluded. The exact robust-regression routine, weight function and tuning choices are not identified.

dependent_variable.name: TXFO
dependent_variable.definition: Current foreign tax expense (Compustat TXFO), scaled by total assets. The source gives zero-fill rules for certain missing cases, but also prints a self-referential rule: if TXFO is missing while TXFED and TXWW are observed, set TXFO = TXWW − TXFO. The intended right-hand-side value is not established; this is retained as an unresolved source defect, not corrected.
dependent_variable.formula: TXFO / AT; missing-value rules include the printed self-referential TXFO = TXWW − TXFO assignment (unresolved).

evidence.quote: TXFO is current foreign tax expense (TXFO).
TXFED, TXFO, TXWW , PIDOM, PIFO, PI, XAD, XRD, and DLTT are scaled by total assets (AT).
If TXFO is missing and TXFED is equal to TXWW , then we set TXFO to 0.
If TXFO is missing and PIDOM is equal to PI, then we set TXFO to 0.
If PIFO is missing and TXFED is equal to TXWW , then we set TXFO to 0.
If TXFO is missing and TXFED and TXWW are not missing, we set TXFO to TXWW −TXFO.

independent_variables.name: PIDOM × HAVENYEAR
independent_variables.definition: Product of PIDOM (Domestic pretax income (Compustat PIDOM), scaled by total assets. When PIDOM is missing and PI and PIFO are available, the source imputes PIDOM = PI − PIFO.) and HAVENYEAR (Indicator equal to one if the firm reported at least one material operation in a country classified as a tax haven in year t, and zero otherwise. The static haven list classifies countries identified by at least three of four cited sources as of March 4, 2008.). The authors subtract the mean of all continuous variables before estimating the interaction model; this product is formed from the specified terms, with only continuous components subject to that centering.

evidence.quote: PIDOM ∗ HAVENYEAR
PIDOM is domestic pretax income (PIDOM).
TXFED, TXFO, TXWW , PIDOM, PIFO, PI, XAD, XRD, and DLTT are scaled by total assets (AT).
If PIDOM is missing and PIFO and PI are not missing, then we set PIDOM to PI – PIFO.
Using these data, we set the variable HAVENYEAR equal to 1 if the firm has operations in at least one tax haven country in year t, 0 otherwise.
We consider a country to be a tax haven if it was identified as a haven by at least three of four sources as reported at http://www.globalpolicy.org on March 4, 2008.
HAVENYEAR indicates at least one material operation in a tax haven country in year t listed in the firm’s form 10-K, exhibit 21. Tax haven countries are identified as in table 1.

independent_variables.name: PIFO × HAVENYEAR
independent_variables.definition: Product of PIFO (Foreign pretax income (Compustat PIFO), scaled by total assets. When PIFO is missing, the source sets it to zero if PIDOM equals PI, or to PI − PIDOM if PIDOM and PI are observed.) and HAVENYEAR (Indicator equal to one if the firm reported at least one material operation in a country classified as a tax haven in year t, and zero otherwise. The static haven list classifies countries identified by at least three of four cited sources as of March 4, 2008.). The authors subtract the mean of all continuous variables before estimating the interaction model; this product is formed from the specified terms, with only continuous components subject to that centering.

evidence.quote: PIFO ∗ HAVENYEAR
PIFO is foreign pretax income (PIFO).
TXFED, TXFO, TXWW , PIDOM, PIFO, PI, XAD, XRD, and DLTT are scaled by total assets (AT).
If PIFO is missing and PIDOM is equal to PI, then we set PIFO to 0.
If PIFO is missing and PIDOM and PI are not missing, then we set PIFO to PI – PIDOM.
Using these data, we set the variable HAVENYEAR equal to 1 if the firm has operations in at least one tax haven country in year t, 0 otherwise.
We consider a country to be a tax haven if it was identified as a haven by at least three of four sources as reported at http://www.globalpolicy.org on March 4, 2008.
HAVENYEAR indicates at least one material operation in a tax haven country in year t listed in the firm’s form 10-K, exhibit 21. Tax haven countries are identified as in table 1.

sample.quote: Our sample consists of all U.S. incorporated firms in the Compustat database between 1995 and 2007 that have at least $10 million in total assets (TA) and a nonmissing CIK number (CIK) so we can link the firm to data from the Securities and Exchange Commission Web site.
We require firms to have nonmissing values of worldwide current tax expense (TXT−TXDI), federal current tax expense (TXFED), and foreign current tax expense (TXFO).

Visual inspection of several form 10-K filings reveals that many of the missing values for these variables in Compustat should be coded as 0. Thus, to increase our sample size, we replace missing values as follows:
We define a firm as multinational if it has a nonzero value of foreign current tax expense ( TXFO ) or pretax foreign income ( PIFO ).
We match each Compustat firm-year to a data set gathered from each firm-year’s exhibit 21 of form 10-K filed on the Securities and Exchange Commission web page at www.sec.gov.
Imposing these requirements on the data translates into a sample of 15,231 firm- years corresponding to 3,433 unique firms.
If TXFO is missing and TXFED and TXWW are not missing, we set TXFO to TXWW −TXFO.

evidence.quote: The importance of tax enforcement in reducing insider income management is probably the most significant finding in this study

Column (1) indicates that the coefficient for Diverge is significant and positive, and only the coefficient for the interaction Diverge × Tax is significant and negative, which suggests that a high rate of tax compliance is more effective than the legal tradition and the efficiency of the judicial system in limiting income management induced by the control divergence.

It should be noted again that although the F -statistic for the collective contribution of the predicted variables is significant at the 1% level, the incremental contributions of Diverge and Tax to explaining cross-sectional variation in income management appear to be modest; the increase in adjusted R <sup>2</sup> from the benchmark model is 5.8%.

independent_variables.definition: Total dollar sensitivity of the top five executives’ portfolio of exercisable options and unrestricted stock to a 1% stock-price increase. independent_variables.name: VESTED STOCK AND OPTION SENSITIVITY
independent_variables.definition: Total dollar sensitivity of the top five executives’ portfolio of exercisable options and unrestricted stock to a 1% stock-price increase. The unrestricted-stock component changes by 1% of year-end market value; each exercisable option uses the same one-year approximation, e^(−dT)N(Z) × (stock price × 0.01), with d, T, N, and Z defined by the paper. Values are aggregated across the top five executives. review_notes: Source-first scope: the paper’s abstract and introduction make the fraud–equity-incentive relation its central question and explicitly compare both matched and unmatched control samples. The principal models are the full-control specifications for SENSITIVITY and VESTED STOCK AND OPTION SENSITIVITY in each design (Table 5 columns B/D; Table 6 columns B/D). The unmatched sample is a fully estimated logit comparison discussed in the abstract, not only a descriptive comparison. The no-control columns A/C are nested estimates; Table 4 is descriptive, and Table 7’s ex-post stock sales/option exercises are a separate follow-up question.

The table captions identify logit as the actual estimator. The paper shows chi-square p-values but does not state the covariance/standard-error correction. The only displayed equation (1) is conceptual; complete RHS terms come from Tables 5 and 6.

FINANCING has a strict-versus-weak inequality discrepancy at −0.5; Altman’s Z construction is not printed. The paper describes 1st/99th-percentile winsorization in Table 4 descriptive statistics but does not say whether this preprocessing is applied to Table 5/6 regression inputs.
results_review_notes: All four frozen full-control baseline columns are extracted: Table 5 B/D (matched) and Table 6 B/D (unmatched). Other table columns and additional analyses are excluded.

Table 4 descriptive values are retained for the accused-fraud, matched nonfraud, and unmatched nonfraud samples. Mean/median difference p-values are excluded as hypothesis tests; the separate matching-only TOTAL ASSETS row is excluded because it is not a retained RHS variable.
Individual coefficient p-values are copied directly from the reported Chi-Square p-value columns; no unreported coefficient statistic or degrees of freedom is inferred.
Source definitions retain the unresolved strict/inclusive FINANCING threshold and do not provide the exact ALTMAN’S Z construction.

Source-first comparison found that two Table 6 column B cells in the matching prior enrichment had been copied from column D; corrected CEO=CHAIR and NUMMTGS to the original Table 6 B cells. Table 4 descriptive values, roles, stable IDs, sample groups, and links were source-checked.

evidence.quote: Credit Rating: The numerical equivalent of S&P, Moody’s, Fitch, or DPR senior debt rating. It is set as equal to 1 for the highest senior debt rating, through 27 for the lowest senior debt rating. For firms not rated by S&P, we assign the Moody’s senior debt rating; for firms not rated by either S&P or Moody’s, we assign the Fitch senior debt rating; finally, for firms not rated by S&P, Moody’s, or Fitch, we assign the DPR senior debt rating. We use a conventional conversion scheme to match ratings from all four rating agencies. The corporate credit rating variable is set to 28 for firms without an available S&P, Moody’s, Fitch, or DPR debt rating. Credit ratings are collected from the S&P Historical Rating Database and from the Mergent FISD database. Financial Covenants: The number of financial covenants imposed by the loan agreement.

review_notes: Source-first scope: the abstract and introduction frame one principal question—how low financial reporting quality changes lenders’ trade-off between accounting-based and non-accounting-based monitoring terms. The within-sample design and main results test this across the primary contractual outcomes: financial covenants, price, security, general covenants, maturity, and financial-ratio performance pricing. Retain Table 3 col. 1, Table 4 col. 1, Table 5 cols. 1–3, and Table 6 col. 1. The general-covenant and maturity models are explicitly design tests of substitute monitoring mechanisms. Exclude relationship-lender interactions, ICW-severity interactions, restatement comparisons, difference-in-differences, simultaneous-equation/SUR fits, and other robustness analyses as later moderation, comparison, endogeneity, or robustness designs.

Table 5 RHS inventory was checked against the rendered PDF page 17 because the extracted table text did not preserve all column positions. Financial Covenants appears in column 3 (maturity) only; it is not an RHS term in column 2 (general covenants).

Method remains unknown for the Table 3 and Table 4 primary regressions and Table 5 cols. 2–3. The authors print linear specifications and label the analyses regressions, but do not name those primary estimators. Poisson models are described for the separate restatement comparison and as untabulated re-estimates of covenant models. Probit is explicitly reported for Table 5 col. 1 and Table 6 col. 1.

scope.quote: Specifically, we hypothesize and find that the bias component of the book-to-market ratio has a more persistent cross-sectional association with future book return on equity than does the lag component.

We now use multivariate regression to test the ability of BC and LC to predict ROE beyond current ROE.

review_notes: Source-first baseline choice: the paper labels January 10, 2002 document shredding as the primary market-reaction event. Table 9’s two Jan10-specific cross-sectional regressions directly test the Houston-office and fee determinants for that event, using the two- and three-day CAR windows. The underlying full event-study mean/sign tests are not regressions and were not converted into equations. The Feb. 4 date-specific columns, pooled two-date columns, and other event/switching/industry-portfolio analyses are follow-up comparisons and were excluded from this single principal regression family.

The Jan10 CAR dependent variables require firm-specific expected returns from the market model; that per-firm fitted return model is retained as a supporting construction. The event-period CAR is a deterministic sum of abnormal returns, not another regression.

Needs review: underlying estimators are not named; Table 9 gives t-values without specifying the standard-error correction or clustering; the market-model estimation window and per-firm daily N are unreported; Salegrow’s exact computation is not stated; and the Afee numerator wording conflicts across the sample description, Table 2, and Table 9.
results_review_notes: Table 9 contains the selected January 10-only baseline columns; the February 4 columns and pooled two-date fits are excluded.

Table 2 supplies fee components and total assets, and Table 5 supplies broader-sample CAR means. No direct descriptive summaries for sales growth or leverage were located in the relevant descriptive tables/sections searched (pages 10, 13–15 and 23).

The exact Afee numerator is unresolved: the source uses “total audit fee” while its sample discussion describes audit, information-systems and other-fee components and Table 2 distinguishes Audit fee from Total fee.
The Table 2 dollar fee rows are raw fiscal-2000 amounts, not the fee-to-assets ratios used in Table 9; total assets are a broader-sample denominator component.

Table 8 distribution summaries for the selected CAR outcomes are retained in a separate group at the authors’ decimal-return scale; Table 5 reports the same window means as percentages. No arithmetic scale conversion was applied.

calculation_provenance.policy: strict; no guessed degrees of freedom or normal approximations

We estimate model (1) for subsamples of observations with and without incentives to avoid losses.

review_notes: Source-first scope: the introduction states the principal research issue as whether SFAS 131 improves investors’ and analysts’ ability to predict firm performance. Section 5.2.1 and Table 4 directly test the first analyst-access question: whether analyst earnings and revenue forecasts reflect the new segment information before its public release. Retain its parallel AEF and ARF outcomes, both equation (1) comparisons (SFAS 14 versus SFAS 131 mechanical forecast inputs), and pooled equation (2) interaction fits. Section 5.2.2 calls the post-release forecast-accuracy analysis the next question; the later trading-rule, mechanical-forecast-difference determinants, and monitoring analyses are follow-ups to separate questions, so they are outside this selected family.

Appendix B forecast definitions are supplied in the current independently checked reading derivative and have been expanded here. They are deterministic measurement inputs, not fitted construction regressions, so no supporting regression dependency is needed. Preserve the source’s signed SALEDEV cutoff versus “within 5%” prose, unspecified constant growth rate for segments without an SIC code, literal negative-earnings branches/equality gaps, EARNDEV correction rules, and Table 3 ×100 versus Table 4 dollar-per-share scaling conflict.

The paper identifies these specifications only as regressions; the underlying estimator is not reported. The Table 4 fits have exact per-fit Ns from the coordinator-verified transcription appended to physical reading page 29. Adoption years vary across firms, so no single calendar window is reported.

Section 3 explicitly calls Tables 1 and 2 the primary tests. Retain the full all-quarter pooled specification for both outcomes as parallel main proxies. review_notes: Source-first scope: the abstract and introduction identify development and comparison of performance-matched discretionary-accrual measures as the contribution. Section 3.2 specifies the Jones and modified-Jones measurement regressions, then compares performance matching with the alternative regression-based ROA approach. Retain the actual fitted construction specifications: Jones and modified-Jones equation (6), plus current- and lagged-ROA versions of both equation (7) approaches. Matching is a post-fit residual difference, not a separate regression. Later simulation t-tests, serial-correlation analyses, and sensitivity applications evaluate the measures and are outside this extraction.

The paper identifies annual cross-sectional regression fits but does not identify their underlying estimator, so method remains null. Each fit repeats by year and two-digit SIC code; exact per-cell Ns are not reported, so sample_size is null. For modified-Jones variants, the source defines the substituted term as DSALES−DAR but does not separately restate DAR scaling; that field-specific gap is retained.
results_review_notes: The six assigned baseline IDs are the Jones/modified-Jones and ROA-augmented measurement equations. Table 1 Panel A does not report fitted equation coefficients; results remain not_reported for the coefficients, intercepts, and parameter-level inference.

The six Table 1 Panel A discretionary-accrual rows (Jones, modified Jones, and the four ROA-augmented variants) are regression residuals derived from the fitted equations, not upstream inputs or data-value summaries of the retained TA_{i,t} dependent variables. Those six descriptive groups and their links are excluded. The exact Total accruals row and source-backed included/excluded total-accrual sample-note summaries remain retained.
The other four performance-matched measures and Panel B stratified subsamples remain outside the inventory-frozen selected family/column scope.

scope.quote: The first objective of this paper is to develop empirical methods to detect real activities manipulation. I examine cash flow from operations (CFO), production costs, and discretionary expenses, variables that should capture the effect of real operations better than accruals. Next, I use these measures to detect real activities manipulation around the zero earnings threshold.
For my primary tests, suspect firm-years are firm-years reporting small annual profits.
H1A. After controlling for sales levels, suspect firm-years exhibit at least one of the following: unusually low cash flow from operations (CFO) OR unusually low discretionary expenses.
H2A. After controlling for sales levels, suspect firm-years exhibit unusually high production costs.

scope.quote: The first objective of this paper is to develop empirical methods to detect real activities manipulation. I examine cash flow from operations (CFO), production costs, and discretionary expenses, variables that should capture the effect of real operations better than accruals. Next, I use these measures to detect real activities manipulation around the zero earnings threshold.
For my primary tests, suspect firm-years are firm-years reporting small annual profits.
H1A. After controlling for sales levels, suspect firm-years exhibit at least one of the following: unusually low cash flow from operations (CFO) OR unusually low discretionary expenses.
H2A. After controlling for sales levels, suspect firm-years exhibit unusually high production costs.

review_notes: Scope: selected the first contribution stated in the introduction—the total-AQ cost-of-capital tests—in its full specification: Table 2 Panel B / Eq. (2), Table 2 Panel C / Eq. (3), and Table 3 Panel A / Eq. (7). Eq. (1) is included as the AQ-measure construction dependency; Eq. (6) is included because the authors report Eq. (7) incremental adjusted R-squared relative to it.

The introduction also calls innate-versus-discretionary pricing a second contribution. Its later Hypothesis 2 decomposition (Section 5, Table 4), alternative AQ measures, unreported rating tests, quintile beta sort, and lower-order CAPM specifications are excluded as a distinct later decomposition, robustness/application, or preliminary/nested specification under the one-principal-family selection rule.

The paper does not name the within-fit estimator for Eq. (1), Eqs. (2)–(3), or Eqs. (6)–(7). Fama–MacBeth identifies the time-series inference for annual tests, not the underlying annual estimator. The Beta control in Eq. (3) comes from firm-specific CAPM fits described in words; the firm-level equation is not printed.

Table 2’s quintile heading says Q1 is the high AQ score and Q5 the low AQ score, while the text calls Q5 the poorest-quality group and the raw AQ measure is residual standard deviation with larger values indicating poorer quality. The numerical decile-rank direction for Eqs. (2)–(3) remains ambiguous.
results_review_notes: The selected baseline family is Table 2 Panel B, Table 2 Panel C, and Table 3 Panel A, three-factor-plus-AQfactor. Other Table 2 quintile outcomes, alternate asset-pricing columns, decomposition tables, and subsequent analyses are not added.
Table 1 summaries are retained only for selected outcomes, model variables, and upstream raw versions/components. No table values were recalculated.

Table 1 does not report direct data summaries for IntCov, Beta, monthly excess returns, SMB, HML, or AQfactor; the AQ summary is an upstream sorting input to AQfactor, not a direct AQfactor return summary.

Table 2 Panel B retains the printed coefficient cells. The AQ result discussion converts 0.14 across nine AQ decile differences to 126 basis points, indicating that Panel B coefficients are displayed in percentage-point units relative to CostDebt’s ratio scale; the coefficient multiplier records that source-supported scale.

review_notes: Source-first scope: Section 2.2.1 says the current-performance/readability relationship is unclear and economically slight, then identifies future performance—especially earnings persistence—as the better setting for testing the management-obfuscation question. The selected principal family is therefore Table 4 Panels A/B, whole-report Fog and Length, positive current-earnings firms, with separate t+1 and t+2 dependent-variable fits. Table 3 current-earnings/readability is excluded as a subordinate current-performance test despite its abstract summary.

Within Table 4, whole-report Fog and whole-report Length are the principal parallel readability proxies. MD&A/Notes-only columns and Panel C’s joint section comparison are excluded as section-level partition/follow-up analyses; Table 5 loss-firm results, Table 3’s change specification and profit/loss replacement, Section 5 lexical features, and later options/return tests are also outside this principal family.

The Table 4 note explicitly lists RET_VOL and its interaction with earnings, so it is retained. Table 3 is excluded under the source-first scope; although its footnote enumeration omits RET_VOL while surrounding text refers back to Table 2 determinants and the note defines RET_VOL, no Table 3 RHS is carried into the selected record.

The supplied reading’s coordinator-verified math transcription resolves OCR corruption in Table 4: Fog uses a multiplier of 0.4, DIV uses Compustat data21>0, and SIZE/MTB use multiplication of data25 and data199. Those exact supplied-source transcriptions are used.

The estimator is not named. Year and industry dummies are included; standard errors are clustered by two-digit SIC industry. The Table 4 note uses signed ACC while Section 4.2 prose says ABSACC, so that source conflict is preserved. The denominator year for earnings scaling and the log bases for NBSEG/NGSEG are not specified.

The descriptives summarize current Earnings(t), not the future earnings outcomes at t+1 or t+2; they do not describe any constructed Earnings-by-readability or Earnings-by-control interaction. No missing interaction statistics were calculated from component summaries.

Table 1/2 do not provide direct descriptive rows for the ACC or DIV controls. Table 1 reports market value of equity as a raw version of SIZE and as an input to MTB; table-note transformation definitions are preserved in the variable links.

dependencies.quote: Discretionary accruals are estimated using the cross-sectional Jones (1991) model

The abnormal CFO (R_CFO), abnormal production costs (R_PROD) and abnormal discretionary expenses (R_DISX) are computed as the difference between the actual values and the normal levels predicted from Eqs. (3), (6), and (8).

For our first measure, RM_1, consistent with Zang (2006), we first multiply abnormal discretionary expenses by negative one (so that the higher amount, the more likely it is that the firm is cutting discretionary expenses) and add it to abnormal production costs.

For the second measure, RM_2, again consistent with Zang (2006), we first multiply abnormal cash flows from operations and abnormal discretionary expenses by negative one and then aggregate them into one measure.

For our first measure, RM_1, consistent with Zang (2006), we first multiply abnormal discretionary expenses by negative one (so that the higher amount, the more likely it is that the firm is cutting discretionary expenses) and add it to abnormal production costs.

scope.quote: This paper investigates the relation between accrual reliability and earnings persistence.
Our empirical tests employ a comprehensive categorization of accounting accruals in which each accrual category is rated according to its reliability.
The third major contribution of our work is to corroborate and extend Sloan’s findings regarding market efficiency with respect to information in accruals.
Our second prediction is that (g22g1) will be more negative for less reliable accruals.
The univariate regressions have two shortcomings. First, they do not allow for formal statistical tests of differences in the r2 estimates across accrual components.

review_notes: Source-first selection: the abstract and introduction identify the relation between accrual reliability and earnings persistence as the central question. The retained main model is Table 5 Panel C’s final joint OLS regression using the extended balance-sheet decomposition. The source says the univariate regressions cannot test coefficient differences; the joint specification includes all components. Table 5 Panels A/B are benchmarks and coarser preceding decompositions; the univariate rows are preliminary comparisons. Table 6’s longer horizon, Table 7’s further tests, and Table 8’s stock-return/mispricing analysis are later or downstream questions.

The source-defined operating and financing uses of “short-term investments” differ by context: current operating assets use the combined cash and short-term investments field (Compustat item 1), while financing FINA identifies short-term investments as item 193. DSTI is mapped to item 193 in its financing-asset context. This follows the paper’s respective definitions and the supplied verified reading.
Table 5 reports 108,617 firm-years across 40 annual cross-sections, but not the observation count for any single annual fit; sample_size is null.
results_review_notes: Table 4 Panel A reports source descriptives for every retained predictor and the next-year ROA outcome; liability variables are preserved in the positive raw form as reported.

review_notes: Source-first scope: the paper asks whether conservatism has changed over time and lists four measure families. Equation (1)/Table 5 is the only explicitly estimated regression family; it evaluates the earnings–return association and its change across periods. The other measure families are reported through accrual summaries, distributional statistics, and market-to-book summaries rather than additional estimated equations. No fitted construction is required for Equation (1).

Section 4.3 describes average annual measures over five-year intervals, while Table 5 reports an overall fit and subperiod results with N and coefficient statistics. The supplied text does not resolve whether the equation was fit annually and averaged within each interval or pooled within each interval; the fitting procedure remains unresolved.
results_review_notes: All Equation (1) coefficient estimates and t-values are retained for the Table 5 overall period and nine subperiod columns.
Table 5 sample N, adjusted R², relative bad/good-news sensitivity, bad/good-news R² ratio, and total-bias cells are retained as auxiliary rows within their existing fit result sets.

The source states that annual b1 is equal across later and earlier years is rejected at 1%; exact test details are absent, so only the prose conclusion is retained in an auxiliary cross-period comparison record.
The source prose mean of the earnings-to-price ratio, 0.09, is retained as a dependent-variable descriptive with N/time scope left unclear; Table 1 ROA means are not linked to Equation (1) variables.
Subperiod estimation is marked unclear because Section 4.3 describes average annual measures over five-year intervals but does not resolve annual averaging versus pooled estimation.

review_notes: Source-first scope: the stated primary goal is to compare the Cross-sectional Jones and Cross-sectional Modified Jones models with their time-series counterparts. Table 7 is selected as the full-control logit comparison after the contingency-table and univariate logit screens. Industry, DeAngelo, and Healy are introduced as additional models evaluated for completeness, so they are excluded from the retained principal family; the Big-Six split and later sensitivity tests are also outside this family.

Table 7 prints the fourth model block with a duplicate “Cross-sectional Jones Model” label. It is mapped to the Cross-sectional Modified Jones model based on its position in the four-model Jones-family comparison and the paper’s explicit taxonomy; this source-label ambiguity is preserved and requires review.

Equation and total-accrual math use the coordinator-verified transcription tails in the supplied reading derivative, including Equation 7’s minus change-in-current-liabilities term and component definitions. The supplied derivative remains the paper_text_file.
results_review_notes: The fourth selected Table 7 block is assigned to the frozen Cross-sectional Modified Jones model by sequence, while the printed Table 7 label repeats “Cross-sectional Jones Model”; this source discrepancy is preserved in that result set.

scope.quote: In Table 2 we report results for regressions where we explain our textual outcomes using variables such as size, auditor, NYSE membership, complexity in terms of numbers of business segments or operating segments, market-to-book ratio, leverage, intangibles, and losses.
While those variables are significant cross-sectional determinants of textual attributes, including them in a regression framework does not explain the trend in disclosure characteristics over time.

method.quote: In Table 2 we report results for regressions where we explain our textual outcomes using variables such as size, auditor, NYSE membership, complexity in terms of numbers of business segments or operating segments, market-to-book ratio, leverage, intangibles, and losses.

sample.quote: We generate a database of text using SEC 10-K filings spanning the years 1996 to 2013.
Control variables in our reported analyses are obtained from CRSP and Compustat.
Following Loughran and McDonald (2014) we remove firms with negative market-to-book ratios.
The intersection of our data constraints results in a sample of 10,452 firms and 75,991 firm-years.
Before analyzing any 10-K filings, we exclude all amended and small business
those filed before June 1, 1996
documents containing fewer than 3,000 words
missing basic data from Compustat (assets, net income, shares outstanding, price, and book value of equity).

sample.quote: We generate a database of text using SEC 10-K filings spanning the years 1996 to 2013.
Control variables in our reported analyses are obtained from CRSP and Compustat.
Following Loughran and McDonald (2014) we remove firms with negative market-to-book ratios.
The intersection of our data constraints results in a sample of 10,452 firms and 75,991 firm-years.
Before analyzing any 10-K filings, we exclude all amended and small business
those filed before June 1, 1996
documents containing fewer than 3,000 words
missing basic data from Compustat (assets, net income, shares outstanding, price, and book value of equity).
Observations 75,991 75,991 75,991

dependent_variable.name: Ln(Liquidity Factor + 1)
dependent_variable.definition: Natural logarithm of one plus the score of the first and only factor with eigenvalue greater than one, extracted by factor analysis from four quarterly liquidity proxies: the median quoted bid-ask spread; the share of trading days with zero returns; the median Amihud price-impact measure (daily absolute stock return divided by U.S.-dollar trading volume, omitting zero-return days); and estimated total round-trip trading costs (bid-ask spreads, commissions, and implicit costs such as short-sale constraints or taxes).
dependent_variable.formula: ln(FactorScore_1([BidAskSpread, ZeroReturns, PriceImpact, TotalTradingCosts]) + 1)

evidence.quote: the Liquidity Factor equal to the factor scores extracted from the four individual measures bid-ask spreads, zero returns, price impact, and total trading costs using factor analysis
the factor scores from the first (and only) factor with an Eigenvalue greater than one as dependent variable
Zero Returns is the proportion of trading days with zero daily stock returns out of all potential trading days in a given quarter.
Price Impact is the quarterly median of the Amihud (2002) illiquidity measure (i.e., daily absolute stock return divided by US$ trading volume).

To avoid the misclassification of days with no or low trading activity (i.e., days potentially yielding a price impact of zero), we omit zero-return days from the computation of the quarterly medians.

Total Trading Costs are an estimate of the total round trip transaction costs (including bid-ask spreads, commissions, and implicit costs from shortsale constraints or taxes) based on a quarterly time-series regression of daily stock returns on the aggregate market returns (Lesmond et al., 1999).
Because the Liquidity Factor can assume negative values we add one to the raw score before computing the natural logarithm.

review_notes: Source-first selection: the paper frames the main question as whether the liquidity effects around mandatory IFRS adoption are attributable to IFRS or concurrent reporting-enforcement changes. The principal full-sample comparison is Table 3, Eq. (2), column (6): the authors’ three-group quarterly-trend design, with bid-ask spread and the aggregate liquidity factor as parallel main outcomes. Column (7) is explicitly a sensitivity check; the later regulatory-quality, voluntary-adopter, and asynchronous-enforcement tests are follow-ups outside this selected family.

Added the required supporting fit for Total Trading Costs because that estimated measure is an input to the retained Liquidity Factor. The source describes a quarterly log-likelihood regression system but does not print its complete equation/system; the support record is flagged for review rather than reconstructed from the cited literature.
results_review_notes: Only the two frozen Table 3 column (6) baseline models are included. Other Table 3 columns, additional sensitivity tests, alternative country partitions and later tests are outside this enrichment.

The coefficients and Wald difference-test p-values are copied as printed. The p-values from the test of the IFRSEU_ENF/IFRSEU_nonENF difference are stored as separate auxiliary tests, not attached to either individual coefficient.
Table 3 includes but does not report the intercept or country, industry and quarter-year fixed-effect coefficients.
Table 2 Panel B Pearson correlations were visually checked but are not represented as descriptive_statistics; the frozen results rules exclude correlations from the descriptive statistic rows.

The verified reading text transcribes the superscript significance stars as “nnn, nn, and n”; the original page image displays the glyphs as ***, **, and *. The legend retains the visually verified star markers, with the reading-text quote retained for exact text validation.

scope.quote: net operating assets scaled by total assets is a strong negative predictor of long-run stock returns.

The level of net operating assets scaled by beginning total assets (hereafter NOA) is a strong and robust negative predictor of future stock returns for at least three years after balance sheet information is released.
The effect also remains strong after including various past return measures and current-period operating accruals in Fama and MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions.
By applying the Fama–MacBeth (1973) regressions, we evaluate the relation between NOA and subsequent returns with an expanded set of controls
In the Model 3 regressions, NOA in each of the panels is highly significantly negatively related to cross-sectional stock returns

review_notes: Source-first selection: the abstract and introduction present scaled NOA as a strong negative predictor of subsequent stock returns. Table 5 Model 4 is the final full-control Fama–MacBeth specification, including both Accruals and NOA with standard asset-pricing controls; Panels A–C repeat it at 1-, 2-, and 3-fiscal-year accounting-predictor lags. Table 7 Panel A repeats Table 5 Panel A Model 4 and is retained only as a duplicate location. Portfolio sorts, alternate NOA definitions, components, and Mishkin forecasts are follow-up analyses.

The source reports Fama–MacBeth monthly cross-sectional regressions but does not identify the estimator used in each monthly cross-section, the return convention for the dependent variable, or exact monthly fit N. The Table 5-specific Ret(-36:-13) window ends at t−13; Section 3.2 on physical page 13 describes the same variable label through t−12, so the timing discrepancy remains flagged.
results_review_notes: Only the frozen Table 5 Model 4 baseline across Panels A–C is extracted. Table 7 Panel A duplicates Table 5 Panel A Model 4 and is not added as another result set; robustness and additional tests are outside scope.
The 438 count refers to monthly coefficient estimates in the Fama–MacBeth time-series averages, not firm-month observations.

Table 1 Panel A/B means and medians are reported for NOA-sorted annual portfolios; decile-specific Ns are not reported, and contemporaneous NOA/Accruals summaries are not treated as exact summaries of lagged predictors.

Table 1 has no distributional summary rows for monthly stock returns or the past-return controls. Table 2 reports correlations, not variable descriptives; those values are not treated as descriptive statistics.

The Table 5 note defines Ret(−36:−13) through t−13, while Section 3.2 on physical page 13 says the same labeled window runs through t−12. Preserve the Table 5 label and note for the selected coefficient rows and flag the source conflict.

Table 1 NOA and Accruals summaries are contemporaneous NOA-ranking-year portfolio values, not exact summaries of the lagged 1–3-year regressors. Their uncertain local links and the different sample relation are retained with the timing limitation explicit.

estimation_procedure.description: Full-sample determinant regression of current-report Fog on the three earnings-change groups. For each cutoff, MBE marks ΔEPS in the interval from zero through 1, 2, or 3 cents; NegEarnChg marks ΔEPS below zero; the baseline group is firms that beat prior-year EPS by more than the cutoff. Columns I–III repeat this specification across the three MBE cutoffs. The authors also report an F test of β1−β2=0 comparing the MBE and NegEarnChg coefficients.

scope.quote: We explore how the readability of annual reports varies with earnings management.
In this paper, we examine whether managers use of complex disclosures goes beyond the presence of “legalese”, but also whether they use complex disclosure to hide information from investors.
Table 4 presents our first test of Hypothesis 1.
The definition of EM in Equation (1) in this analysis is whether a firm met or just beat past year’s earnings.
Panel A presents the results from the full sample.
To address this ambiguity, we repeated our analyses using smaller matched samples, with results shown in Panels B and C of Table 4.

review_notes: Source-first selection: the abstract frames the main question as whether suspected earnings management makes MD&A disclosures harder to read. scope.quote: This study examines whether application of IFRS by non-US firms results in accounting amounts comparable to those resulting from application of US GAAP by US firms.

We use two approaches to assess comparability, accounting system comparability and value relevance comparability. For both, we find that IFRS firms’ accounting amounts have greater comparability with those of US firms when IFRS firms apply IFRS than when they applied non-US domestic standards.

The first approach we use to assess comparability, which we label accounting system comparability, defines accounting amounts as being comparable if an economic outcome (e.g., stock price) estimated based on the mapping from accounting amounts (e.g., earnings) to that economic outcome of one system is the same as the estimated economic outcome based on the mapping of the other system (De Franco et al., 2011). See Appendix A for details and Tables 3 and 4 for the related findings.

method.quote: To implement this step, we estimate the following pairs of stock price and stock return regressions, pooling observations across firms and over time, where i and t refer to firm and year, respectively.

equation.quote:
COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Accounting system US price mapping A1a and fitting scope, physical PDF page 23):
AppendixA says mappings are estimated separately for US and IFRS firms, pooling observations across firms and over time. A1a: P_it^US = beta0^US + beta1^US*BVE_it^US + beta2^US*NI_it^US + epsilon_it^US. The fitted regressions are accounting-system mappings, not the later deterministic cross-prediction equations.

sample.quote: To test our predictions in Section 3, we use a matched sample design, whereby for each IFRS firm we select a US firm in the same industry as the IFRS firm whose size as measured by equity market value is closest to the IFRS firm’s at the end of the year of its adoption of IFRS (Barth et al., 2008).
Next, we eliminate from the sample any matched pair for which the size difference exceeds 50% in absolute value.
Our analyses include all firm– years for which the IFRS firm and its matched US firm both have data.

We limit IFRS firms to those that do not cross-list in the US to eliminate effects on the IFRS accounting amounts associated with the reconciliation requirement (Harris and Muller, 1999; Lang et al., 2006).
Pre-adoption sample years potentially range from 1992 through 2005. Post-adoption sample years potentially range from 1996 through 2009.
The resulting sample of IFRS firms comprises 3400 firms that adopted IFRS between 1995 and 2006 and 17,714 firm–year observations, of which 8214 are post-IFRS adoption and 9500 are pre-adoption.

scope.quote: This study examines whether application of IFRS by non-US firms results in accounting amounts comparable to those resulting from application of US GAAP by US firms.

We use two approaches to assess comparability, accounting system comparability and value relevance comparability. For both, we find that IFRS firms’ accounting amounts have greater comparability with those of US firms when IFRS firms apply IFRS than when they applied non-US domestic standards.

The first approach we use to assess comparability, which we label accounting system comparability, defines accounting amounts as being comparable if an economic outcome (e.g., stock price) estimated based on the mapping from accounting amounts (e.g., earnings) to that economic outcome of one system is the same as the estimated economic outcome based on the mapping of the other system (De Franco et al., 2011). See Appendix A for details and Tables 3 and 4 for the related findings.

method.quote: To implement this step, we estimate the following pairs of stock price and stock return regressions, pooling observations across firms and over time, where i and t refer to firm and year, respectively.

equation.quote: A1b is the same two-RHS price mapping for IFRS. For each system s in US/IFRS, A2a/b is RETURN_it^s=beta0^s+beta1^s*(NI_it/P_(i,t-1))^s+beta2^s*(DeltaNI_it/P_(i,t-1))^s+beta3^s*LOSS_it^s+beta4^s*LOSS_it^s*(NI_it/P_(i,t-1))^s+beta5^s*LOSS_it^s*(DeltaNI_it/P_(i,t-1))^s+epsilon. The fitted LOSS interactions use current t, not t-1. A3a/b is CF_(i,t+1)^s=beta0^s+beta1^s*(NI_it/TA_(i,t-1))^s+epsilon.
We estimate Eqs. (A1a), (A2a), and (A3a) including industry fixed effects and Eqs. (A1b), (A2b), and (A3b) including country and industry fixed effects.

sample.quote: To test our predictions in Section 3, we use a matched sample design, whereby for each IFRS firm we select a US firm in the same industry as the IFRS firm whose size as measured by equity market value is closest to the IFRS firm’s at the end of the year of its adoption of IFRS (Barth et al., 2008).
Next, we eliminate from the sample any matched pair for which the size difference exceeds 50% in absolute value.
Our analyses include all firm– years for which the IFRS firm and its matched US firm both have data.

We limit IFRS firms to those that do not cross-list in the US to eliminate effects on the IFRS accounting amounts associated with the reconciliation requirement (Harris and Muller, 1999; Lang et al., 2006).
Pre-adoption sample years potentially range from 1992 through 2005. Post-adoption sample years potentially range from 1996 through 2009.
The resulting sample of IFRS firms comprises 3400 firms that adopted IFRS between 1995 and 2006 and 17,714 firm–year observations, of which 8214 are post-IFRS adoption and 9500 are pre-adoption.

scope.quote: This study examines whether application of IFRS by non-US firms results in accounting amounts comparable to those resulting from application of US GAAP by US firms.

We use two approaches to assess comparability, accounting system comparability and value relevance comparability. For both, we find that IFRS firms’ accounting amounts have greater comparability with those of US firms when IFRS firms apply IFRS than when they applied non-US domestic standards.

The first approach we use to assess comparability, which we label accounting system comparability, defines accounting amounts as being comparable if an economic outcome (e.g., stock price) estimated based on the mapping from accounting amounts (e.g., earnings) to that economic outcome of one system is the same as the estimated economic outcome based on the mapping of the other system (De Franco et al., 2011). See Appendix A for details and Tables 3 and 4 for the related findings.

method.quote: To implement this step, we estimate the following pairs of stock price and stock return regressions, pooling observations across firms and over time, where i and t refer to firm and year, respectively.

For each system s in US/IFRS, A2a/b is RETURN_it^s=beta0^s+beta1^s*(NI_it/P_(i,t-1))^s+beta2^s*(DeltaNI_it/P_(i,t-1))^s+beta3^s*LOSS_it^s+beta4^s*LOSS_it^s*(NI_it/P_(i,t-1))^s+beta5^s*LOSS_it^s*(DeltaNI_it/P_(i,t-1))^s+epsilon. The fitted LOSS interactions use current t, not t-1. A3a/b is CF_(i,t+1)^s=beta0^s+beta1^s*(NI_it/TA_(i,t-1))^s+epsilon.

sample.quote: To test our predictions in Section 3, we use a matched sample design, whereby for each IFRS firm we select a US firm in the same industry as the IFRS firm whose size as measured by equity market value is closest to the IFRS firm’s at the end of the year of its adoption of IFRS (Barth et al., 2008).
Next, we eliminate from the sample any matched pair for which the size difference exceeds 50% in absolute value.
Our analyses include all firm– years for which the IFRS firm and its matched US firm both have data.

We limit IFRS firms to those that do not cross-list in the US to eliminate effects on the IFRS accounting amounts associated with the reconciliation requirement (Harris and Muller, 1999; Lang et al., 2006).
Pre-adoption sample years potentially range from 1992 through 2005. Post-adoption sample years potentially range from 1996 through 2009.
The resulting sample of IFRS firms comprises 3400 firms that adopted IFRS between 1995 and 2006 and 17,714 firm–year observations, of which 8214 are post-IFRS adoption and 9500 are pre-adoption.

scope.quote: This study examines whether application of IFRS by non-US firms results in accounting amounts comparable to those resulting from application of US GAAP by US firms.

We use two approaches to assess comparability, accounting system comparability and value relevance comparability. For both, we find that IFRS firms’ accounting amounts have greater comparability with those of US firms when IFRS firms apply IFRS than when they applied non-US domestic standards.

The first approach we use to assess comparability, which we label accounting system comparability, defines accounting amounts as being comparable if an economic outcome (e.g., stock price) estimated based on the mapping from accounting amounts (e.g., earnings) to that economic outcome of one system is the same as the estimated economic outcome based on the mapping of the other system (De Franco et al., 2011). See Appendix A for details and Tables 3 and 4 for the related findings.

scope.quote: This study examines whether application of IFRS by non-US firms results in accounting amounts comparable to those resulting from application of US GAAP by US firms.

We use two approaches to assess comparability, accounting system comparability and value relevance comparability. For both, we find that IFRS firms’ accounting amounts have greater comparability with those of US firms when IFRS firms apply IFRS than when they applied non-US domestic standards.

The second approach we use to assess comparability, which we label value relevance comparability, defines accounting amounts as being comparable if they explain the same variation in economic outcomes. See Tables 5 and 6 for the related findings.
