evidence.quote: We test for differences in each value relevance metric based on an empirical distribution of the differences obtained from a boot-strapping procedure similar to that employed for tests of significance of accounting system comparability standard deviation differences.

To test for differences in R <sup>2</sup>, we estimate the equations 1000 times, randomly assigning firms to the relevant partitions and base significance tests on the frequency of observing an R <sup>2</sup> difference greater than or equal to the tabulated difference.

Throughout, we use the term significant (marginally significant) to denote a five (ten) percent significance level under a one-sided alternative when we have a signed prediction, and under a two-sided alternative otherwise.

The Table 5 findings support the prediction that value relevance comparability increased after firms adopt IFRS in that comparability increased significantly based on all three metrics, although only marginally so for Cash Flow.

The findings in Table 5 are consistent with our prediction that value relevance is higher for US firms than for IFRS firms before they adopt IFRS in that each of the three value relevance metrics is significantly higher for US firms (0.47 vs. 0.20 for Price, 0.09 vs. 0.07 for Return, and 0.44 vs. 0.20 for Cash Flow).

However, the findings also indicate that after IFRS firms adopt IFRS value relevance is higher for US firms, significantly so for Price (0.53 vs. 0.34) and Cash Flow (0.51 vs. 0.28) but not for Return (0.10 vs. 0.09).

evidence.quote: We test for differences in each value relevance metric based on an empirical distribution of the differences obtained from a boot-strapping procedure similar to that employed for tests of significance of accounting system comparability standard deviation differences.

To test for differences in R <sup>2</sup>, we estimate the equations 1000 times, randomly assigning firms to the relevant partitions and base significance tests on the frequency of observing an R <sup>2</sup> difference greater than or equal to the tabulated difference.

Throughout, we use the term significant (marginally significant) to denote a five (ten) percent significance level under a one-sided alternative when we have a signed prediction, and under a two-sided alternative otherwise.

The Table 5 findings support the prediction that value relevance comparability increased after firms adopt IFRS in that comparability increased significantly based on all three metrics, although only marginally so for Cash Flow.

The findings in Table 5 are consistent with our prediction that value relevance is higher for US firms than for IFRS firms before they adopt IFRS in that each of the three value relevance metrics is significantly higher for US firms (0.47 vs. 0.20 for Price, 0.09 vs. 0.07 for Return, and 0.44 vs. 0.20 for Cash Flow).

However, the findings also indicate that after IFRS firms adopt IFRS value relevance is higher for US firms, significantly so for Price (0.53 vs. 0.34) and Cash Flow (0.51 vs. 0.28) but not for Return (0.10 vs. 0.09).

scope.quote: This study examines whether application of IFRS by non-US firms results in accounting amounts comparable to those resulting from application of US GAAP by US firms.

However, the findings also indicate that after IFRS firms adopt IFRS value relevance is higher for US firms, significantly so for Price (0.53 vs. 0.34) and Cash Flow (0.51 vs. 0.28) but not for Return (0.10 vs. 0.09).

Because large negative stock returns are concentrated in 2007 and 2008, we winsorize variables separately for sample years before and after 2006 to avoid disproportionately winsorizing observations in the later years.

scope.quote: This study examines whether application of IFRS by non-US firms results in accounting amounts comparable to those resulting from application of US GAAP by US firms.

We use two approaches to assess comparability, accounting system comparability and value relevance comparability. For both, we find that IFRS firms’ accounting amounts have greater comparability with those of US firms when IFRS firms apply IFRS than when they applied non-US domestic standards.

The second approach we use to assess comparability, which we label value relevance comparability, defines accounting amounts as being comparable if they explain the same variation in economic outcomes. See Tables 5 and 6 for the related findings.

method.quote: We construct our value relevance comparability metrics based on the explanatory power of regressions of stock price on equity book value and net income, stock return on net income and change in net income, and future operating cash flow on net income.

equation.quote: the nested model that includes only the fixed effects.

sample.quote: For example, when we compare value relevance of IFRS and US firms after the IFRS firms adopt IFRS, we estimate the models using the combined sample of IFRS firms and their matched US firms for years after the IFRS firms adopt IFRS.

To test our predictions in Section 3, we use a matched sample design, whereby for each IFRS firm we select a US firm in the same industry as the IFRS firm whose size as measured by equity market value is closest to the IFRS firm’s at the end of the year of its adoption of IFRS (Barth et al., 2008).
Next, we eliminate from the sample any matched pair for which the size difference exceeds 50% in absolute value.
Our analyses include all firm– years for which the IFRS firm and its matched US firm both have data.

We limit IFRS firms to those that do not cross-list in the US to eliminate effects on the IFRS accounting amounts associated with the reconciliation requirement (Harris and Muller, 1999; Lang et al., 2006).
Pre-adoption sample years potentially range from 1992 through 2005. Post-adoption sample years potentially range from 1996 through 2009.
The resulting sample of IFRS firms comprises 3400 firms that adopted IFRS between 1995 and 2006 and 17,714 firm–year observations, of which 8214 are post-IFRS adoption and 9500 are pre-adoption.

other.description: Table 2 column (2) replaces Early Years with Year One through Year Five indicators and is described as a justification for the three-year cutoff; column (1) is retained as the primary Early Years specification.

evidence.quote: To provide justification for using the first three years of service as the cutoff for defining Early Yearsit, we estimate Equations (3) and (4) after replacing Early Yearsit with indicator variables for each of the first five years of CEOs’ service

scope.quote: This study examines changes in CEOs’ incentive to manage their firms’ reported earnings during their tenure. Earnings overstatement is greater in the early years than in the later years of CEOs’ service, and this relation is less pronounced for firms with greater external and internal monitoring.
Hypothesis H1: Earnings overstatement is greater in the early years of CEOs’ service than in the later years of CEOs’ service.
Panels A and B of Table 2 report the regression results of the discretionary accruals model and the abnormal discretionary expenses model, respectively.

equation.quote: Discretionary Accrualsit = a0 + a1Early Yearsit + a2CEO Ownershipit + a3CEO Ageit + a4LnMVEquityit + a5MarketBookRatioit + a6Litigation Riskit + a7Leverage it + a8Institutional Ownershipit + a9Merger&Acquisitionit + a10Issuerit + a11ROAit + a12Lossit + a13CFOit + a14Lagged Accrualsit + a15Lagged NOAit + a16 Total Asset Growthit + a17Employment Growthit+ it (3)

sample.quote: For the years 1992 to 2010, we obtain data on CEO tenure, CEO age, and CEO ownership from ExecuComp, financial statement data from Compustat, return data from CRSP, institutional holding data from Thomson Reuters 13f File, analyst forecast data from IBES Summary, and board and audit committee independence data from RiskMetrics.
Our final sample for the discretionary accruals models contains 20,206 firm-year observations, representing 4,625 CEOs and 2,704 firms.

review_notes: Source-first selection: the introduction identifies early-versus-later CEO tenure earnings overstatement as the central question and H1; discretionary accruals and abnormal discretionary expenses are parallel outcomes. Retained the full-control Table 2 column (1) models for those two outcomes. The monitoring interaction tests are introduced separately as H2 after the source states the primary early-versus-later prediction, so they are excluded from this principal family.

Table 2 column (2) replaces the three-year Early Years indicator with separate first-five-year indicators to justify the cutoff; it is not an additional baseline. Equations (1) and (2) are retained as supporting construction regressions because their fitted residuals are the dependent variables in the selected Table 2 models. They are separately estimated in two-digit SIC industry-year groups with a minimum of ten observations; this is repeated fitting, not fixed effects.

The final-year/horizon tests in Table 4 are separately introduced after H1; long-tenure, reversal, R&D-only, write-off and other sensitivity analyses are excluded. The first-five-year coefficient screen and H2 monitoring interaction tests are also excluded.

The paper reports Huber–White standard errors clustered by firm, but does not name the coefficient estimator used for any retained application. OLS is not inferred from the equations or residual construction.

Per-fit N is exact for the reported Table 2 regressions and is copied from their observation rows. The individual Equation (1) and (2) industry-year fits have varying N; only the minimum of ten observations per group is reported, so sample_size is null for each repeated construction equation.

Equation (4) is transcribed as printed: b0 through b9 followed by a10 and a11. The supplied reading and source PDF agree; the mixed coefficient labels are not a missing-equation issue and do not imply cross-equation restrictions. Lagged NOA's sales deflator period remains unspecified.
results_review_notes: The two selected Table 2 column (1) regressions and all reported control coefficients/intercepts are included. Column (2) per-year tenure specifications and later robustness/subgroup regressions are excluded.
Table 1 descriptives cover all variables in the retained column (1) models; its Final Year row was omitted because that term is included only in the excluded column (2).

The paper requires data for the outcomes and controls, total assets above US$100 million, less than 80% zero-return days in the total event window, excludes voluntary adopters, and removes countries with fewer than 150 firm-years; the return/volume data also require at least 40 observations in each pre- and post-event non-event period.
models.method_details: Pooled full-sample firm-level regression; column (3) is the full specification with firm-level and country-level controls.

independent_variables.name: CEO_PAYSLICE
independent_variables.definition: CEO total compensation as a percentage of aggregate top-five executive compensation. Compensation includes salary, bonus, other annual pay, total value of restricted stock granted, Black-Scholes value of stock options granted, long-term incentive payouts, and all other total compensation. The number of executives is adjusted to five: if fewer than five are disclosed, the remaining positions are assigned compensation equal to the lowest-paid disclosed executive; if more than five are disclosed, only the top five are retained.
independent_variables.formula: CEO total compensation / adjusted aggregate total compensation of the top five executives; total compensation includes salary, bonus, other annual pay, restricted stock grant value, Black-Scholes stock-option grant value, long-term incentive payouts, and all other total compensation.

evidence.quote: The slice of the CEO’s total compensation in total top five executives’ compensation after adjusting the number of executives disclosed in proxy statements if a firm discloses more or less than five executives.

The first measure is the CEO’s percentage of aggregate top five executives’ total compensation, which includes salary, bonus, other annual pay, the total value of restricted stock granted, the Black-Scholes value of stock options granted, long-term incentive payouts, and all other total compensation (CEO_PAYSLICE).

Specifically, if fewer than five executives’ compensations are disclosed in a given year, we assume that the remaining top five undisclosed executives receive the same level of compensation as the lowest-paid executive among those disclosed in the proxy statements.
If proxy statements disclose more than five executives in a given year, we keep the compensation for the top five executives.

estimation_procedure.description: Conditional logistic regression on the matched manipulation/control sets. The conditional likelihood is based on the probability of being a manipulation firm given that one of the firms in each matched set is a manipulation firm. Matching is on SIC-based industry and total assets at 80–120% of the manipulation firm in the year before the manipulation period; if more than two controls are available, the two closest in assets are retained. The selected specification is the full Table 4 Panel A column (4) model for H1–H3.

For each manipulation firm, we identify firms in ExecuComp in the same industry and with total assets in the range of 80–120 percent of the manipulation firm’s total assets in the year prior to the start of the manipulation period.
We follow Frankel et al.’s (2002) SIC-based industry classification scheme.
If there are more than two matches, we keep the two matches with closest total assets in the year immediately before the manipulation years.

scope.quote: In this study, we examine whether industry specialization of auditors and low balling affect the association between auditor tenure and earnings quality.

estimation_procedure.description: Truncated regression of ABSTDA on auditor tenure and the controls in Equation (2). This is the non-specialist estimation; the authors state that their inferences on the specialization comparison are mainly based on the specialist/non-specialist subsample analyses. Specialization is defined from Big N auditors’ share of client total assets in two-digit SIC industries; the auditor with the highest industry share is the specialist.

evidence.quote: Since absolute values of discretionary accruals used as a dependent variable are truncated at zero, a truncated regression approach is adopted to arrive at unbiased estimates of coefficients in the model.
Consequently our inferences are mainly drawn based on the sub-sample analyses.

preprocessing.description: All continuous variables are winsorized at three standard deviations.

evidence.quote: All continuous variables are winsorized at three standard deviations.

scope.quote: In this study, we examine whether industry specialization of auditors and low balling affect the association between auditor tenure and earnings quality.
main tests are based on the discretionary accruals model suggested by Ball and Shivakumar (2006).
We expect the coefficient for Tenure to be negative, suggesting shorter tenure is associated with higher discretionary accruals, i.e. lower earnings quality.
Additionally, we expect this association to be significantly weaker for firms audited by industry specialists.
We conduct tests based on both specialist and non-specialist sub-samples, as well as on the full sample with an interaction term between tenure and specialists.
Consequently our inferences are mainly drawn based on the sub-sample analyses.

method.quote: Estimations are based on truncated regression approach.

sample.quote: This study is based on a sample of firms from 1993 to 2004.
We include only firms that are audited by Big 6/5/4 auditors
Firms with mergers and acquisitions (M&A) are dropped from the sample
Our final sample consists of 32,777 firm-year observations.
Out of the total sample, 24,433 firm-year observations are audited by non-specialists and 8344 firm-year observations by industry specialists.
A Big N audit firm’s industry specialization is measured based on its share of clients’ total assets in the two-digit SIC industry group

scope.quote: In this study, we examine whether industry specialization of auditors and low balling affect the association between auditor tenure and earnings quality.
main tests are based on the discretionary accruals model suggested by Ball and Shivakumar (2006).
We expect the coefficient for Tenure to be negative, suggesting shorter tenure is associated with higher discretionary accruals, i.e. lower earnings quality.
Additionally, we expect this association to be significantly weaker for firms audited by industry specialists.
We conduct tests based on both specialist and non-specialist sub-samples, as well as on the full sample with an interaction term between tenure and specialists.
Consequently our inferences are mainly drawn based on the sub-sample analyses.

evidence.quote: ReadIndex is the first principal component of the following measures of readability: Flesch-Kincaid readability, LIX readability, RIX readability, Gunning Fog readability, ARI readability, and SMOG readability.

estimation_procedure.description: The source estimates the earnings-persistence equation repeatedly across horizons h=1–5. Table 2 Panel B reports separate fits in all five earnings-volatility quintiles; Table 3 reports each horizon for the full sample and the highest- and lowest-volatility quintiles. Table 3 per-fit observation counts for horizons 1–5 are full sample [9,102; 7,502; 6,147; 5,011; 4,032], highest quintile [1,682; 1,314; 1,029; 822; 659], and lowest quintile [1,899; 1,620; 1,365; 1,140; 922]. Table 2 Panel A’s full-sample h=1 fit is the same fit as Table 3 Panel A at h=1. Table 2 tests the Q1–Q5 persistence difference with a simple t-test from a pooled Q1/Q5 regression including a Q5 intercept dummy and an Earnings_t-by-Q5 slope term; adjusted-R² differences use 1,000 simulated pseudo-quintile splits. These are inference procedures, not extra baseline outcomes.

preprocessing.description: Earnings is deflated by average total assets. The source truncates the top and bottom 1% of earnings, accruals, and CFO in sample construction. Earnings-volatility groups use the firm-specific standard deviation of deflated earnings over the most recent five years.

evidence.quote: Earnings, accruals and cash flow from operations (CFO) are deflated using average assets.
To avoid the influence of extreme observations, we truncate the top and bottom 1% of earnings, accruals and cash flows from operations.
Vol(Earnings) is defined as the firm-specific standard deviation of Earnings over the most recent 5 years.

scope.quote: The empirical specifications focus on establishing the relation between earnings volatility and short- and long-term earnings predictability.
Table 2 presents the persistence coefficients and R <sup>2</sup> of regressions of 1-year-ahead earnings on current earnings.
Table 3 presents results for 5-year-ahead prediction of earnings, conditional on earnings volatility.

equation.quote: Results for the earnings persistence regression: Earningst+1 1⁄4 a+b Earningst+e.
Table3 panels A(full sample), B(highest earnings-volatility quintile), C(lowest quintile) each display five regressions: Earnings_(t+h)=alpha+beta*Earnings_t, h=1,2,3,4,5.

sample.quote: Firms in the full sample are randomly assigned into two sub-samples. We use the first sub-sample (observations 1⁄4 11,061) for a comprehensive exploratory analysis of the predictive power of earnings volatility for earnings predictability
After all requirements, the final sample includes 22,113 firm-years over 1988–2004.

Number-of-observation rows for h1..5 respectively: A=[9102,7502,6147,5011,4032]; B=[1682,1314,1029,822,659]; C=[1899,1620,1365,1140,922]. These are reported counts for the corresponding horizon/group fits, not a single N to use for every grouped fit.

missing_fields.method: The source does not identify the estimator actually used for the principal Table 2 and Table 3 regression applications.
missing_fields.sample_size: This entry represents fits across horizons and groups, so the scalar is null. Table 3 reports the per-fit counts listed in the estimation procedure; Table 2 Panel B does not report per-quintile N in the supplied reading.

results_missing_fields.intercept: The equations include an intercept α, but the selected Table 2 and Table 3 panels do not report its estimate.
results_missing_fields.standard_error: Individual standard errors are not printed; the tables report only that each persistence coefficient is significant at the 0.001 level.
results_missing_fields.t_statistic: Individual coefficient t-statistics are not reported; degrees of freedom and the reference distribution for the blanket coefficient significance statement are unspecified.
results_missing_fields.table2_panelB_middle_quintile_N: Table 2 Panel B does not report per-quintile observation counts; Table 3 supplies h=1 counts for the full sample and extreme quintiles only.
results_missing_fields.estimator: The paper reports regressions but does not identify the estimator used for the principal Table 2 and Table 3 fits.
results_missing_fields.fixed_effects: Fixed effects are not specified for the selected principal Table 2 and Table 3 fits.

results_review_notes: Table 2 Panel A and Table 3 Panel A h=1 report the same full-sample fit; Table 2 Panel B Q1 and Q5 h=1 likewise duplicate Table 3 Panels C and B. Duplicate locations are attached to one result set per fit.
The one-year Table 2 Panel B Q2–Q4 coefficients are reported without per-quintile sample counts. Table 3 reports per-horizon counts for the full sample and extreme quintiles only.

Per-fit adjusted R-squared values remain fit summaries outside this coefficient-focused enrichment; the printed Q1−Q5 adjusted-R-squared difference and p-value are retained as an auxiliary comparison on vol_q1_h1, with vol_q5_h1 as counterpart.
The Table 1 Vol(Earnings) row describes the sample-grouping variable, not a retained equation variable, so it is not linked to Earnings_t or a future-earnings outcome.

evidence.quote: In this case, the null hypothesis is that earnings volatility is unrelated to earnings predictability, and the test statistic is the difference in adjusted R <sup>2</sup> between earnings volatility quintiles 1 and 5.
We repeat this procedure 1000 times, yielding a 1000-observation empirical distribution of R <sup>2</sup> differences under the null.

review_notes: The source-selected principal question is the relation between earnings volatility and short- and long-term earnings predictability (abstract/introduction and Sections 3.2–3.3). Table 2 Panel B and Table 3 are one repeated earnings-on-earnings regression family across volatility groups and horizons; duplicated full-sample one-year fits are represented once. Table 4 is retained separately because its dependent variable is the five-year sum of future earnings.

Analyst-forecast-error analyses are later Section 5 tests of users’ understanding, while accrual, earnings-level, CFO-volatility and later robustness analyses are comparison or supplemental tests; they are outside the selected principal family.
The estimator for the principal regression applications remains unreported in the supplied source. This is the unresolved issue keeping status at needs_review.
results_review_notes: Only the two frozen baseline model families are extracted: one-year persistence across volatility quintiles and horizons 1–5 for the full and extreme-quintile samples, plus the five-year summed-earnings regression in Table 4 Panels A–C. Later robustness, portfolio, analyst-forecast, and additional tests are outside scope.

Per-fit adjusted R-squared values remain model-fit summaries outside this coefficient-focused enrichment. The Table 2 Q1−Q5 and Table 4 difference-from-Panel-B adjusted-R-squared summaries and p-values are retained as auxiliary comparisons on existing fits, with named counterparts.

Vol(Earnings) is a sample-grouping variable, not a retained equation predictor; it is not linked to Earnings_t or a future-earnings outcome. Table 1 does not provide a separate summary for the future-earnings outcomes.
The Table 4 persistence-difference method conflict is preserved: its note says bootstrap while page 11 prose says t-test. The method, reference, tail, df, and subtraction order remain unresolved.

scope.quote:
This study’s objectives are to use a consistent general theoretical framework to

(1) explain results documented in the recent literature on the relation between MTB and

asymmetric timeliness, and so provide a deeper understanding of the two measures;
and
(2) generate and test new predictions about the relations between MTB and

(a) the timeliness of good news
(b) the timeliness of bad news, and

(c) asymmetric timeliness
(d) and how those relations vary with the horizon used to estimate timeliness and

asymmetric timeliness.
To investigate the association between asymmetric timeliness and beginning MTB, we estimate the following regression:

The coefficient b1 represents the association between MTB and earnings timeliness with respect to good news. The coefficient g1 measures the association between asymmetric timeliness of earnings and MTB.

scope.quote:
This study’s objectives are to use a consistent general theoretical framework to

(1) explain results documented in the recent literature on the relation between MTB and

asymmetric timeliness, and so provide a deeper understanding of the two measures;
and
(2) generate and test new predictions about the relations between MTB and

(a) the timeliness of good news
(b) the timeliness of bad news, and

(c) asymmetric timeliness
(d) and how those relations vary with the horizon used to estimate timeliness and

asymmetric timeliness.
The relation between historical asymmetric timeliness and ending MTB is examined with the following regression:
Hypothesis 2c. The association between asymmetric timeliness (g) and MTB at the end of the estimation period is more positive the longer the estimation period.

review_notes: The Eq. (3) paragraph and Table 5A give incompatible horizon ranges; the primary Table 5A specification is recorded as j=0–4 and the source conflict is preserved.

results_review_notes: The frozen Table 5A columns and variable note support j=0–4, which are extracted. The prose immediately following Equation (3) says j varies from 0 to 2; that horizon discrepancy remains unresolved.

review_notes: The selected principal family is the paper’s central MTB–asymmetric-timeliness relation: Table 4A tests beginning-of-period MTB rank against future good-news, bad-news, and asymmetric timeliness; Table 5A tests ending-of-period MTB rank against historical timeliness. The horizons are part of these designs.

Tables 2–3 report initial Basu regressions across horizons without MTB rank; Tables 4B–5B are explicitly descriptive extreme-quintile comparisons, and the later goodwill analysis is robustness. These are not the primary regression family selected from the stated objective and hypotheses.

The underlying estimator within each annual Fama–Macbeth cross-section is not identified. Source conflicts in the Eq. (2) denominator/forward-return timing and Eq. (3) horizon range remain flagged; status is needs_review.
results_review_notes: Only the frozen Table 4A forward and Table 5A historical baseline families are extracted. Separate extreme-MTB-quintile Tables 4B/5B and other analyses are outside the selected locations.
All 7 RHS terms and intercepts are extracted for k=1–3 and j=0–4. Reported b1+g1 combinations and adjacent-horizon differences are kept as auxiliary estimates with their own printed t-statistics.

Table 1 summaries are retained for the raw MTB ratio, market value denominator, horizon-matched earnings and returns. Indicator and interaction descriptives are not reported and are not calculated from the raw summaries.
Forward outcome/return timing conflicts and the Table 4A b1+g1 cell/prose discrepancy are documented rather than reconciled.

models.model_label: Pooled cross-sectional earnings forecast, Eq. (1)
models.sample_description: NYSE, Amex, and Nasdaq common shares with CRSP share codes 10 or 11 (excluding ADRs, closed-end funds, and REITs) at the CRSP/Compustat intersection. For each forecast origin year t from 1968 to 2008, the authors estimate pooled regressions on the preceding ten years and forecast earnings at horizons τ=1,…,5 using year-t inputs. Firms need nonmissing year-t predictors to receive forecasts. The paper does not report the exact observation count for any year/horizon training fit.
models.method_details: The authors identify pooled cross-sectional regressions but do not name the underlying estimator. Do not infer OLS from the linear equation. Each year’s fit uses the previous ten years; the paper reports time-series averages of the annual coefficients and Newey–West t-statistics for those annual coefficient estimates.

scope.quote: In this paper, we propose a new approach to estimate the ICC. We use earnings forecasts generated by a cross-sectional model instead of analysts’ forecasts to proxy for cash flow expectations.

We estimate model-based earnings forecasts for up to five years into the future and then use those earnings forecasts to compute the ICC for more than 170,000 firm-year observations over the period 1968–2008.
Cross-sectional earnings regressions, 1968–2008.

sample.quote: Our sample includes all NYSE, Amex, and Nasdaq listed securities with sharecodes 10 or 11 (i.e., excluding ADRs, closed-end funds, and REITs) that are at the intersection of the CRSP monthly returns file from July 1963 to June 2009 and the Compustat fundamentals annual file from 1963 to 2009.

models.model_label: Conditional logit of the going-private decision, full matched sample
models.sample_description: Full pre- and post-SOX matched case-control sample: 237 going-private firms and 237 non-going-private controls (N=474). Each control is matched to a going-private firm using prior-year market value and SIC industry; when a four-digit SIC match is unavailable, the authors use three- or two-digit SIC. The market-value caliper is |ln(firm market value) - ln(control firm market value)| < ln(4), using natural logarithms. Filings run from January 1998 through May 2005; the sample includes both pre- and post-SOX proposal-announcement periods.

scope.quote: In this paper, we provide evidence on the effect of SOX on firms that are close to the public/private margin; that is, firms for which the net benefits of being public are relatively small. Specifically, we examine firms’ going-private decisions, and ask how this choice was affected by SOX.

We pose three main questions regarding SOX and the going-private decision. First, to what extent was SOX associated with an increase in the number of firms electing to go private? Second, did the factors associated with firms’ decisions to go private change around the passage of SOX? Third, did the determinants of going-private announcement returns change around the passage of SOX?
Given our interest in how SOX has changed the public/private margin, we examine whether the characteristics related to the likelihood of firms going private differ in the pre- and post-SOX periods.
In Table 8, we present the results of the logit regressions. Column (1) includes all firms, Column (2) includes pre-SOX firms only, and Columns (3)–(5) include post-SOX firms only.

independent_variables.name: EPL_n × DlnSALE_{n,i,t}
independent_variables.definition: Interaction of the country-level aggregate EPL strictness index and current-year log-change in deflated sales. EPL is the late-1990s country index computed as the average of regular-employee EPL (REGEPL) and temporary-employee EPL (TEMPEPL), each scaled 0–6 with higher values denoting stricter protections. EPL and continuous controls are mean-centered before estimation.

evidence.quote: ðb1 þg1EPLn þl1GDPGROWTHn,t þl2AINT n,i,t þl3LAW nÞDln SALEn,i,t
EPLn aggregate index of employment protection legislation (EPL) in country n in late 1990s, computed as (REGEPLnþ TEMPEPLn)/2 following OECD (2004)
The indexes range from 0 to 6, and higher scores represent stricter EPL.

evidence.quote: l1GDPGROWTHn,t

the average annual GDP growth ranges from 1.1% in Italy to 6.2% in Ireland
To facilitate the interpretation of the estimates, in all regressions, we rescale the continuous control variables and EPL index to have mean zero.

estimation_procedure.description: Hierarchical linear Model A combines the level-1 firm cost-stickiness equation with country-level slope equations. The combined regression is estimated by OLS under the authors’ stated mean-zero, exogeneity assumptions; country-level random slope shocks enter the composite error. This is one pooled firm-year fit across countries and years, not a regression repeated separately by country or year. Table 5 column (a) is the main 1990–2008 sample; other columns are time-period or US-exclusion sensitivity checks. Inference uses two-way clustering by country and year.

scope.quote: Central to the economic theory of sticky costs is the proposition that managers consider adjustment costs when changing resource levels. We test this proposition using employment protection legislation (EPL) provisions in different countries as a proxy for labor adjustment costs.

By combining Eq. (1) with (2a) and (2b), we obtain our main estimation model. Model A

dependent_variable.name: ln(1 + NYAM equal-weighted 12-anomaly hedge-portfolio return)_t
dependent_variable.definition: Natural log of one plus the monthly NYAM EW hedge-portfolio return. The EW return is the equal-weighted average of the 12 individual high-characteristic-decile-minus-low-characteristic-decile hedge returns for SIZE, BM, R1, R212, TURN, ILLIQ, ACC, AG, ISSUE, IVOL, PROFIT, and SUE. The corresponding characteristic definitions are: SIZE: Natural logarithm of the firm's equity market value; Table 2 describes market capitalization in billions of dollars.; BM: Logarithm of book equity for the fiscal year-end in a calendar year divided by market equity at the end of December of that year. The source does not specify the logarithm base.; R1: Stock return from the immediately preceding month. For the monthly cross-sectional regressions, the source says R1 is already lagged one month, so it is used at t−1.; R212: Cumulative return over the 11 months ending at the beginning of the previous month (months t−12 through t−2). The paper does not state the compounding/aggregation formula.; TURN: Logarithm of share turnover, measured as monthly trading volume divided by total shares outstanding. The Section 2 definition supplies the log transformation; the Table 2 note states the underlying ratio without restating the log, which is an omission rather than an incompatible definition. The source does not specify the logarithm base.; ILLIQ: Monthly mean across trading days of the absolute daily stock return divided by daily dollar trading volume, multiplied by 10^6. D is the number of trading days in month t.; ACC: Change in non-cash current assets, minus change in current liabilities excluding short-term debt and taxes payable, minus depreciation expense; divided by average total assets.; AG: Year-on-year percentage change in total assets.; ISSUE: Change in shares outstanding from 11 months ago. The source does not report a denominator or further scaling.; IVOL: Within-month standard deviation of residuals from a Fama–French (1993) three-factor regression estimated with daily data.; PROFIT: Earnings divided by book equity, with earnings defined as income before extraordinary items.; SUE: Most recently announced quarterly earnings less earnings four quarters earlier, standardized by the standard deviation estimated over the prior eight quarters.. Each characteristic is winsorized each month at the 0.005 and 0.995 fractiles. Portfolio sorts use lagged characteristic values; Section 4.1 does not give one uniform numerical lag for every characteristic.
dependent_variable.formula: ln(1 + R_EW,t), where R_EW,t = (1/12) * sum over the 12 individual anomaly hedge-portfolio returns.

dependent_variable.formula: R*_{jt} = R_{jt} − RF_t − Σ[k=1..5] β_{jk,t−1} F_{kt}, where RF is the one-year T-bill rate and F_k is factor realization plus associated risk premium.

review_notes: Source-first scope: retain Table 3 full-period attenuation trends for the two outcomes the introduction identifies as central: anomaly hedge-portfolio returns (Panel A) and monthly Fama–MacBeth characteristic premiums (Panel B). Include 12 anomaly-specific series plus the equally weighted hedge composite for NYAM; use the Table 2 monthly cross-sectional regression as required construction for Panel B.

Population choice: NYAM is the paper’s stated base sample (1976–2011). Nasdaq results are reported in parallel but use a shorter sample beginning in 1983; under the principal-base-sample boundary, they are not included as an additional family. Table 4–6 discovery/period/decimalization and arbitrage-proxy analyses are follow-up explanations and are excluded.

Table 3 hedge outcomes are raw returns. Do not import the factor risk adjustment used for the FM characteristic-premium outcome into the hedge-return trends. The supplied source states an equally weighted high-decile-long/low-decile-short formation rule, but the later R1 interpretation describes the reverse direction while attaching it to the same negative Table 2 return; preserve this genuine conflict.

The source gives log turnover in its Section 2 definition and gives the underlying monthly volume/shares ratio in Table 2/3 notes; the latter does not state an incompatible unlogged transformation. BM and TURN log bases are unreported; R212 aggregation and ISSUE denominator/scaling are also unreported.

Recursive fitted inputs retained: first-pass full-sample factor regressions generate the risk-adjusted return used in monthly Fama–MacBeth cross-sections; daily FF3 residual fits generate IVOL. The IVOL fit is linked to its hedge return and the EW composite. No method is inferred from linear appearance or from a family name.

review_notes: Principal family selected from the abstract/introduction and primary design: Equation (6), Table 6 future-performance regressions. The introduction frames the central contribution as the association of real activities manipulation with firms just meeting earnings benchmarks and the subsequent performance of those firms; Equation (6) directly tests that question. The eight t+1 columns are retained as parallel outcomes (AdjROA, AdjCFO) and RM measures (R&D, SG&A, production, aggregate). Earlier benchmark-incidence tests, descriptive analyses, and the asset-RM column in the separate hypothesis-1 analysis are outside this principal family. Equation (6) states i=1,2,3, but the paper calls t+2/t+3 results robustness and Table 6 reports t+1, so later horizons are not separate baseline entries.

Source conflict: Equation (6) and the Table 6 coefficient row identify the current performance control as AdjROA_t, while the equation printed in the Table 6 header labels it ROA_t. The extraction uses AdjROA_t, supported by Equation (6) and the row label, and preserves the header conflict in model review notes.

Source numbering conflict: the Aggregate RM definition calls its production component “production model 3” multiplied by −1, while the displayed production-cost regression is Equation (4), and individual Production RM definitions identify model 4. The aggregate construction therefore preserves the paper’s wording and flags the inconsistent model number; the production-cost fit is retained as the required construction dependency.

Equation (1) timing conflict: its paragraph says estimates cover 1988–2000, while the general Table 1 estimation description states 1988–2002 for equations 1–4. Both statements are preserved for the R&D construction fit.
results_review_notes: Retained family is the eight Table 6 t+1 fits only: four RM samples in Panel A and the same four in Panel B. Untabulated t+2 and t+3 results and Table 5 correlations are excluded.

models.model_label: Signed abnormal accruals — LAW
models.sample_description: Firm-year observations from the COMPUSTAT Global Industrial and Commercial file, 1996–2004. The sample requires fully consolidated audited observations with nonmissing dependent and independent variables, retains countries with investor-protection measures, and excludes Japan, South Korea, India, Pakistan, and financial institutions. It also removes the top and bottom 1 percent of abnormal accruals and observations with absolute studentized residuals greater than 3. At least three consecutive years of data are required to construct abnormal accruals, making 1996 the first test year.
models.method_details: The paper describes equation (1) as a fixed-effects model with year-specific dummies and two-digit-SIC industry dummies, but does not identify the underlying estimator from the allowed vocabulary.

dependent_variable.name: AB_ACCR
dependent_variable.definition: Signed abnormal accruals for firm i in year t, scaled by lagged total assets. The measure is actual total accruals less predicted total accruals. Total accruals are (earnings before extraordinary items − operating cash flows) / lagged total assets; earnings before extraordinary items are net income (#32) less extraordinary items (#33). Operating cash flows and current accruals are defined in the CFO entry. Predicted accruals are [sales_t × (current accruals_t−1 / sales_t−1) − gross PPE_t × (depreciation_t−1 / gross PPE_t−1)] / lagged total assets, where depreciation_t−1 is Compustat item #11 less item #13, with missing amortization item #13 set to zero; gross PPE is item #77 and lagged total assets item #89. Missing deferred-tax, untaxed-reserve, and minority-interest values used in operating cash flows are treated as zero. The construction is formula-based; the paper reports no fitted construction regression.
dependent_variable.formula: AB_ACCR_it = actual total accruals_it − predicted total accruals_it; actual total accruals_it = (earnings before extraordinary items_it − operating cash flows_it) / total assets_i,t−1; predicted total accruals_it = [sales_it × (current accruals_i,t−1 / sales_i,t−1) − gross PPE_it × ((D&A #11 − amortization #13)_i,t−1 / gross PPE_i,t−1)] / total assets_i,t−1.

independent_variables.name: CFO
independent_variables.definition: Operating cash flows for firm i in year t scaled by lagged total assets. The paper defines operating cash flows as earnings before extraordinary items plus depreciation and amortization (#11), changes in deferred income tax (#105), untaxed reserve (#108), other liabilities (#109), and minority interest (#27), minus current accruals. The sixpoint index

This index is based on six specific elements of investor protection dealing with the
ability of outside (minority) investors to challenge the control of the firm by managers
and dominant (inside) owners. Country-level scores can range from 0 to 6 based on the
sum of six indicator variables that reflect shareholder rights: (a) the ability to vote by
mail, (b) the ability to gain control of shares during the shareholders’ meeting, (c) the
possibility of cumulative voting for directors, (d) the ease of calling an extraordinary
shareholders’ meeting, (e) the availability of mechanisms allowing minority
shareholders to make legal claims against directors, and (f) shareholders have
preemptive rights that can be waived only by a shareholders’ vote. Larger values of the
antidirector rights’ index indicate that minority shareholders are better protected
against expropriation by management and controlling shareholders.

The sixpoint index

This index is based on six specific elements of investor protection dealing with the
ability of outside (minority) investors to challenge the control of the firm by managers
and dominant (inside) owners. Country-level scores can range from 0 to 6 based on the
sum of six indicator variables that reflect shareholder rights: (a) the ability to vote by
mail, (b) the ability to gain control of shares during the shareholders’ meeting, (c) the
possibility of cumulative voting for directors, (d) the ease of calling an extraordinary
shareholders’ meeting, (e) the availability of mechanisms allowing minority
shareholders to make legal claims against directors, and (f) shareholders have
preemptive rights that can be waived only by a shareholders’ vote. Larger values of the
antidirector rights’ index indicate that minority shareholders are better protected
against expropriation by management and controlling shareholders.

dependent_variable.name: AB_ACCR
dependent_variable.definition: Signed abnormal accruals for firm i in year t, scaled by lagged total assets. The measure is actual total accruals less predicted total accruals. Total accruals are (earnings before extraordinary items − operating cash flows) / lagged total assets; earnings before extraordinary items are net income (#32) less extraordinary items (#33). Operating cash flows and current accruals are defined in the CFO entry. Predicted accruals are [sales_t × (current accruals_t−1 / sales_t−1) − gross PPE_t × (depreciation_t−1 / gross PPE_t−1)] / lagged total assets, where depreciation_t−1 is Compustat item #11 less item #13, with missing amortization item #13 set to zero; gross PPE is item #77 and lagged total assets item #89. Missing deferred-tax, untaxed-reserve, and minority-interest values used in operating cash flows are treated as zero. The construction is formula-based; the paper reports no fitted construction regression.

models.method_details: The paper describes equation (1) as a fixed-effects model with year-specific dummies and two-digit-SIC industry dummies, but does not identify the underlying estimator from the allowed vocabulary.

dependent_variable.name: AB_ACCR
dependent_variable.definition: Signed abnormal accruals for firm i in year t, scaled by lagged total assets. The measure is actual total accruals less predicted total accruals. Total accruals are (earnings before extraordinary items − operating cash flows) / lagged total assets; earnings before extraordinary items are net income (#32) less extraordinary items (#33). Operating cash flows and current accruals are defined in the CFO entry. Predicted accruals are [sales_t × (current accruals_t−1 / sales_t−1) − gross PPE_t × (depreciation_t−1 / gross PPE_t−1)] / lagged total assets, where depreciation_t−1 is Compustat item #11 less item #13, with missing amortization item #13 set to zero; gross PPE is item #77 and lagged total assets item #89. Missing deferred-tax, untaxed-reserve, and minority-interest values used in operating cash flows are treated as zero. The construction is formula-based; the paper reports no fitted construction regression.
dependent_variable.formula: AB_ACCR_it = actual total accruals_it − predicted total accruals_it; actual total accruals_it = (earnings before extraordinary items_it − operating cash flows_it) / total assets_i,t−1; predicted total accruals_it = [sales_it × (current accruals_i,t−1 / sales_i,t−1) − gross PPE_it × ((D&A #11 − amortization #13)_i,t−1 / gross PPE_i,t−1)] / total assets_i,t−1.

models.sample_description: Full earnings-conservatism firm-year sample, 1995–2004, from COMPUSTAT Global Industrial and Commercial and Global Issue files. It requires fully consolidated audited observations with nonmissing dependent and independent variables, retains countries with investor-protection measures, and excludes Japan, South Korea, India, Pakistan, and financial institutions. It also removes the top and bottom 1 percent of annual returns and earnings per share before extraordinary items and observations with absolute studentized residuals greater than 3. The sample requires at least two consecutive years of data, making 1995 the first test year; the earnings-conservatism analysis is smaller because it requires additional stock-return data.

standard_errors.details: Rogers (1993) inference is robust to heteroscedasticity and clustered by country; footnote 10 states the 42 country clusters yield 42 degrees of freedom for t-statistics.

evidence.quote: robust to heteroscedasticity and country clustering

The Rogers 1993 approach treats each country as a
cluster and estimates the variance as if there were only 42 observations and the

evidence.quote: La Porta et al. (1998) develop what they
The sixpoint index

This index is based on six specific elements of investor protection dealing with the
ability of outside (minority) investors to challenge the control of the firm by managers
and dominant (inside) owners. Country-level scores can range from 0 to 6 based on the
sum of six indicator variables that reflect shareholder rights: (a) the ability to vote by
mail, (b) the ability to gain control of shares during the shareholders’ meeting, (c) the
possibility of cumulative voting for directors, (d) the ease of calling an extraordinary
shareholders’ meeting, (e) the availability of mechanisms allowing minority
shareholders to make legal claims against directors, and (f) shareholders have
preemptive rights that can be waived only by a shareholders’ vote. Larger values of the
antidirector rights’ index indicate that minority shareholders are better protected
against expropriation by management and controlling shareholders.

standard_errors.details: Rogers (1993) inference is robust to heteroscedasticity and clustered by country; footnote 10 states the 42 country clusters yield 42 degrees of freedom for t-statistics.

evidence.quote: robust to heteroscedasticity and country clustering

The Rogers 1993 approach treats each country as a
cluster and estimates the variance as if there were only 42 observations and the

review_notes: Selected the paper’s three stated earnings-quality analyses as the principal full-sample regression families: signed abnormal accruals (equation 1/Table 4), loss reporting (equation 2/Table 5), and earnings conservatism (equation 3/Table 6). The introduction names these three outcomes, and the research-design/results sections test each against investor-protection proxies; each table reports five proxy-specific full specifications. This is a substantive earnings-quality study, not a method-development paper.

The signed abnormal-accrual measure is computed by the paper’s reported formula from prior-year ratios and accounting items; no fitted construction regression is reported, so no supporting regression dependency is added. Later separate Big 4 and non-Big 4 sample partitions described after Table 6 are follow-up partitions and are excluded from the principal family.

The supplied reading text renders equation operators in equations (1)–(3) as hyphens, while visual inspection of physical PDF pages 14, 16, and 17 confirms plus signs; equation_text uses the printed PDF notation and quotations remain literal to the supplied reading.

Equation (3) prints MB*DR for both β25 and β26, but Table 6 reports MB*DR and MB*R as separate coefficient rows. The equation text preserves the printed duplicate; the 27-term RHS inventory follows Table 6, and the discrepancy is flagged for review.
Equation (2) prints P(LOSS=1) equal to a linear predictor while Table 5 labels the models logistic regression. The equation is preserved as printed, and no inverse-logit link is added.

Footnote 5 specifies all six ANTI_DIR rights and the 0–6 score; footnotes 6, 8, and 9 clarify the analysis windows and missing-value handling for depreciation and operating cash flows. Footnote 10 says country-clustered Rogers t-statistics use 42 country degrees of freedom, whereas Table 5 reports asymptotic z-statistics; this inference discrepancy is preserved for review. The supplied reading text on page 31 is corrupted after the first footnote 6 sentences; the physical PDF page was inspected, and citations use only intact supplied text.

models.model_label: Absolute value of unexpected accruals
models.sample_description: Industry- and size-matched firm-year sample of Big 6 clients during 1986–1995. Candidates are U.S. corporations on the Compustat full-coverage and research files with no fiscal-year-end change during the ten-year period. The screened sample excludes observations without Compustat financial data or an identifiable auditor, non-Big-6 audits, modified opinions within two years of fiscal year-end, and auditor changes within one year of fiscal year-end. Short-tenure firms are matched to medium- and long-tenure firms in the same fiscal year and four-, three-, or two-digit SIC industry depending on availability, using the closest book value of total assets. The final matched sample also excludes observations in the extreme one percent of variables used to test the hypotheses. This test uses the unexpected-accrual sample.

scope.quote: We measure conditional conservatism using Basu’s (1997) asymmetric timeliness coefficient, Ball and Shivakumar’s (2005) accrual-based measure of asymmetric timeliness, and Khan and Watts’ (2009) firm–year measure of conditional conservatism.
To test whether more conservative firms experience lower crash risk, we first estimate the following augmented Basu (1997) model following the method of Francis and Martin (2010):
Model (2) reports the results of estimating Eq. (9) with firm fixed effects

dependencies.quote: The firm-specific weekly return, denoted by W, is defined as the natural log of one plus the residual return from the following expanded market model regression

CRASHt+1 is an indicator variable equal to one if a firm experiences one or more firm-specific weekly returns falling 3.2 or more standard deviations below the mean firm-specific weekly return for fiscal year t + 1, and zero otherwise
NCSKEWt is the negative coefficient of skewness of firm-specific weekly returns in fiscal year t
SIGMAt is the standard deviation of firm-specific weekly returns in fiscal year t
RETt is the average firm-specific weekly return in fiscal year t times 100
COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Firm-specific weekly return conversion, physical PDF page 15): W_j,tau = ln(1 + epsilon_j,tau).

scope.quote: We measure conditional conservatism using Basu’s (1997) asymmetric timeliness coefficient, Ball and Shivakumar’s (2005) accrual-based measure of asymmetric timeliness, and Khan and Watts’ (2009) firm–year measure of conditional conservatism.
To test whether more conservative firms experience lower crash risk, we first estimate the following augmented Basu (1997) model following the method of Francis and Martin (2010):
Model (2) reports the results of estimating Eq. (9) with firm fixed effects
and all other control variables except OPAQUE

NCSKEWt is the negative coefficient of skewness of firm-specific weekly returns in fiscal year t

scope.quote: We measure conditional conservatism using Basu’s (1997) asymmetric timeliness coefficient, Ball and Shivakumar’s (2005) accrual-based measure of asymmetric timeliness, and Khan and Watts’ (2009) firm–year measure of conditional conservatism.
Our second set of tests use the Ball–Shivakumar (2005, 2006, 2008) accrual-based measure of asymmetric timeliness to examine the impact of conditional conservatism on future crash risk.
Table 4 are largely the same as in Table 3, except for the difference in the conservatism measurement

The four control blocks apply to the control-variable vector as printed.
Similar to the Basu regression tests, we also replace CRASH with NCSKEW in Eq. (10) to examine the relation between conservatism and negative firm-specific return skewness.

sample.quote: sample period is from 1964 to 2007.
Observations 88,734

dependencies.quote: The firm-specific weekly return, denoted by W, is defined as the natural log of one plus the residual return from the following expanded market model regression

CRASHt+1 is an indicator variable equal to one if a firm experiences one or more firm-specific weekly returns falling 3.2 or more standard deviations below the mean firm-specific weekly return for fiscal year t + 1, and zero otherwise
NCSKEWt is the negative coefficient of skewness of firm-specific weekly returns in fiscal year t
SIGMAt is the standard deviation of firm-specific weekly returns in fiscal year t
RETt is the average firm-specific weekly return in fiscal year t times 100
COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Firm-specific weekly return conversion, physical PDF page 15): W_j,tau = ln(1 + epsilon_j,tau).

Principal question selected from the abstract/introduction and Section 3 before reviewing the prior result: whether conditional conservatism predicts lower future crash risk. The paper tests this with Basu, Ball–Shivakumar, and Khan–Watts conservatism measures and both CRASH and NCSKEW proxies. Retained the full-sample full-control firm-fixed-effect columns (2) in Tables 3 and 4 and full-control column (2) in Table 5, with one model per primary proxy. Excluded reduced-sample OPAQUE columns, the Table 3/4 no-firm-fixed-effect comparisons, Table 5 controls-only columns, marginal-effect analysis, later information-asymmetry interactions, and robustness/time-trend tests.

The first-sweep result omitted the fitted expanded weekly market model (Equation (7)), although its residuals are transformed into W and generate the retained CRASH, NCSKEW, SIGMA, and RET variables. Added one repeated firm-year supporting fit and linked each dependent baseline to the W-derived variables it uses.
results_review_notes: Table 1 values are copied for retained variables and their directly related model terms. Main-sample controls and future crash-risk measures use Table 1 N=114,548; the Basu-specific X/R/D group uses N=95,938; the Ball–Shivakumar TCA/∆REV/GPPE/DCF/CF group uses N=88,734.

Table 2 correlations and Table 5 Panel B economic-significance quantities are outside descriptive-statistics scope. OPAQUE and robustness-only quantities are excluded because they do not occur in the assigned selected column (2) baselines.
No means, standard deviations, percentiles, interaction summaries, p-values, or other statistics were calculated from other values.

scope.quote:
In testing whether economies of scale exist for tax planning, I first perform
empirical tests on a broad sample of U.S. domestic and multinational corporations.
I then focus the analysis on a subsample of U.S. multinational corporations only.
I estimate the following ordinary least squares (OLS) regression using a broad sample of firms to test Hypotheses 1, 2, and 3:

I use two different proxies for foreign operations in the empirical tests. I use the MNC dummy variable in (1) to determine whether multinational firms have lower or higher ETRs than other firms. I use the ratio of foreign assets to total worldwide assets, FOROPER, in (2) below to determine whether firms with more extensive foreign operations have lower or higher ETRs than other firms:
While MNC tests whether systematic differences exist between the ETRs of multinational and domestic-only companies, FOROPER tests whether economies of scale exist for foreign tax planning.

Table 5 presents
results of regressions of worldwide ETRs on test and control variables, for a sample
of multinational corporations only. In particular, Table 5 presents estimated coefficients for (3) and (4). I perform these regressions to determine whether the relations between ETRs and the extent of foreign operations in a sample of multinational corporations only are different from the broader sample of firms.

Table 6 presents results of regressions of U.S. and foreign ETRs on test and
control variables for the sample of multinational corporations only. In particular,
Table 6 presents estimated coefficients for (5) and (6). I perform these regressions
to determine whether the relations between ETRs and test variables differ between
the U.S. and foreign tax jurisdictions.

estimation_procedure.description: Matched difference-in-differences design. Each mandatory-IFRS adopter is matched without replacement to a benchmark firm in the same industry and legal-enforcement category, minimizing the penalty ((MVI−MVB)/MVI)^2 + ((BTMI−BTMB)/BTMI)^2 + ((NII−NIB)/NII)^2. MVI/MVB is the adopter/benchmark market value of equity, BTMI/BTMB is their book-to-market ratio, and NII/NIB is their income before extraordinary items scaled by average total assets; each measure is averaged over the three years before the adopter’s adoption year. The rule-of-law score for 2005 defines strong (above 1.30) and weak (below 1.30) enforcement. The authors relax the industry match for 26 adopters but retain the legal-enforcement category. The estimation panel is balanced with three pre-adoption years (2002–2004) and two post-adoption years (2006–2007); 2005 is omitted. The treatment contrast is Post × IFRS.

scope.quote: We study the effects of mandatory IFRS adoption on three groups of accounting quality metrics: income smoothing, reporting aggressiveness, and earnings management to meet or beat a target.
Furthermore, we find that the effects we observe hold mainly for IFRS adopters in strong enforcement countries.
We focus on an important institutional factor that has been shown to significantly affect accounting quality: the strength of legal enforcement.
Given these competing predictions, we use two-tailed tests to provide evidence on the effects of IFRS adoption for firms in strong enforcement countries.
In addition to smoothing reported income managers can target salient earnings benchmarks.

We consider two earnings benchmarks, the positive earnings threshold and the analyst consensus earnings forecast, and test whether firms appear more likely to manage earnings toward these benchmarks following IFRS adoption.
We also include industry fixed effects and estimate (3) using logistic regression.

estimation_procedure.description: Matched difference-in-differences design. Each mandatory-IFRS adopter is matched without replacement to a benchmark firm in the same industry and legal-enforcement category, minimizing the penalty ((MVI−MVB)/MVI)^2 + ((BTMI−BTMB)/BTMI)^2 + ((NII−NIB)/NII)^2. MVI/MVB is the adopter/benchmark market value of equity, BTMI/BTMB is their book-to-market ratio, and NII/NIB is their income before extraordinary items scaled by average total assets; each measure is averaged over the three years before the adopter’s adoption year. The rule-of-law score for 2005 defines strong (above 1.30) and weak (below 1.30) enforcement. The authors relax the industry match for 26 adopters but retain the legal-enforcement category. The estimation panel is balanced with three pre-adoption years (2002–2004) and two post-adoption years (2006–2007); 2005 is omitted. The treatment contrast is Post × IFRS.

scope.quote: We study the effects of mandatory IFRS adoption on three groups of accounting quality metrics: income smoothing, reporting aggressiveness, and earnings management to meet or beat a target.
Furthermore, we find that the effects we observe hold mainly for IFRS adopters in strong enforcement countries.
We focus on an important institutional factor that has been shown to significantly affect accounting quality: the strength of legal enforcement.
Given these competing predictions, we use two-tailed tests to provide evidence on the effects of IFRS adoption for firms in strong enforcement countries.
In addition to smoothing reported income managers can target salient earnings benchmarks.

We consider two earnings benchmarks, the positive earnings threshold and the analyst consensus earnings forecast, and test whether firms appear more likely to manage earnings toward these benchmarks following IFRS adoption.
We also include industry fixed effects and estimate (3) using logistic regression.

estimation_procedure.description: Matched difference-in-differences design. Each mandatory-IFRS adopter is matched without replacement to a benchmark firm in the same industry and legal-enforcement category, minimizing the penalty ((MVI−MVB)/MVI)^2 + ((BTMI−BTMB)/BTMI)^2 + ((NII−NIB)/NII)^2. MVI/MVB is the adopter/benchmark market value of equity, BTMI/BTMB is their book-to-market ratio, and NII/NIB is their income before extraordinary items scaled by average total assets; each measure is averaged over the three years before the adopter’s adoption year. The rule-of-law score for 2005 defines strong (above 1.30) and weak (below 1.30) enforcement. The authors relax the industry match for 26 adopters but retain the legal-enforcement category. The estimation panel is balanced with three pre-adoption years (2002–2004) and two post-adoption years (2006–2007); 2005 is omitted. The treatment contrast is Post × IFRS.

scope.quote: We study the effects of mandatory IFRS adoption on three groups of accounting quality metrics: income smoothing, reporting aggressiveness, and earnings management to meet or beat a target.
Furthermore, we find that the effects we observe hold mainly for IFRS adopters in strong enforcement countries.
We focus on an important institutional factor that has been shown to significantly affect accounting quality: the strength of legal enforcement.
Given these competing predictions, we use two-tailed tests to provide evidence on the effects of IFRS adoption for firms in strong enforcement countries.
In addition to smoothing reported income managers can target salient earnings benchmarks.

We consider two earnings benchmarks, the positive earnings threshold and the analyst consensus earnings forecast, and test whether firms appear more likely to manage earnings toward these benchmarks following IFRS adoption.
We also include industry fixed effects and estimate (3) using logistic regression.

estimation_procedure.description: Matched difference-in-differences design. Each mandatory-IFRS adopter is matched without replacement to a benchmark firm in the same industry and legal-enforcement category, minimizing the penalty ((MVI−MVB)/MVI)^2 + ((BTMI−BTMB)/BTMI)^2 + ((NII−NIB)/NII)^2. MVI/MVB is the adopter/benchmark market value of equity, BTMI/BTMB is their book-to-market ratio, and NII/NIB is their income before extraordinary items scaled by average total assets; each measure is averaged over the three years before the adopter’s adoption year. The rule-of-law score for 2005 defines strong (above 1.30) and weak (below 1.30) enforcement. The authors relax the industry match for 26 adopters but retain the legal-enforcement category. The estimation panel is balanced with three pre-adoption years (2002–2004) and two post-adoption years (2006–2007); 2005 is omitted. The treatment contrast is Post × IFRS.

scope.quote: We study the effects of mandatory IFRS adoption on three groups of accounting quality metrics: income smoothing, reporting aggressiveness, and earnings management to meet or beat a target.
Furthermore, we find that the effects we observe hold mainly for IFRS adopters in strong enforcement countries.
We focus on an important institutional factor that has been shown to significantly affect accounting quality: the strength of legal enforcement.
Given these competing predictions, we use two-tailed tests to provide evidence on the effects of IFRS adoption for firms in strong enforcement countries.
Next, we examine whether the adoption of IFRS is associated with an increase in signed accruals after controlling for other determinants.
We also include industry fixed effects and estimate (4) using OLS regressions.

estimation_procedure.description: Matched difference-in-differences design. Each mandatory-IFRS adopter is matched without replacement to a benchmark firm in the same industry and legal-enforcement category, minimizing the penalty ((MVI−MVB)/MVI)^2 + ((BTMI−BTMB)/BTMI)^2 + ((NII−NIB)/NII)^2. MVI/MVB is the adopter/benchmark market value of equity, BTMI/BTMB is their book-to-market ratio, and NII/NIB is their income before extraordinary items scaled by average total assets; each measure is averaged over the three years before the adopter’s adoption year. The rule-of-law score for 2005 defines strong (above 1.30) and weak (below 1.30) enforcement. The authors relax the industry match for 26 adopters but retain the legal-enforcement category. The estimation panel is balanced with three pre-adoption years (2002–2004) and two post-adoption years (2006–2007); 2005 is omitted. The treatment contrast is Post × IFRS.

Given these competing predictions, we use two-tailed tests to provide evidence on the effects of IFRS adoption for firms in strong enforcement countries.

independent_variables.name: OC_CJRS_{t-1}
independent_variables.definition: Lagged CEO-level modified Malmendier–Tate option-based overconfidence indicator. Average annual option moneyness is realizable value per exercisable option divided by estimated average exercise price; the latter is fiscal-year-end share price less realizable value per option. A CEO is overconfident after holding options more than 100 percent in the money at least twice during the sample period; the indicator is one beginning with the first qualifying occurrence and zero otherwise.
independent_variables.formula: RV/option = total realizable value of exercisable options / number of exercisable options; average exercise price = fiscal-year-end stock price − RV/option; moneyness = RV/option / average exercise price; OC_CJRS=1 from first occurrence after ≥2 option-holding observations with moneyness>100%, else 0

evidence.quote: First, we compute the realizable value per option as the total realizable value of the exercisable options divided by the total number of exercisable options.
Second, we estimate the average exercise price of the options by subtracting the realizable value per option from the stock price at the fiscal year-end.
Finally, the average percent moneyness of the options is calculated as the per-option realizable value divided by the estimated average exercise price.
we require that the CEOs hold stock options at least twice during our sample period that are more than 100 percent in the money.
The measure OC_CJRS takes the value of one beginning with the first time the CEO exhibits the above option-holding behavior and zero otherwise

independent_variables.name: OC_CJRS_{t-1}
independent_variables.definition: Lagged CEO-level modified Malmendier–Tate option-based overconfidence indicator. Average annual option moneyness is realizable value per exercisable option divided by estimated average exercise price; the latter is fiscal-year-end share price less realizable value per option. A CEO is overconfident after holding options more than 100 percent in the money at least twice during the sample period; the indicator is one beginning with the first qualifying occurrence and zero otherwise.
independent_variables.formula: RV/option = total realizable value of exercisable options / number of exercisable options; average exercise price = fiscal-year-end stock price − RV/option; moneyness = RV/option / average exercise price; OC_CJRS=1 from first occurrence after ≥2 option-holding observations with moneyness>100%, else 0

evidence.quote: First, we compute the realizable value per option as the total realizable value of the exercisable options divided by the total number of exercisable options.
Second, we estimate the average exercise price of the options by subtracting the realizable value per option from the stock price at the fiscal year-end.
Finally, the average percent moneyness of the options is calculated as the per-option realizable value divided by the estimated average exercise price.
we require that the CEOs hold stock options at least twice during our sample period that are more than 100 percent in the money.
The measure OC_CJRS takes the value of one beginning with the first time the CEO exhibits the above option-holding behavior and zero otherwise

independent_variables.name: OC_CJRS_{t-1}
independent_variables.definition: Lagged CEO-level modified Malmendier–Tate option-based overconfidence indicator. Average annual option moneyness is realizable value per exercisable option divided by estimated average exercise price; the latter is fiscal-year-end share price less realizable value per option. A CEO is overconfident after holding options more than 100 percent in the money at least twice during the sample period; the indicator is one beginning with the first qualifying occurrence and zero otherwise.
independent_variables.formula: RV/option = total realizable value of exercisable options / number of exercisable options; average exercise price = fiscal-year-end stock price − RV/option; moneyness = RV/option / average exercise price; OC_CJRS=1 from first occurrence after ≥2 option-holding observations with moneyness>100%, else 0

evidence.quote: First, we compute the realizable value per option as the total realizable value of the exercisable options divided by the total number of exercisable options.
Second, we estimate the average exercise price of the options by subtracting the realizable value per option from the stock price at the fiscal year-end.
Finally, the average percent moneyness of the options is calculated as the per-option realizable value divided by the estimated average exercise price.
we require that the CEOs hold stock options at least twice during our sample period that are more than 100 percent in the money.
The measure OC_CJRS takes the value of one beginning with the first time the CEO exhibits the above option-holding behavior and zero otherwise

review_notes: Source-first scope: retain Table 3, the main full-sample analysis. The introduction says the central result is robust across the three overconfidence measures and three crash-risk measures; Table 3 supplies the nine corresponding outcome/proxy fits. The CEO-turnover change analysis, cross-sectional moderators, and later robustness tests are not included.

Equation (2) is printed on source page 10 and is used for the Table 3 fits. The supplied page-10 reading has corrupted mathematical glyphs; physical PDF page 10 was rendered and visually checked. The displayed equation has an intercept, one CEO-overconfidence measure at t−1, controls at t−1, and an error. Table 3 supplies the full control-variable inventory.

Retain the exact Table 3 per-column counts: CRASH 17,513 / 16,254 / 16,254; NCSKEW 17,568 / 16,299 / 16,299; DUVOL 17,568 / 16,299 / 16,299. The paper does not explain the difference between its page-6 base counts (17,568 and 16,229 for the additional OC measures) and the column counts; no cause is inferred.

Equation (1) is a required fitted input because it constructs firm-specific weekly returns used in all three crash-risk outcomes. The verified reading supplies the coordinator-checked equation transcription. The paper does not name the estimator or report the number of firm-year fits; its 26-observation rule is only a minimum.

The excess-investment residual regression is required to form OC_SZ/OC_MSZ and is included as a supporting fit. Its estimator, exact sample, growth definitions, and regression grouping are not reported. The OPAQUE discretionary-accrual construction and INCENTIVE_STK operational formula also remain partly unspecified in this paper.

review_notes: Scope selected from the paper: retain the two-stage governance/accounting-discretion design, all four accounting-discretion proxies shown in the principal Tables 3–5 (|ABACC|, SMOOTH, FREQ, DISCIND), and the three distinct future-performance outcomes. The authors say DISCIND is the measure they primarily discuss for parsimony, but also present each component in every table and acknowledge its separate interpretation; this extraction therefore preserves the parallel main proxies. Later restatement, cluster, serial-correlation, and other sensitivity analyses are excluded.

Source conflict: printed equation (5) omits MGR, but Table 3 reports MGR in each regression. Equation (6) sums governance coefficients j=8 through 17 and, using the printed Eq. (5) mapping, excludes MGR; the paper does not reconcile this.

Source conflict: the Table 1 note defines R&D in STCLAIM as R&D expense scaled by total assets, while section 4 says R&D/sales. The Table 1 AUDEXP note uses a 15% sales-share threshold, while section 4 uses a 15% firm-count threshold.

Source issue: endnote 6 says ROA is also included in the normal-accrual fit in equation (3), but the printed equation (3) omits it. Equation (7a) and (7b) also print gamma_2 on both the risk and current-performance terms, while Table 4 reports them separately. These labels are preserved without correction.

The paper calls the reported models regressions but does not name the estimator. Footnote 15 describes an untabulated FIML/GLS/AR(1) alternative as a serial-correlation sensitivity analysis; it is not assigned to the published tables.

Table 5 source conflict: the four columns are labeled |ABACC|, SMOOTH, FREQ, and DISCIND, but the table note states that hedge portfolios are sorted on DISCIND. The sort basis for columns 1–3 is unresolved; no alternate measure is silently substituted.

The source writes BM as #60/#24 × #25 without parentheses; its intended grouping is not specified. FREQ is the fraction of prior 12 quarterly surprises, while the paper does not state how missing quarters are handled within that window.

review_notes: Source-first scope: Table 5 equation (4) is the principal family testing whether the Big 6 auditor effect on DAC differs between income-increasing (Cp) and income-decreasing (Cg) incentive settings. The full sample is retained as the benchmark; Cp and Cg are co-primary directional populations needed for the central question. Eq. (2) DAC construction and annual Eq. (3) probit fits are required supporting regressions. Table 3 mean comparisons, the pooled Eq. (3) probit (not used to form retained Mills ratios), AWCA, alternate incentive proxies, and later sensitivity partitions are excluded.

Applied the sweep clarification distinguishing a substantive empirical question from development of an input measure: the paper asks a substantive audit-effectiveness question, and Eq. (2) is supporting because its residual is the retained DAC outcome. No scope revision was needed for the first two checkpointed substantive studies.

Table 5 reports aggregate observation totals across 15 annual fits; per-year second-stage N is unknown. The annual probit support is also repeated by year with no per-year N. The pooled first-stage probit is reported in Table 4, but does not generate the inverse Mills ratios used in Table 5 and is excluded.

Table 5 note refers to the auditor-choice model as equation (4), but equation (4) is the accrual-choice equation; the definitions and procedure identify the probit in equation (3) as the source of Lambda.

Equation (4) prose defines CFO as operating cash flows scaled by total assets, while the Table 5 row label specifies lagged total assets; the table-specific scaled measure is retained with the discrepancy flagged.

The pooled and annual Table 4 estimates are alternative presentations of equation (3); the retained annual probits are the ones actually used in the Table 5 selection correction. Equation (2) is estimated separately by two-digit SIC and year; Cp/Cg classification is at firm-year level, as endnote 18 clarifies.
