sample.quote: Our initial sample includes all firm-years for which a 10-K report with at least 3,000 words was filed during 1994–2014.

Specifically, for each firm-year observation, we match weekly returns to the fiscal year if the last trading day of a calendar week falls within the 12-month period ending three months after the firm’s fiscal year-end.
We then delete observations with non-positive total assets, financial firms (Standard Industrial Classification, or SIC, codes 6000–6999)
utilities firms (SIC codes 4900– 4999), low-priced firms (fiscal year-end price lower than $1), observations with fewer than 26 weeks of stock return data
The above procedure yields our sample of 52,879 firm-year observations for 7,012 unique firms.

sample.quote: Our initial sample includes all firm-years for which a 10-K report with at least 3,000 words was filed during 1994–2014.

Specifically, for each firm-year observation, we match weekly returns to the fiscal year if the last trading day of a calendar week falls within the 12-month period ending three months after the firm’s fiscal year-end.
We then delete observations with non-positive total assets, financial firms (Standard Industrial Classification, or SIC, codes 6000–6999)
utilities firms (SIC codes 4900– 4999), low-priced firms (fiscal year-end price lower than $1), observations with fewer than 26 weeks of stock return data
The above procedure yields our sample of 52,879 firm-year observations for 7,012 unique firms.

review_notes: Table 3 is the principal full-sample family: Equation (4) tests modified Fog readability against one-year-ahead crash risk using NCSKEW, DUVOL, and CRASH as parallel outcomes. The Introduction separately highlights the earnings-management interaction and later tables test cross-sectional partitions; those are other contributions/secondary tests rather than additional baseline outcomes for the selected readability-to-crash-risk question.

The Table 3 baseline contains all 16 RHS terms in Equation (4), including OPAQUE squared, and includes year and industry fixed effects, an unreported intercept, and standard errors clustered by firm. The three columns each report N=52,879.

Supporting fitted inputs include the expanded index model that generates W, the modified-Jones fit that generates ABACC for OPAQUE, and the CAPM beta fit used for BETA. The paper does not report the modified-Jones equation or CAPM equation/estimator; the expanded index model estimator is also unspecified. These remain explicit gaps.

The source gives conflicting MODFOG word-list thresholds: the measurement section says at least three syllables, whereas the Table 3 note and Appendix say the words exceed three syllables. The exact threshold is unresolved. The HHI share formula and the industry classification used for fixed effects are also not stated.
results_review_notes: Table 1 Panel A has the same 52,879-observation full sample as Table 3; each row retains N, mean, standard deviation, Q1, median, and Q3 as printed. RAWFOG is linked only as the upstream raw version of MODFOG. The reported OPAQUE row is exact for OPAQUE and a component of the retained squared term; no squared-term statistics were calculated.
Table 1 Panel B reports one-year-ahead outcome means by MODFOG tercile. Tercile N is not reported. The high-versus-low p-values are univariate tests and were not recorded as data-value descriptives.
The Table 3 notes explicitly identify the intercept as unreported; all 16 frozen predictors are tabulated in each selected outcome column. Year and industry fixed effects are reported as Yes.

The original Table 3 p. 47 PDF is the authority for superscript star counts; several markers were omitted or garbled in the verified text. The current extraction preserves the viewed table markers and p. 48 legend.

Table 1 Panel B reports univariate means of crash outcomes by MODFOG tercile but omits tercile sample Ns; the retained groups preserve this limitation and do not copy Panel B p-values as data descriptives.
The Table 3 p. 47 note says the 2,028 words exceed three syllables, while the method section pp. 14–15 says at least three syllables; the frozen specification’s threshold ambiguity is preserved.

Excludes merger/acquisition firms, SIC 6000–6999 financial services and 9000–9999 nonclassifiable establishments, first-year auditor engagements, completed auditor–client relationships shorter than five years (retaining years 2–5 for relationships lasting at least five years), and firms whose nondiscretionary EPS already exceeds the consensus forecast. models.method_details: Probit model for MBE in the pooled full-sample column of Table 4.

dependent_variable.name: MBE
dependent_variable.definition: Indicator equal to one when forecast error (actual EPS minus the median consensus forecast, divided by beginning-of-fiscal-year stock price) is nonnegative while adjusted forecast error is negative. The paper specifies the median consensus forecast closest to the earnings announcement and I/B/E/S actual EPS from the Historical Summary tape for forecast-error calculations. ADJFE is NDEPS minus the median forecast; NDEPS equals actual EPS minus discretionary accruals per share (equivalently, cash flow from operations plus nondiscretionary accruals per share). Thus positive discretionary accruals allow the firm to cross the forecast threshold. Zero otherwise.
dependent_variable.formula: 1{FE ≥ 0 and ADJFE < 0}; FE = (actual EPS − median forecast) / beginning-of-year stock price; ADJFE = NDEPS − median forecast; NDEPS = actual EPS − DA per share.

evidence.quote: MBE - equals 1 if forecast error is non-negative and adjusted forecast error (earnings less discretionary accruals less analysts forecast) is less than zero; 0 otherwise
MBE - 1 if positive discretionary accruals are used to meet or beat analysts earnings forecast; 0 otherwise

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Nondiscretionary EPS and adjusted forecast error, physical PDF page 8): NDEPS = Actual EPS - Discretionary accruals per share; equivalently Cash flow from operations + Nondiscretionary accruals per share. ADJFE = NDEPS - Median consensus analysts forecast. These are deterministic transformations, not extra estimated regressions.
Forecast error is calculated as the difference between actual earnings per share and median forecasted earnings per share, divided by the stock price as of the beginning of the fiscal year
We use the median consensus forecast closest to the earnings announcement date and the I/B/E/S actual earnings per share from the I/B/E/S Historical Summary tape in our calculation of forecast error

dependent_variable.name: MBE
dependent_variable.definition: Indicator equal to one when forecast error (actual EPS minus the median consensus forecast, divided by beginning-of-fiscal-year stock price) is nonnegative while adjusted forecast error is negative. The paper specifies the median consensus forecast closest to the earnings announcement and I/B/E/S actual EPS from the Historical Summary tape for forecast-error calculations. ADJFE is NDEPS minus the median forecast; NDEPS equals actual EPS minus discretionary accruals per share (equivalently, cash flow from operations plus nondiscretionary accruals per share). Thus positive discretionary accruals allow the firm to cross the forecast threshold. Zero otherwise.
dependent_variable.formula: 1{FE ≥ 0 and ADJFE < 0}; FE = (actual EPS − median forecast) / beginning-of-year stock price; ADJFE = NDEPS − median forecast; NDEPS = actual EPS − DA per share.

evidence.quote: MBE - equals 1 if forecast error is non-negative and adjusted forecast error (earnings less discretionary accruals less analysts forecast) is less than zero; 0 otherwise

ADJFE = NDEPS - Median consensus analysts forecast. These are deterministic transformations, not extra estimated regressions.
Forecast error is calculated as the difference between actual earnings per share and median forecasted earnings per share, divided by the stock price as of the beginning of the fiscal year

The pre-/post-SOX columns are H1a partitions and later forecast-error/discretionary-accrual sensitivity tests are excluded.

Equation (1) is retained as the required supporting Jones fit because its residual DA is used to calculate NDEPS, ADJFE, and MBE. The verified reading transcription confirms only PPE and ΔREV as substantive predictors plus an ordinary constant; all variables are scaled by average assets, with no statement that the constant is scaled.

The Jones estimator is not identified. Table 4 reports two-way cluster-robust inference for cross-sectional and time-series dependence but does not name cluster identifiers. The model includes two-digit SIC industry indicators, but the research-design definitions say 52 while the Table 4 note says 53 industry codes.

The HORIZON definition for the main model (months to earnings announcement) differs from the Table 2 descriptive note (months to fiscal year-end). The Table 3 variable definition referenced by Table 4 is used for the baseline, with the timing difference retained as an unresolved source issue. SHORT is defined as >1 and <4 in Equation (3) and as 3 years or less in the appendix; excluding first-year engagements makes the definitions equivalent for the retained sample.
The per-share conversion of the Jones residual DA for NDEPS is not reported, so the source does not fully specify this outcome construction.
results_review_notes: The selected frozen baseline family is the full-sample pooled Table 4 columns (1) and (2). Pre-SOX and post-SOX columns (3)–(6), later cutoff tests, and other robustness analyses are outside the selected baseline family.

Table 4 reports industry and yearly indicators as included and explicitly states their parameter estimates/statistics are not reported; this is retained as a result-set note rather than treated as a missing substantive predictor.

Table 4 reports coefficients and z-scores, states z-scores use two-way cluster-robust standard errors, and defines two-tailed significance markers. Standard errors and normal-reference p-values are derived from the printed z-scores under the conventional zero-null coefficient Wald relation; markers remain source-specific bounds.
Table 2 forecast-horizon descriptives use fiscal year-end as the starting date, whereas the Table 3/Table 4 model definition uses earnings-announcement date; the descriptive link remains unclear.

The Table 1 Panel C “% of firms” header is retained literally alongside observation counts; its denominator convention is unresolved. Table 2 absolute discretionary-accrual and absolute forecast-error rows are not direct inputs to the retained MBE definition and are not linked. The Table 3 Pearson correlation matrix is excluded as a correlation table, not a descriptive summary.

The source labels the Table 2 ratio as net income/average total assets (ROA), while the model variable definition says income before extraordinary items/average total assets; preserve the source wording in the descriptive-row note.

scope.quote: Specifically, I test the following joint hypothesis: If analysts, because of behavioral biases, underreact to new information when revising their forecasts, they will underreact even more in cases of greater information uncertainty. As a result, analysts will revise their forecasts in the same direction in the future, and the revision will be stronger for firms with greater information uncertainty.

The testable implication is that greater information uncertainty leads to more positive (negative) forecast errors and subsequent forecast revisions following good (bad) news relative to firms about which there is less information uncertainty

scope.quote: Specifically, I test the following joint hypothesis: If analysts, because of behavioral biases, underreact to new information when revising their forecasts, they will underreact even more in cases of greater information uncertainty. As a result, analysts will revise their forecasts in the same direction in the future, and the revision will be stronger for firms with greater information uncertainty.

The testable implication is that greater information uncertainty leads to more positive (negative) forecast errors and subsequent forecast revisions following good (bad) news relative to firms about which there is less information uncertainty

scope.quote: Specifically, I test the following joint hypothesis: If analysts, because of behavioral biases, underreact to new information when revising their forecasts, they will underreact even more in cases of greater information uncertainty. As a result, analysts will revise their forecasts in the same direction in the future, and the revision will be stronger for firms with greater information uncertainty.

The testable implication is that greater information uncertainty leads to more positive (negative) forecast errors and subsequent forecast revisions following good (bad) news relative to firms about which there is less information uncertainty

scope.quote: Specifically, I test the following joint hypothesis: If analysts, because of behavioral biases, underreact to new information when revising their forecasts, they will underreact even more in cases of greater information uncertainty. The testable implication is that greater information uncertainty leads to more positive (negative) forecast errors and subsequent forecast revisions following good (bad) news relative to firms about which there is less information uncertainty

review_notes: Source-first scope: the introduction states the central joint hypothesis that greater information uncertainty amplifies analysts’ underreaction, producing more positive (negative) forecast errors and subsequent revisions after good (bad) news (page 3). The paper directly tests that question in Table 4, Panels A and B, with separate bad- and good-news annual cross-sections; retain the final full-control model C for each of the two parallel outcomes in each news group. Table 2’s unconditional underreaction comparison, Table 3 portfolio sorts, reduced models A/B, size-as-alternative-proxy tests, and later robustness/subsample analyses do not replace this principal uncertainty test.

Equation (1) is reproduced with the printed duplicate α7 label on the REV−8,−4×RET_6 and REV−8,−4×VOL terms. Table 4 independently lists both RHS terms; the duplicate label does not remove either term or establish that their estimated coefficients are constrained equal.

The source identifies Fama–MacBeth annual cross-sectional estimation/inference, but does not clearly name the estimator used for the annual cross-sections. It also reports average annual N by news group (748 bad news; 600 good news), not an exact N for each retained fit. The DNAS input’s rank treatment in the triple interaction is not separately specified.

scope.quote: e follow De Franco et al. (2011) in measuring targets’ financial statement comparability. Similar to

HYPOTHESIS 1a. Target firms’ pre-acquisition financial statement comparability is positively related to

acquirer abnormal returns around acquisition announcements.

HYPOTHESIS 1b. Target firms’ pre-acquisition financial statement comparability is positively related to

expected synergies from business combinations.

HYPOTHESIS 1c. Target firms’ pre-acquisition financial statement comparability is positively related to

post-acquisition operating performance of the acquirer.

Table 3 presents regression results of our tests examining the relation between target firms’ financial


statement comparability and the efficiency of acquisition decisions: model (1) uses _ACQ_CAR_ (acquirer’s three

day announcement returns); model (2) uses SYNERGY (three-day value-weighted returns of acquirer and target);


and model (3) uses ∆ ROA (change in ROA from the pre- to post-acquisition period).


Using the three-day announcement period abnormal returns of the acquirer as the measure of


acquisition efficiency, the coefficient on target comparability is positive (0.017) and statistically significant at


the 5 percent level ( t -stat = 2.04) after controlling for acquirer, target, and deal characteristics. These results


support our first hypothesis that acquirers’ announcement returns are positively related to the pre-acquisition


level of targets’ financial statement comparability. In terms of economic significance, the acquirers’ three-day


announcement returns for targets that exhibit higher financial statement comparability are, on average, 1.7


percent higher than for targets that exhibit less financial statement comparability. <sup>21</sup> The model (1) results also


indicate that the market’s assessment of the quality of the acquisition as reflected in the acquirer’s three-day


announcement period abnormal return is significantly positively related to acquirer’s Tobin’s Q and leverage.

scope.quote: e follow De Franco et al. (2011) in measuring targets’ financial statement comparability. Similar to

HYPOTHESIS 1a. Target firms’ pre-acquisition financial statement comparability is positively related to

acquirer abnormal returns around acquisition announcements.

HYPOTHESIS 1b. Target firms’ pre-acquisition financial statement comparability is positively related to

expected synergies from business combinations.

HYPOTHESIS 1c. Target firms’ pre-acquisition financial statement comparability is positively related to

post-acquisition operating performance of the acquirer.

Table 3 presents regression results of our tests examining the relation between target firms’ financial


statement comparability and the efficiency of acquisition decisions: model (1) uses _ACQ_CAR_ (acquirer’s three

day announcement returns); model (2) uses SYNERGY (three-day value-weighted returns of acquirer and target);


and model (3) uses ∆ ROA (change in ROA from the pre- to post-acquisition period).


Using the three-day announcement period abnormal returns of the acquirer as the measure of


acquisition efficiency, the coefficient on target comparability is positive (0.017) and statistically significant at


the 5 percent level ( t -stat = 2.04) after controlling for acquirer, target, and deal characteristics. These results


support our first hypothesis that acquirers’ announcement returns are positively related to the pre-acquisition


level of targets’ financial statement comparability. In terms of economic significance, the acquirers’ three-day


announcement returns for targets that exhibit higher financial statement comparability are, on average, 1.7


percent higher than for targets that exhibit less financial statement comparability. <sup>21</sup> The model (1) results also


indicate that the market’s assessment of the quality of the acquisition as reflected in the acquirer’s three-day


announcement period abnormal return is significantly positively related to acquirer’s Tobin’s Q and leverage.

Equation(1): Earnings_it = alpha_i + beta_i*Return_it + epsilon_it. Earnings is quarterly net income before extraordinary items divided by market equity at the end of the previous quarter. Return is the buy-and-hold raw stock return during quarter t. The time-series fit uses the16quarters before acquisition announcement with a minimum of14quarters. Fit separately for each firm. Sixteen is the intended window,14the eligibility minimum; do not assert exactly16usable observations for every fit.

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Equations2-4 comparability construction, physical PDF page 18):
Equation(2): E(Earnings^i_i,t) = alpha_hat_i + beta_hat_i*Return_it. Equation(3): E(Earnings^i_j,t) = alpha_hat_j + beta_hat_j*Return_it. Both mappings apply firm i returns; superscript i denotes the return source, subscript denotes the accounting-system parameter source. Equation(4): CompAcct_ijt = (1/tau)*sum_t^tau abs(E(Earnings^i_i,t)-E(Earnings^i_j,t)). Absolute-value bars were checked in enlarged source crop. Following prose multiplies this average absolute difference by -1 so greater/less-negative values mean greater comparability, then averages pair scores across all other same-two-digit-SIC firms to construct TRG_COMP. Equations2-4 are deterministic uses of Equation1 estimated coefficients, not additional fitted regressions.

scope.quote: e follow De Franco et al. (2011) in measuring targets’ financial statement comparability. Similar to

HYPOTHESIS 1a. Target firms’ pre-acquisition financial statement comparability is positively related to

acquirer abnormal returns around acquisition announcements.

HYPOTHESIS 1b. Target firms’ pre-acquisition financial statement comparability is positively related to

expected synergies from business combinations.

HYPOTHESIS 1c. Target firms’ pre-acquisition financial statement comparability is positively related to

post-acquisition operating performance of the acquirer.

Table 3 presents regression results of our tests examining the relation between target firms’ financial


statement comparability and the efficiency of acquisition decisions: model (1) uses _ACQ_CAR_ (acquirer’s three

day announcement returns); model (2) uses SYNERGY (three-day value-weighted returns of acquirer and target);


and model (3) uses ∆ ROA (change in ROA from the pre- to post-acquisition period).


Using the three-day announcement period abnormal returns of the acquirer as the measure of


acquisition efficiency, the coefficient on target comparability is positive (0.017) and statistically significant at


the 5 percent level ( t -stat = 2.04) after controlling for acquirer, target, and deal characteristics. These results


support our first hypothesis that acquirers’ announcement returns are positively related to the pre-acquisition


level of targets’ financial statement comparability. In terms of economic significance, the acquirers’ three-day


announcement returns for targets that exhibit higher financial statement comparability are, on average, 1.7


percent higher than for targets that exhibit less financial statement comparability. <sup>21</sup> The model (1) results also


indicate that the market’s assessment of the quality of the acquisition as reflected in the acquirer’s three-day


announcement period abnormal return is significantly positively related to acquirer’s Tobin’s Q and leverage.

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Equation1 firm earnings-return construction, physical PDF page 17):
Equation(1): Earnings_it = alpha_i + beta_i*Return_it + epsilon_it. Earnings is quarterly net income before extraordinary items divided by market equity at the end of the previous quarter. Return is the buy-and-hold raw stock return during quarter t. The time-series fit uses the16quarters before acquisition announcement with a minimum of14quarters. Fit separately for each firm. Sixteen is the intended window,14the eligibility minimum; do not assert exactly16usable observations for every fit.

COORDINATOR-VERIFIED MATHEMATICAL TRANSCRIPTION (Equations2-4 comparability construction, physical PDF page 18):
Equation(2): E(Earnings^i_i,t) = alpha_hat_i + beta_hat_i*Return_it. Equation(3): E(Earnings^i_j,t) = alpha_hat_j + beta_hat_j*Return_it. Both mappings apply firm i returns; superscript i denotes the return source, subscript denotes the accounting-system parameter source. Equation(4): CompAcct_ijt = (1/tau)*sum_t^tau abs(E(Earnings^i_i,t)-E(Earnings^i_j,t)). Absolute-value bars were checked in enlarged source crop. Following prose multiplies this average absolute difference by -1 so greater/less-negative values mean greater comparability, then averages pair scores across all other same-two-digit-SIC firms to construct TRG_COMP. Equations2-4 are deterministic uses of Equation1 estimated coefficients, not additional fitted regressions.

Equation (1) is the sole fitted regression among the comparability equations; Equations (2)–(4) are deterministic. Table 3 is coded OLS based on the paper’s direct OLS-derived-weight explanation for the Table 3 coefficients in footnote 21. Robust standard errors are recorded separately. Estimators for the supporting firm-specific earnings-return and SYNC regressions remain unidentified.

In our primary analysis we use textual analysis techniques to compare a firm’s risk factor disclosures in the current year and in the next year
The two modification measures complement each other. Modif is comprehensive and jDLengthj is intuitive for interpretation.
We estimate equation (2) using No-letter Firms (hereinafter “sample firms”).
The first four models examine one spillover channel at a time; the last model includes all the spillover variables.

estimation_procedure.description: Cross-sectional regression of suppliers’ two-day market-adjusted returns at customer QEAs for customer-supplier pair observations. Event day 0 is the QEA day when announced before market open; after-close and non-trading-day announcements are shifted to the next trading day. Observations are excluded if the supplier QEA precedes the customer QEA or if their QEAs are within three days. This model is the full specification for its selected economic-bond dimension; there are no repeated fits or separate grouping dimensions.

evidence.quote: The table reports the results of cross-sectional regressions of suppliers’ two-day market-adjusted returns at the time of their customers’ quarterly earnings announcements (QEAs)

If a customer’s QEA was made before the market opened on a given day, we treat that day as day 0; after the market closed on a given day, we treat the following trading day as day 0; or on a non-trading day we treat the next trading day as day 0.
To ensure that a customer’s QEA is not preempted by the information contained in a supplier’s QEA, we exclude observations where a supplier’s QEA precedes that of its customer in a given quarter.
we omit observations where suppliers and customers QEAs fall within three days of one another.

scope.quote: merely documenting such information externalities is not the central focus of our study. Instead, our interest lies in developing and testing hypotheses about the economic determinants of these information externalities.
Under Hypothesis 2a, the information externality experienced by a supplier due to its customer’s QEA is increasing in the dependence of the supplier on its customer, which is proxied by PCT_SALES.
Under Hypothesis 2b, the supplier’s information externality is increasing in the customer’s exposure to its supplier, an effect which is captured by RATIO.
We view the economic bond between a supplier and a customer from two perspectives.
First, we predict that the more dependent a supplier is on its customer
Second, we predict that the information investors glean from a customer’s QEA will depend on the customer’s exposure to the supplier.

To ensure that a customer’s QEA is not preempted by the information contained in a supplier’s QEA, we exclude observations where a supplier’s QEA precedes that of its customer in a given quarter.

Source-first scope: the introduction explicitly frames the information-environment analysis around two main outcomes, the adverse-selection component of the spread (GHLAMBDA) and ERCs. Retain the full eight-quarter comment-letter-firm specification for each: Table 3 Panel B column (1) and Table 4 column (2). The source calls the propensity-score matched comparison a robustness check and the one-quarter window a causality-confidence analysis; these, the Table 4 reduced SUE-only column, amendment/content analyses, and voluntary-disclosure alternative explanation are excluded.

The two retained outcome regressions use the authors’ described pre/post Equation (1) design; the paper does not identify the underlying estimator. Firm/year fixed effects and firm-clustered heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors are reported.

Supporting fits are retained for the actually estimated GHLAMBDA stock-month construction and the fitted controls PERSIST, PREDICT, and BETA. Equation (2) uses the supplied coordinator-verified mathematical transcription. The persistence fit is described in prose; the BETA fit is identified as a market model but its equation and underlying estimator are not reported.
results_review_notes: The selected baseline results are Table 3 Panel B column (1), the comment-letter-firm eight-quarter information-asymmetry model, and Table 4 column (2), the comment-letter-firm full ERC model. Matched-sample, one-quarter, baseline-only, and appendix models are excluded.

Table 3 Panel A provides pre/post descriptives for every retained GHLAMBDA outcome and predictor. The ERC model has no directly relevant descriptive-statistics table located; Appendix A1 descriptives concern the separate propensity-score determinant models and are not linked to this baseline.

Table 3 reports firm and year fixed effects as included, but does not tabulate individual fixed-effect coefficients. Table 4 column (2) also omits a standalone intercept; the source does not say whether a constant is absorbed by fixed effects.

Both result tables identify t-statistics, firm-clustered robust standard errors, and two-tailed marker thresholds. Formal test-family labels and degrees of freedom are not reported; exact p-values are not inferred from markers.

GHLAMBDA is described as the quarterly average of lambda after multiplying retained monthly lambda estimates by 1,000 for presentation; all table estimates and descriptives are preserved on the source-reported scale.

Table 3 Panel A provides the complete descriptive rows for GHLAMBDA and its six information-asymmetry controls in pre/post quarters. Table A1 Panel A and Panel D also summarize retained SIZE in distinct firm-year matching samples; those four SIZE rows are kept in separate groups with the source-stated timing and different-sample relation. No source descriptive rows were found for CAR, SUE, POST, or the other ERC-only baseline terms.

independent_variables.name: V/P_{t−1}
independent_variables.definition: Prior-year value-to-market measure of growth opportunities: VAIP divided by market value of equity, calculated as Compustat price item 25 multiplied by shares item 199. VAIP uses book equity, operating income after depreciation, dividends, a 12% discount rate, and abnormal-earnings persistence ω=0.62 (the original text labels the parameter x).
independent_variables.formula: V/P_{t−1} = VAIP_{t−1} / (item25 × item199); VAIP = (1−αr)BV + α(1+r)X − αrd; α=ω/(1+r−ω), r=0.12, ω=0.62

evidence.quote: V/P is a measure of growth opportunities. It is calculated as the ratio of the value of the firm (VAIP) and market value of equity

V/P is V_AIP divided by market value of equity, where market value of equity = Compustat item25 * item199 (multiplication, not subtraction). V_AIP = (1-alpha*r)*BV + alpha*(1+r)*X - alpha*r*d; alpha = omega/(1+r-omega), r=0.12, omega=0.62.
BV is the book value of common equity (item 60), d is annual dividends (item 21) and X is operating income after depreciation (item 178)
The displayed Table2 specification uses V/P_(t-1).

independent_variables.name: Good_itτ

evidence.quote: Good itτ = 1 if FE itτ is positive, and 0 otherwise

FE itτ is the forecast error defined as realized EPS for firm i in quarter t + τ minus the corresponding consensus analyst forecast of EPS, deflated by the firm’s stock price at the end of fiscal quarter t + τ
FE is the earnings surprise divided by the stock price at the end of the final month of the fiscal quarter for which earnings is being forecast
We winsorize the 1% tails of this variable to mitigate outlier problems

standard_errors.details: The authors adjust t- and F-statistics for cross-correlation caused by repeated appearances of the same return observations. The all-20-quarter t-statistic adjustment factor is unclear in the supplied reading text: it reads “divide by 20,” while visual inspection of PDF page 17 appears to show √20. F-statistics are reported as divided by 20 at the five-year level.

evidence.quote: The t -statistics and F -statistics are adjusted for cross-correlation in the residuals resulting from multiple appearances of the Rit observations
regressions, we divide by 20
The F -statistics are adjusted in a similar manner, dividing by 4 at the annual level and 20 at the five-year level
Ritτ = α

estimation_procedure.description: Pool available quarterly returns and earnings surprises over the 20 quarters after each firm-quarter growth-portfolio formation. The same quarterly return can enter multiple growth-formation windows, up to 20 times in the five-year fit.

evidence.quote: We therefore track stock return and earnings surprise characteristics for the 20 quarters that follow the measurement of the growth/value characteristics
Growth portfolios are formed at the beginning of Year 1
τ indexes the 20 subsequent quarters

estimation_procedure.description: Table 5 runs the full Eq. (2) separately for BETA and STDERET outcomes and for keyword-count versus all-word-count versions. It uses the level of post-disclosure risk at t+1 and includes the corresponding t risk control; the authors say this specification captures a change in risk while allowing the lagged-risk coefficient to vary. RF_DISC is interpreted as the unexpected portion conditional on pre-disclosure risk controls, rather than as a separately residualized first-stage measure in this baseline. The outcome window begins two trading days after the 10-K release and spans 250 trading days.

evidence.quote: In our second hypothesis, we predict that risk factor disclosures are positively associated with post-disclosure market-based measures of firm risk (i.e., beta and stock return volatility).
our measure for risk factor disclosures (RF_DISC) captures the portion of risk factor disclosures that are ‘‘unexpected.’’

Second, we model our dependent variable as the level of post-disclosure risk at time t ? 1. By including a control for the level of risk at time t, this ensures that our model is capturing the change in the risk measure subsequent to the release of the risk factor disclosure.

estimation_procedure.description: Table 5 runs the full Eq. (2) separately for BETA and STDERET outcomes and for keyword-count versus all-word-count versions. It uses the level of post-disclosure risk at t+1 and includes the corresponding t risk control; the authors say this specification captures a change in risk while allowing the lagged-risk coefficient to vary. RF_DISC is interpreted as the unexpected portion conditional on pre-disclosure risk controls, rather than as a separately residualized first-stage measure in this baseline. The outcome window begins two trading days after the 10-K release and spans 250 trading days.

evidence.quote: In our second hypothesis, we predict that risk factor disclosures are positively associated with post-disclosure market-based measures of firm risk (i.e., beta and stock return volatility).

estimation_procedure.description: Table 5 runs the full Eq. (2) separately for BETA and STDERET outcomes and for keyword-count versus all-word-count versions. It uses the level of post-disclosure risk at t+1 and includes the corresponding t risk control; the authors say this specification captures a change in risk while allowing the lagged-risk coefficient to vary. RF_DISC is interpreted as the unexpected portion conditional on pre-disclosure risk controls, rather than as a separately residualized first-stage measure in this baseline. The outcome window begins two trading days after the 10-K release and spans 250 trading days.

evidence.quote: In our second hypothesis, we predict that risk factor disclosures are positively associated with post-disclosure market-based measures of firm risk (i.e., beta and stock return volatility).
our measure for risk factor disclosures (RF_DISC) captures the portion of risk factor disclosures that are ‘‘unexpected.’’

Second, we model our dependent variable as the level of post-disclosure risk at time t ? 1. By including a control for the level of risk at time t, this ensures that our model is capturing the change in the risk measure subsequent to the release of the risk factor disclosure.
BETAit11 is the firm’s coefficient loading on the market excess return (Fama & French) for the 250 trading day period beginning two trading days after the 10-K release.
STDERETit11 is the standard deviation of daily abnormal stock returns for the 250 trading day period beginning two trading days after the 10-K release.

The abstract and introduction define the central substantive question as whether discretionary-accrual boosting explains the earnings kink (physical pp. 1–3). The paper is not presented as a method paper: it tests the earnings-management explanation, and introduces the revised accrual proxy as one of four checks addressing the possibility that its proxy lacks power (p. 3).

Table 1 is a genuine fitted comparison, not just a borrowed calibration: the authors extend Jones and estimate four incremental accrual specifications across 637 two-digit-SIC/year groups, comparing mean coefficients and adjusted R² (pp. 4–8). The forward-looking variant is developed as a more explanatory DA construction. Under the frozen principal-question rule and scope clarification 01, however, these fits are indispensable measurement constructions supporting the substantive kink question, not its principal regression family.

The direct central tests are Table 3's comparisons of small-profit firms with all other firms and with small-loss firms (pp. 12–15). Table 3 reports differences in means and explicitly identifies its test statistics as t-tests (p. 14), so there is no eligible principal regression baseline to extract. Equations (3)–(4) construct DA inputs for those non-regression comparisons; under the frozen rule, construction fits cannot replace an absent baseline family or be retained as supporting models without one.

Table 2's earnings-component persistence regressions are introduced as a test validating the DA proxy's transitory component (p. 8; Table 2 pp. 10–11). The SEC enforcement and future-performance analyses are additional proxy-power checks (pp. 3, 8–9); Table 4 future-performance comparisons are also differences in means (pp. 13, 16). These validation/follow-up tests do not become the baseline for the central earnings-kink question. Thus the main empirical analysis contains no eligible baseline regression.

review_notes: Source-first scope: the abstract proposes a new method for estimating the relation between investment and uncertainty of future benefits; the introduction identifies the R&D-versus-capital-expenditure comparison as the central question. Section 4.1 explicitly says Tables 3 and 4 report the main results: Table 3 estimates the relation using current outlays and Table 4 uses capitalized R&D and net PP&E. Table 3 Panels A and B are retained as parallel deflator specifications (BVE and price), and Table 4 Panel B is retained as the co-primary cumulative-investment specification. The full table equations include advertising expense; the reduced Eq. (5) is augmented in most empirical analyses. Other sensitivity specifications and research-design extensions beyond Tables 3 and 4 are excluded.

The paper names annual cross-sectional regressions but not the underlying estimator. The note that the procedure is similar to Fama–MacBeth does not establish that the annual fits use that estimator. Newey–West inference with five lags applies to mean coefficients across the 21 annual fits.
The paper gives aggregate panel counts (Table 3: 42,776 and 40,569; Table 4: 29,408), not exact per-year regression Ns, so sample_size is null for each repeated specification.

The paper gives conflicting leverage descriptions (Eq. (5) p. 7, data definition p. 10, and table notes pp. 15–16). The equations use an explicit natural-log market-value variable, but the Table 3 label says billions while the data formula does not give a conversion factor. The per-share conversion denominator/date is not specified for investment outlays and asset variables.
Winsorization wording differs between the general data section (p. 11) and the table-specific notes (pp. 15–16). The result records the table-specific rule and flags the discrepancy for review.

The capitalized R&D variable uses five years of historical R&D with 20% annual straight-line depreciation, but the paper does not print exact year-by-year weights or the per-share denominator; the variable definition preserves the stated construction and flags these omitted details.
descriptive_reason: Table 1 reports the retained current-outlay outcomes, predictors, controls and current R&D flow; Table 4 Panel A reports the retained capitalized R&D, PPE and grossed-up earnings-SD variables. Other-family variables and the parallel variance outcome were excluded.
results_review_notes: All reported regression parameters and controls are represented for the three frozen baseline specifications, including intercepts.
Coefficient-distribution SDs and quartiles are retained under reported_distribution, separate from data-variable descriptives and from standard errors.
No p-values, degrees of freedom, directions, tests or sample statistics were calculated by the extractor; only printed values and frozen derived quantities are used.

models.model_label: Pooled full-control regression of RPOJ
models.sample_description: Pooled I/B/E/S firm-year panel from 1984–1998. Selection requires at least five analyst forecasts, market capitalization of at least $100 million, CRSP daily and monthly returns, Compustat annual accounting data, eps1>0, eps2>0, and a five-year or long-term growth estimate. Table 4 reports 15,872 observations; earlier source tables report 15,585, an unresolved discrepancy.
models.method_details: The paper reports pooled regressions but does not identify the underlying estimator; OLS is not inferred.

dependent_variable.name: RPOJ
dependent_variable.definition: Risk premium (implied cost of equity less the 10-year US Treasury yield) inferred from the Ohlson–Juettner pricing relation. P0 is current price; eps1 and eps2 are one- and two-year-ahead EPS; dps1 is eps1 multiplied by current payout. The implementation uses the average of STG=(eps2−eps1)/eps1 and I/B/E/S five-year LTG as the short-term growth input, sets nominal perpetual growth gamma−1=rf−3%, and measures the RP on June 30. Current payout is dps0/eps0 when eps0>0; otherwise dps0/(0.06×total assets); payout ratios are winsorized to [0,1], held constant for future periods, and stock buybacks are ignored.
dependent_variable.formula: RP = re − rf; re = A + sqrt(A^2 + (eps1/P0) × (g2 − (gamma−1))); A = 0.5 × [(gamma−1) + dps1/P0]; g2_impl = (((eps2−eps1)/eps1) + LTG)/2; gamma−1 = rf − 3%; dps1 = eps1 × payout ratio.

evidence.quote: P0 = eps1/r_e + [eps2-eps1-r_e*(eps1-dps1)]/[r_e*(r_e-g_p)]. Substituting g_p=gamma-1 gives r_e = A + sqrt(A^2 + (eps1/P0)*(g2-(gamma-1)))
For implementation the authors use the average of forecast two-year growth and five-year growth as their short-term growth estimate.
The dependent risk premium is inferred cost of equity minus the prevailing10-year Treasury bond yield.
The inputs to the OJ model are P0, eps1, short-term growth g2, perpetual growth g, and dps1
We winsorize the payout ratios to lie between 0 and 1.
As in Gebhardt et al. (2001), we infer the risk premium on June 30 of each year.

dependent_variable.name: RPRIV1
dependent_variable.definition: Risk premium implied by residual-income valuation, defined as implied cost of equity less the 10-year US Treasury yield. Price equals current book value plus present value of residual earnings. Inputs are price, eps1, eps2, annualized five-year growth, industry median ROE, current book value and payout. Forecast eps3 is eps2×(1+five-year growth); from years 4–12 ROE reverts linearly to the industry median, and residual earnings are constant thereafter. RIV1 uses the moving median ROE of up to the prior 10 years excluding negative-ROE firms. Future payout is held at the current ratio; current payout is dps0/eps0 for positive eps0 and dps0/(6% of assets) otherwise, winsorized [0,1], with buybacks ignored. Book values use clean-surplus updates between earnings announcement and month+4 after fiscal year-end, then Compustat values. Risk premia are measured June 30.

dependent_variable.name: RPRIV2
dependent_variable.definition: Risk premium implied by residual-income valuation, defined as implied cost of equity less the 10-year US Treasury yield. Price equals current book value plus present value of residual earnings. Inputs are price, eps1, eps2, annualized five-year growth, industry median ROE, current book value and payout. Forecast eps3 is eps2×(1+five-year growth); from years 4–12 ROE reverts linearly to the industry median, and residual earnings are constant thereafter. RIV2 uses the moving median ROE over up to the prior 10 years for all industry firms including loss-making firms, and winsorizes that median at the risk-free rate and 20%. Future payout is held at the current ratio; current payout is dps0/eps0 for positive eps0 and dps0/(6% of assets) otherwise, winsorized [0,1], with buybacks ignored. Book values use clean-surplus updates between earnings announcement and month+4 after fiscal year-end, then Compustat values. Risk premia are measured June 30.

independent_variables.name: EARNVAR
independent_variables.definition: Single factor measuring earnings variability. Inputs are log MAE (mean absolute analyst-forecast error over the previous five years scaled by mean absolute realized EPS over that period), log EPSVAR (coefficient of variation in EPS over the previous five years), and log DISP (dispersion in analyst forecasts; its lookback is not stated). One factor explains more than 65% of variance, with reported loadings 0.95, 0.90 and 0.80, respectively. Components are normalized to zero mean and unit standard deviation; the factor can be negative.
independent_variables.formula: Factor-analysis score on ln(MAE), ln(EPSVAR), ln(DISP); reported loadings 0.95, 0.90 and 0.80 respectively; exact score construction not reported.

evidence.quote: The three variables we consider are: MAE, the mean absolute error in annual analysts forecasts over the previous five years scaled by the mean absolute realized EPS over the period; EPSVAR, the coefficient of variation in EPS over the previous five years; and DISP, the dispersion in analyst forecasts.
We take logs of these variables to reduce the effects of outliers and then run a factor analysis. A single factor accounts for more than 65% of the variance.
The loadings on the three measures are 0.95, 0.90, and 0.80, respectively, on the logs of MAE, EPSVAR, and DISP.
EARNVAR is a factor that measures earnings variability and can be negative because all factor components are normalized to have zero mean and unit standard deviation.

independent_variables.name: UNA1
independent_variables.definition: The Table 6 row is labeled UNA1; the paper’s variable definitions call the proxy UNA. UNA is the in-sample rank of negative verifiable net assets (VNA), where VNA is [cash plus all investments and advances, less debt and preferred equity] divided by [assets less liabilities]. The negative rank increases with the unverifiability of net assets.
independent_variables.formula: in_sample_rank(−[(cash + all investments and advances − debt − preferred equity) / (assets − liabilities)])

evidence.quote: UNA: We compute the ratio of [cash ? all investments and advances - debt preferred equity] to [assets - liabilities]. The denominator in this ratio is total net assets, while the numerator is intended to proxy for that component of net assets whose fair-values are likely most verifiable (Richardson et al. 2005). Thus this ratio is intended to capture the verifiability of net assets (VNA). Items excluded from the numerator include plant and equipment, receivables, payables, inventories, advances, etc. Fair-value estimates of these items are likely less verifiable than cash, investments, debt, and preferred equity. Thus as the VNA ratio decreases, subjectivity in estimating the fair value of goodwill is expected to increase. To obtain a measure that increases in the subjectivity of estimating the fair value of goodwill, we multiply VNA by -1. We then rank the resulting value in-sample and denote it UNA, where ‘‘UNA’’ refers to the unverifiability of net assets.

independent_variables.name: UNA1
independent_variables.definition: The Table 6 row is labeled UNA1; the paper’s variable definitions call the proxy UNA. UNA is the in-sample rank of negative verifiable net assets (VNA), where VNA is [cash plus all investments and advances, less debt and preferred equity] divided by [assets less liabilities]. The negative rank increases with the unverifiability of net assets.
independent_variables.formula: in_sample_rank(−[(cash + all investments and advances − debt − preferred equity) / (assets − liabilities)])

evidence.quote: UNA: We compute the ratio of [cash ? all investments and advances - debt preferred equity] to [assets - liabilities]. The denominator in this ratio is total net assets, while the numerator is intended to proxy for that component of net assets whose fair-values are likely most verifiable (Richardson et al. 2005). Thus this ratio is intended to capture the verifiability of net assets (VNA). Items excluded from the numerator include plant and equipment, receivables, payables, inventories, advances, etc. Fair-value estimates of these items are likely less verifiable than cash, investments, debt, and preferred equity. Thus as the VNA ratio decreases, subjectivity in estimating the fair value of goodwill is expected to increase. To obtain a measure that increases in the subjectivity of estimating the fair value of goodwill, we multiply VNA by -1. We then rank the resulting value in-sample and denote it UNA, where ‘‘UNA’’ refers to the unverifiability of net assets.

evidence.quote: time-series means of the estimated coefficients
autocorrelation-corrected t-statistics

test_context.notes: The source reports time-series mean coefficients from monthly cross-sectional regressions and autocorrelation-corrected t-statistics on those means. The within-month estimator and autocorrelation correction/bandwidth are not identified. The t label supports a Student-t reference under the frozen rule, but degrees of freedom and sidedness remain unknown; no exact p-values can be derived. The usual zero-coefficient null on the reported mean coefficient supports helper derivation of a standard error from the printed coefficient/t-statistic pair; the derived SE is not author-reported.

review_notes: Table 9 reports coefficient time-series means and autocorrelation-corrected t-statistics, not per-month coefficient estimates. No per-month N or aggregate regression N is shown.

Table 9 labels REV3 as cumulative price-deflated forecast revisions in the past three months, while page 9 displays a j=0..3 sum without an averaging divisor and nearby prose calls it an average over three months. This source construction conflict is preserved; no formula was changed.

missing_fields.standard_error: Table 9 reports the time-series mean coefficient and autocorrelation-corrected t-statistic, but no separately reported standard error.
missing_fields.p_value: Table 9 reports no exact coefficient p-values; no point p-value is derivable with unknown df and sidedness.

review_notes: Scope: Table 9, Panels A and B, is selected as the direct firm-level regression family for the two central effects stated in the abstract and introduction: lower future returns at high IU and stronger price/earnings momentum effects at high IU. The monthly cross-sectional specifications include the IU group indicators and momentum interactions, with Size and BM controls. Panel A uses price momentum; Panel B uses earnings momentum; each is reported for two IU group constructions. Earlier portfolio-sort tables, the later three-factor risk-adjustment regressions of portfolio returns (Tables 7–8), and the earnings-announcement event study (Table 10) are not construction regressions required by Table 9.

Needs review: the paper calls its cross-sectional regressions “Fam-MacBeth, 1973 type” but does not identify the estimator used within each month. The verified displayed REV formula sums j=0 through 3, while the prose and Table 9 note describe a three-month average/cumulative measure; that discrepancy is preserved.
descriptive_reason: Table 1 is the relevant descriptive table for raw components of the retained IU indicators. Its Firm Age, Volatility, and Volume rows are included; Duration is an alternative IU proxy not used as an input to any selected Table 9 specification, and size, BM, J6, and REV3 have no variable-summary rows in the inspected source. Pairwise correlations are excluded.
results_review_notes: The displayed REV3 definition is internally inconsistent: the methods prose calls it the average revision over the past three months, while the displayed formula sums j=0 through 3 without a divisor. The frozen base retains this source conflict; no change to the definition or fitted estimates was made.

Table 9 contains the selected mean cross-sectional coefficient fits. Earlier portfolio sorts, Table 7–8 risk-adjustment regressions, and Table 10 earnings-announcement tests remain outside the frozen baseline family.

review_notes: Scope: Table 4 Panel A levels is selected as the primary full-sample H1 market-reaction family. The two displayed columns are the absolute three-day abnormal return and abnormal trading volume; the text presents the latter as an alternative market-reaction measure. The analyst-risk assessment is H2 and a later separate sample, while Table 3 reports determinants of an already constructed Specificity measure; neither is required to construct a Table 4 regressor. The pseudo analyses and proprietary-cost partitions are excluded. The CAR outcome and |CAREA| control both require the Fama–French expected-return construction, which is retained as a supporting dependency with its unreported equation details flagged.

Needs review: Table 4’s note says Panel B uses changes analyses, but the visible table contains only the two displayed levels columns, and the main text calls the changes analysis an untabulated sensitivity test. The source does not reconcile those statements; the extraction retains the supported full-sample levels fits. The underlying regression estimator is not named. The Fama–French three-factor equation, inputs, fitting window, and sample are not reported.
descriptive_reason: Table 2 Panel A supplies pre-winsorization statistics for the retained market-reaction outcome and all 22 RHS variables; its N=14,865 is a group-level sample count, with no per-variable N cells. Table 2 Panel B contributes summaries only for the 14 predictors shared with the retained fits, in the distinct narrower analyst-match sample (N=627); the panel N is group-level, not a per-variable count. Table 1 by-year/by-industry values for Specificity and Item 1A section length are retained as stratified summaries, with the percentage scale and uncertain stop-word treatment preserved. Table 2 Panel C correlations, sample-share percentages, analyst-only variables and downstream analyst outcomes are excluded. No descriptive row for ABVOL was found.
results_review_notes: All source-reported values were copied without recomputing summaries or changing scales; table-specific rounding and the 0.054 prose mean for Specificity are preserved.
The source reports the Table 4 two-tailed t-statistics and significance markers, with no degrees of freedom; the frozen rule uses Student-t and the helper does not infer point p-values.

Table 2 Panel A and Panel B sample Ns are recorded at group level and not duplicated as variable-level n statistics. Table 1 observation counts are retained because the source prints an observations cell for each year/industry stratum.
The Table 2 Panel A Specificity mean is 0.05; the discussion separately reports 0.054. Both source values are preserved without recomputation.

independent_variables.definition: Operating income per share (#177), matched to the applicable basic/diluted IBES definition, less applicable GAAP EPS. If a diluted value is needed, #177 is adjusted using the most recent annual basic-shares-to-diluted-shares factor (#54/#171). The resulting amount is scaled by total assets per share at quarter t.
independent_variables.formula: Operating Income (#177) − GAAP Earnings (#19 or #9); for diluted #177, use the stated annual #54/#171 dilution factor; then scale by total assets per share at quarter t.

evidence.quote: Special Items 1⁄4 Operating Income - GAAP Earnings.

Operating Income is the applicable basic or diluted income per share (matched to the IBES definition) before special items, extraordinary items, and discontinued operations (Compustat data item #177).

Since #177 is only reported on a primary basis, we adjust it to a diluted basis by using the implied dilution factor from the most recent annual basic shares outstanding (#54) divided by annual diluted shares outstanding (#171) reported by Compustat.

Since Compustat does not report quarterly operating income per share on a diluted basis, we adjust it to a diluted basis, if necessary, by using the most recent annual dilution factor, computed from basic shares outstanding (data item #54) and diluted shares outstanding (data item #171).
GAAP Earnings is the applicable basic or diluted income per share (matched to the IBES definition) before extraordinary items and discontinued operations (#19 or #9).
All variables are calculated as per share amounts, which are then scaled by total assets per share at the end of the initial fiscal quarter (data item #9/data item #15).

evidence.quote: Special Items 1⁄4 Operating Income - GAAP Earnings.

Operating Income is the applicable basic or diluted income per share (matched to the IBES definition) before special items, extraordinary items, and discontinued operations (Compustat data item #177).

Since #177 is only reported on a primary basis, we adjust it to a diluted basis by using the implied dilution factor from the most recent annual basic shares outstanding (#54) divided by annual diluted shares outstanding (#171) reported by Compustat.

Since Compustat does not report quarterly operating income per share on a diluted basis, we adjust it to a diluted basis, if necessary, by using the most recent annual dilution factor, computed from basic shares outstanding (data item #54) and diluted shares outstanding (data item #171).
GAAP Earnings is the applicable basic or diluted income per share (matched to the IBES definition) before extraordinary items and discontinued operations (#19 or #9).

estimation_procedure.description: Equations (3) and (4) are a recursive Mishkin pricing/forecasting system, estimated simultaneously by generalized nonlinear least squares (GNLS) on the persistence-matched HIO/LIO sample. The forecasting equation estimates γ0, γ1, γ1H, γ2, and γ2H. The pricing equation uses observed Earn(t+1), current Accruals and CashFlows (including their H interactions), the forecasting intercept γ0, and market-implied γ* persistence parameters. The likelihood-ratio tests compare forecast and market-implied accrual-persistence weights: γ1 = γ1* for LIO and γ1+γ1H = γ1*+γ1H* for HIO; the relative efficiency ratios are also compared across groups. LIO firms are matched to HIO firms within ±0.03 on firm-specific accrual persistence.

Table 5’s matched Mishkin system is selected because Table 4’s unmatched HIO/LIO contrast is explicitly confounded by different accrual persistence and the authors re-estimate the system after matching within ±0.03. The firm-specific matching regressions are required selection dependencies.

Table 7 return regressions test the related H2b hedge-return implication and are outside this single principal H2a family. H1 persistence comparisons, the unmatched Table 4 screen, hedge sorts, H3 trading tests, and later applications are excluded.

independent_variables.name: GSCORE
independent_variables.definition: Additive index equal to the sum of the eight binary growth-fundamental signals G1–G8. Each signal defaults to 0 and equals 1 when its stated criterion is met: G1, ROA above the contemporaneous median for low-BM firms in the same two-digit SIC industry; G2, cash-flow ROA above that median; G3, cash-flow ROA above ROA; G4, quarterly ROA variance over the prior four years below that median; G5, variance of quarterly year-over-year sales growth, comparing Q0 with Q−4, over the prior four years below that median; G6–G8, respectively, R&D, capital-expenditure and advertising intensity above their corresponding medians. The intensity measures use beginning assets as denominator. G4 and G5 use quarterly data and require at least six quarters; when the required quarterly data are missing, the signals are coded zero rather than dropping the observation. Industry medians are at the two-digit SIC level within low-BM firms.

evidence.quote: GSCORE is the sum of eight fundamental signals, G1:G8, tailored for growth firms. G1:G8 have a default value of 0 and equal 1 if the following criteria are met respectively.
I define the first growth signal, G1, to equal 1 if a firm’s ROA is greater than the contemporaneous median ROA for all low BM firms in the same industry and 0 otherwise.
ROA, defined as the ratio of net income before extraordinary items scaled by average total assets.
I define the second growth signal, G2, to equal 1 if a firm’s cash flow ROA exceeds the contemporaneous median for all low BM firms in the same industry and 0 otherwise.
G3 is defined to equal if a firm’s cash flow from operations exceeds net income and 0 otherwise.
G4 is defined to equal 1 if a firm’s earnings variability is less than the contemporaneous median for all low BM firms in the same industry and 0 otherwise.
G5 is defined to equal 1 it a firm’s sale growth variability is less than the contemporaneous median for all low BM firms in the same industry and 0 otherwise.

G6, G7 and G8 are defined to equal 1 if a firm’s R&D, capital expenditure and advertising intensity respectively, are greater than the contemporaneous medians of the corresponding variables for all low BM firms in the same industry and 0 otherwise. The intensity of R&D, capital expenditure and advertising are measured by deflating these variables by beginning assets.

The two signals related to naı ̈ve extrapolation, i.e. earnings variability and sales growth variability (G4,G5) are generated from quarterly financials of the past 4 years, with the constraint that at least six quarters information be available.
If these data are missing, the observations are not deleted, but the signals are coded as zeroes.
Industry medians are calculated at the two-digit SIC level within low BM firms.
I measure growth variability as the variance of a firm’s year over year sales growth (Q0 compared to Q)4) over the past 4 years using quarterly information.

research_interest_evidence.quote: Hence, GSCORE adds value even after controlling for size, BM and momentum.

evidence.quote: Low BM firms (22,361 observations)

Financial statement information used in the analysis is based on Year to Date annual financial statements created from quarterly financial statements on or closest to and before December 31st of each year. The time period covered is from 1979 to 2001. Firms with negative book value and firms without at least 2 years of financial information have been deleted. Firms that have BM ratios above the 80th percentile using prior year distributions are classified as high BM, while firms with BM ratios below the 20th percentile using prior year distributions are classified as low BM firms. independent_variables.definition: Total accruals measured 18 months before restatement: earnings before extraordinary items minus cash flow from operations minus cash flow from investing, divided by average total assets. Earnings is Compustat annual data item A18; CFO and CFI are cash-flow statement items A308 and A311; average assets is the average book value of total assets (item A6) during the year.

evidence.quote: We measure accruals 18 months prior to the restatement date
TOTACC 1⁄4 ðEarnings � CFO � CFIÞ=ðAverageAssetsÞ ð2Þ

Earnings is the earnings before extraordinary items (annual data item # A18), and CFO and CFI are the cash flow from operations and cash flow from investing activities, both from the statement of cash flows (# A308 and # A311, respectively). Average assets is the average of the book value of total assets (# A6) during the year.

review_notes: The authors present predictive ability, valuation, and information content as coequal procedures for comparing operating-income measures. Predictive ability is evaluated with prediction-error means and binomial tests, not an estimated regression, so the retained regression families are Eq. (1) valuation and Eq. (2) three-day information content.

For each regression family, the all-three-groups-combined sample is retained with separate STREET and EPSOP regressions as the central competing measurement proxies. Group-specific results are partitions and excluded. The 63-day information-content window is explicitly a replication/sensitivity analysis and excluded.
Eq. (1) estimator is not named, so its method remains null. Eq. (2) is explicitly OLS. CAR is described as market-adjusted but the benchmark-return formula is not reported.
descriptive_reason: The assigned paper's tables report prediction-error tests, regression coefficients, and model-fit comparisons, but no variable means, standard deviations, percentiles, or distributions for the selected baseline outcomes or predictors. Table 1's prediction-accuracy rows are hypothesis-test results, not variable descriptives.
results_review_notes: Table 2 and Table 3 contain selected full-sample baseline fits; the group-specific partitions and 63-day information-content window are not part of the frozen baseline family. Pairwise comparison statistics are preserved as auxiliary rows and recorded once per comparison.

scope.quote: The principal goal is to investigate whether dividends provide information about the quality of reported earnings.

scope.quote: The principal goal is to investigate whether dividends provide information about the quality of reported earnings.
To investigate the general relation between dividend policy and earnings quality, we estimate regressions of future earnings on current earnings using firm-level data
All of the results hold for both one- and two-year-ahead earnings.
To test the prediction that dividends are informative about the quality of firms’ reported earnings more generally, we first estimate the following regression:
We report the results of estimating (1) in Table 4.

review_notes: Principal family: Table 4, Panels A and B, the authors' Eq. (1) earnings-persistence regression. The source identifies future earnings on current earnings, with the dividend indicator and its interaction, as the general test of whether dividends inform earnings quality; it reports both one- and two-year-ahead outcomes over the three named subperiods. Table 3's payout/loss logit addresses a related precursor question; Table 5 examines payout magnitude, Table 6 later payout-policy partitions including repurchases, and Table 8 adds special-item/loss interactions. These are not the selected principal family.
results_review_notes: Table 1 annual DP counts and printed fractions and Table 2 subperiod DP counts and fractions are retained as related descriptive information for the DP indicator. Their DP definition is not confirmed identical to the Table 4 regular-cash-dividend indicator, and their samples/period groups differ from Table 4 fits.

dependent_variable.name: ER_it (mean standardized absolute excess return)
dependent_variable.definition: For firm i at a regular Form 10-K filing date, the mean standardized absolute excess return (SAER) over event days 0 through 3. Daily absolute excess return is the absolute difference between the firm’s CRSP daily total return and the CRSP daily value-weighted total return index. SAER divides this absolute excess return by its standard deviation over the non-information estimation days −10 to −6 and 6 to 10 around filing day 0.
dependent_variable.formula: mean(SAER over event days 0–3); SAER = |CRSP total return − CRSP value-weighted market return| / SD(|daily excess return| over event days −10 to −6 and 6 to 10)

dependent_variable.name: D(DKVCOMP)
dependent_variable.definition: Post-minus-pre change in DKVCOMP, the De Franco-based comparability measure. Firm-specific earnings-on-return coefficients predict earnings for firm i and peer firm j using firm i’s return. Within each period, country, peer-country, and industry cell, the signed measure is minus the average absolute prediction difference across available firm pairs; n_{p,ci,cj,k} is that available-pair count. For same-country comparisons (ci=cj), the paper excludes i=j self-pairs. Higher, less negative values indicate greater comparability. Equation (3) displays the outcome label DVKCOMP, while adjacent prose and Table 2 call the measure DKVCOMP.
dependent_variable.formula: DKVCOMP_post − DKVCOMP_pre; DKVCOMP_{p,ci,cj,k} = −Σ_{i,j}|(α_{p,i,0}+α_{p,i,1}RET_{p,i})−(α_{p,j,0}+α_{p,j,1}RET_{p,i})|/n_{p,ci,cj,k}

evidence.quote: Equation (3) prints DVKCOMP_p,ci,cj,k = -sum_i,j abs(alpha_p,i,0 + alpha_p,i,1*RET_p,i - (alpha_p,j,0 + alpha_p,j,1*RET_p,i))/n_p,ci,cj,k.
DKVCOMP is a comparability measure based on De Franco et al. (2011), where firm-to-firm comparability is assessed by the similarity of firm-level earnings on return regressions.
For both measures, larger (less negative) values indicate more comparable financial accounting information.
n_p,ci,cj,k is the number of available firm pairs within industry k, with i from country ci and j from country cj; when ci=cj, the PDF explicitly requires i != j.

dependent_variable.name: D(CFCOMP)
dependent_variable.definition: Post-minus-pre change in CFCOMP, the cash-flow-based comparability measure. Equation (4) compares the fitted total-accrual-on-CFO functions for firm i and peer firm j at the same firm-i CFO_TA input, averages absolute prediction differences across available firm pairs, and multiplies the average by −1. When ci=cj, the source excludes the same-firm i=j pair. Higher, less negative values indicate greater comparability.
dependent_variable.formula: CFCOMP_post − CFCOMP_pre; CFCOMP_{p,ci,cj,k} = −Σ_{i,j}|(β_{p,i,0}+β_{p,i,1}CFO_TA_{p,i})−(β_{p,j,0}+β_{p,j,1}CFO_TA_{p,i})|/n_{p,ci,cj,k}

evidence.quote: Equation (4): CFCOMP_p,ci,cj,k = -sum_i,j abs(beta_p,i,0 + beta_p,i,1*CFO_TA_p,i - (beta_p,j,0 + beta_p,j,1*CFO_TA_p,i))/n_p,ci,cj,k.
n_p,ci,cj,k is the number of available firm pairs within industry k, with i from country ci and j from country cj; when ci=cj, the PDF explicitly requires i != j.
CFCOMP is a similar construct, where firm-to-firm comparability is assessed by the similarity of firm-level total accruals on cash flow regressions.
For both measures, larger (less negative) values indicate more comparable financial accounting information.

independent_variables.name: IFRS_EFFECT_{ci,cj}
independent_variables.definition: The IFRS-induced change in GAAP_PROX for the country pair. GAAP_PROX is the negative number of GAAP differences between the two countries divided by the maximum number of differences observed across all country pairs; same-country pairs have GAAP_PROX=0. IFRS_EFFECT can be positive or negative and is not a binary treatment indicator.

evidence.quote: We define GAAP_PROX as the negative number of differences divided by the maximum number of differences observed across all country pairs
IFRS_EFFECT captures the change in GAAP_PROX caused by the adoption of IFRS in the treatment countries.
To capture this relation, our main treatment variable is the change of GAAP_PROX between the 2004 and 2008 periods (IFRS_EFFECT).
If both countries are the same, GAAP_PROX takes the value of zero, i.e., the maximum value of GAAP proximity.

Since the adoption of IFRS has affected the GAAP of some treatment countries to become more dissimilar relative to some control countries, values of the IFRS_EFFECT can be negative as well as positive.

review_notes: Principal family: Model (6), Table 2 Panel B, the first-difference IFRS treatment test, with separate outcomes D(DKVCOMP), D(R_DKVCOMP), D(CFCOMP), and D(R_CFCOMP). The abstract and introduction identify the effect of mandatory IFRS adoption on accounting comparability as the central question; the pre-IFRS Model (5) is an identification check and the compliance, moderation, information-transfer, and private-firm analyses are follow-up questions.

Equations (1) and (2) are retained as supporting fits because their firm-period coefficients construct the two underlying comparability measures used in Model (6). The supplied verified transcription identifies these equations and the mathematical forms of Equations (3), (4), and (6); the extraction uses that supplied derivative without self-certifying its math.

The paper does not identify the underlying estimator for Model (6) or the two repeated firm-period measurement fits. The signed direction of the rank transformation is not printed, although the paper says higher values of its measures indicate more comparability. Table 2 reports robust standard errors clustered by country, peer-country, and industry, but does not establish whether these are joint or separate multi-way clusters.

Equation (3) labels its outcome DVKCOMP, while the adjacent prose and Table 2 label the measure DKVCOMP. The extraction follows the prose/table outcome name and preserves the notation discrepancy here. Equation (6) omits a separate ordinary-intercept symbol, while Table 2 reports an Intercept row; the table supports an included intercept.

independent_variables.name: DiscIR_t
independent_variables.definition: Monthly discretionary information-risk factor-mimicking return. Each month, firms are independently ranked into quintiles using their most recent DiscAQ; the factor is average monthly excess return for the top two quintiles minus that for the bottom two. Fiscal-year-t DiscAQ scores are used to form portfolios for the 12-month period beginning in fiscal year t+1. Returns are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles before portfolio formation. DiscAQ is the Eq. (6) residual, based on AQ from Eq. (5); AQ is the time-series standard deviation of Eq. (5) residuals over years t−4 through t.
independent_variables.formula: Winsorize underlying firm returns at the 1st and 99th percentiles before forming quintile portfolios; the factor is the top-two-quintile mean monthly excess return on firms ranked by the most recent metric minus the bottom-two-quintile mean monthly excess return.

evidence.quote: DiscIR and InnateIR are the discretionary and innate information risk factors calculated using the DiscAQ and InnateAQ metrics.
Firms are independently ranked each month into quintiles based on their most recent AQ, DiscAQ, and InnateAQ values.
The information risk factor mimicking returns for AQ, DiscAQ, and InnateAQ are each equal to the difference between the monthly excess returns of the top two quintiles and bottom two quintiles.
fiscal-t metrics are used in twelve-month portfolios starting fiscal t+1.
We winsorize returns at the 1st and 99th percentiles before we form portfolios in order to reduce the effect of outliers.
The residual, l^i,t, from Eq. 6 is the estimate of the discretionary component of firm i’s accrual quality in year t, DiscAQi,t = l^i,t.

independent_variables.name: DiscIR_t
independent_variables.definition: Monthly discretionary information-risk factor-mimicking return. Each month, firms are independently ranked into quintiles using their most recent DiscAQ; the factor is average monthly excess return for the top two quintiles minus that for the bottom two. Fiscal-year-t DiscAQ scores are used to form portfolios for the 12-month period beginning in fiscal year t+1. Returns are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles before portfolio formation. DiscAQ is the Eq. (6) residual, based on AQ from Eq. (5); AQ is the time-series standard deviation of Eq. (5) residuals over years t−4 through t.
independent_variables.formula: Winsorize underlying firm returns at the 1st and 99th percentiles before forming quintile portfolios; the factor is the top-two-quintile mean monthly excess return on firms ranked by the most recent metric minus the bottom-two-quintile mean monthly excess return.

evidence.quote: DiscIR and InnateIR are the discretionary and innate information risk factors calculated using the DiscAQ and InnateAQ metrics.
Firms are independently ranked each month into quintiles based on their most recent AQ, DiscAQ, and InnateAQ values.
The information risk factor mimicking returns for AQ, DiscAQ, and InnateAQ are each equal to the difference between the monthly excess returns of the top two quintiles and bottom two quintiles.
fiscal-t metrics are used in twelve-month portfolios starting fiscal t+1.
We winsorize returns at the 1st and 99th percentiles before we form portfolios in order to reduce the effect of outliers.
The residual, l^i,t, from Eq. 6 is the estimate of the discretionary component of firm i’s accrual quality in year t, DiscAQi,t = l^i,t.

research_interest_evidence.quote: We focus on the component of information risk related to managers’ discretionary accounting choices and test whether the pricing of the discretionary component of information risk (hereafter, discretionary information risk) increases after restatements.
We use two approaches to test whether the factor loading on the DiscIR factor increases after a restatement.
The results, presented in Table 3, show that the increase in the discretionary information risk factor loading is 0.95, significant at the 1% level.
